questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The nerve related to the area marked in the picture has its root value from?
options: Dorsal root ganglia of T1 and T2
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Ventral horn of C4

The above is an image of the left lung with the arrow pointing at the nerve passing anterior to the left hilum. The phrenic nerve passes in front of the left hilum and has its root value from the ventral horn of C4.

In the given image, the left lung is identified by the vertical sequence of structures at the left hilum - pulmonary artery, principal (hyparterial) bronchus, and inferior pulmonary vein. The image also shows an oblique fissure dividing the lung into superior and inferior lobes.

The phrenic nerve, originating from the cervical nerves C3–C5, is a mixed nerve that carries motor fibres to the diaphragm and sensory fibres from the mediastinal pleura, pericardium, and a portion of the peritoneum.

The course of the left phrenic nerve:

Cervical region - both phrenic nerves pass, Anterior to scalenus anterior muscle
Posterior to sternocleidomastoid and inferior belly of omohyoid
Posterior to internal jugular vein, transverse cervical artery, and suprascapular artery
Posterior to the thoracic duct on the left

Root of the neck - It lies medial to the trunks of the brachial plexus in the neck. At the root of the neck, it runs anterior to the second part of the subclavian artery and posterior to the subclavian vein.

Thorax - The phrenic nerve enters the thorax by crossing medially in front of the internal thoracic artery. Within the thorax, the phrenic nerve descends anterior to the pulmonary hilum between the fibrous pericardium and mediastinal pleura, accompanied by the pericardiacophrenic vessels.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Until when can a postpartum intrauterine contraceptive device (IUCD) be inserted?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 48 hours

Postpartum IUCD should be inserted within 48 hours.

An intrauterine contraceptive device (IUCD) prevents the implantation of a fertilized ovum. It does so by acting as a foreign body within the uterine cavity. This leads to increased contractility, tubal peristalsis, and promotes leukocytic infiltration in the endometrium so that the fertilized egg is unable to implant.

Pearl PF1657: Hormonal contraceptives

Oral pills:

* Combined oral contraceptive pills (COC)

* Mala D - Levonorgestrel 0.15 mg + Ethinyl estradiol  0.03 mg + Ferrous fumarate

* Mala N - Levonorgestrel 0.15 mg + Ethinyl estradiol  0.03 mg + Ferrous fumarate (Govt. supply, free of cost)

* Progesterone only pills (POP) - suitable for lactating women

* Norethisterone 350 μg

* Norgestrel 75 μg

* Levonorgestrel (LNG) 30 μg

* Once a month or long-acting pills - highly disappointing results

* Quinestrol (long-acting estrogen) + short-acting progesterone

* Gossypol - male pill : Cottonseed derivative and causes azoospermia and severe oligospermia

* Post-coital pills or interceptive

* Levonorgestrel 0.75 mg, 2 doses, 12 hours apart

* Mifepristone 10-600 mg

* Ulipristal 30 mg, within 5 days of intercourse

* Centchroman 60 mg, 2 tablets, within 24 hrs of intercourse

* GnRH agonists

* CuT IUCD, inserted within 5 days

Injectable contraceptives

* Progesterone only injectables

* DMPA 150 mg IM every 3 months

* NET-EN 200 mg IM every 2 months

* Combined injectables

* Cyclofem - DMPA 25 mg + Estradiol cypionate 5 mg

* Mesigyna - NET-EN 50 mg  + Estradiol valerate 5 mg

Subdermal implants

* Norplant I - Levonorgestrel 35 mg

* Norplant II or Jadelle - 2 rods with levonorgestrel 70 mg in each and released at a rate of 50 μg/day

Others

* Hormonal IUCD - Mirena which contains LNG 52 mg with release rate of 20 μg/day

* Orthoevra patch - Norelgestomin + Ethinyl estradiol weekly for 3 weeks, then patch free for 1 week

* Vaginal ring or Nuvaring - Etonogestrel + ethinyl estradiol daily release, use for 3 weeks with withdrawal for 1 week

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: The most common cause of bladder outlet obstruction in a male child is
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Posterior urethral valve

The most common cause of bladder outflow obstruction in a male child is the posterior urethral valve (PUV).

A PUV is a membranous fold in the posterior urethra which results from the persistence of the urogenital membrane. It is typically located just distal to the verumontanum and is the primary cause of bladder outlet obstruction in newborn males.

Diagnosis is most commonly made antenatally with ultrasound which demonstrates bilateral hydronephrosis, a distended bladder, and a dilated posterior urethra which appears as the keyhole sign on imaging. In severe cases, there is oligohydramnios and pulmonary hypoplasia during the antenatal period.

If the diagnosis is not made antenatally, then babies typically present with urinary tract infections in the neonatal period or with uraemia and renal failure. Clinically, a poor urinary stream, dribbling of urine, and palpable bladder (due to diverticula) can be present.

The investigation of choice is micturating cystourethrography.

The diagnosis is best made during the micturition phase of micturating cystourethrography in lateral or oblique views so that the posterior urethra can be imaged adequately. The following findings are seen:

• Dilatation and elongation of the posterior urethra - equivalent of the ultrasonographic keyhole sign
• Linear radiolucent band corresponding to the valve - seen occasionally
• Vesicoureteral reflux - seen in 50% of patients
• Bladder trabeculation/diverticula

Treatment is initially supportive by inserting a urinary catheter to relieve symptoms of obstruction. Definitive treatment is by urethroscopic destruction of the valves with continuing lifelong supportive treatment of the dilated urinary tract, recurrent urinary infections and uremia.

Other options:

Options B and C- Urethral atresia and anterior urethral valve are rare congenital anomalies that can also lead to urinary obstruction.

Option D- Ureterocele is the cystic enlargement of the intramural ureter. It is common in females. They can present with features of urinary tract infection, bladder obstruction, or ureteral stones. Excretion urography will show cobra head appearance.

The image shown below depicts the "cobra head" sign in a patient with bilateral ureterocele.
questions.learning: Posterior urethral valve — The most common cause of bladder outflow obstruction in a male child is the posterior urethral valve (PUV). A PUV is a membranous fold in the posterior urethra which results from the persistence of the urogenital membrane.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: In which disease among the following, Chloride level in sweat is evaluated?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Cystic fibrosis

Sweat chloride test is the gold standard diagnostic test for cystic fibrosis, reflecting defective chloride transport due to CFTR mutation.

• CFTR dysfunction → impaired chloride reabsorption in sweat glands → increased chloride concentration in sweat
• Sweat chloride level >60 mmol/L is diagnostic (in appropriate clinical setting)

Clinical relevance:

• Used in children with recurrent respiratory infections, failure to thrive, or steatorrhea
• Helps confirm diagnosis early and guide management

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Identify the labelled structure in the image?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Midbrain

The labeled structure is the midbrain.

The midbrain develops from the midbrain vesicle, the cavity of which becomes much reduced to form the cerebral aqueduct or aqueduct of Sylvius.

The midbrain:

* Is of small size and is completely surrounded by cerebrospinal fluid in the subarachnoid space

* Has a cavity called the cerebral aqueduct, which opens above into the third ventricle

* Is located in the posterior cranial fossa

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A woman presents with amenorrhea, headaches, visual disturbances, and milky discharge from the nipples. What is the most appropriate initial investigation to perform?
questions.explanation: The combination of amenorrhea (absent periods) and galactorrhea (milky nipple discharge) is known as the amenorrhea-galactorrhea syndrome. This is most commonly caused by hyperprolactinemia. The presence of headaches and blurred vision (classically bitemporal hemianopia) strongly suggests a prolactin-secreting pituitary adenoma (prolactinoma) that is large enough to compress the optic chiasm. The most appropriate initial test to confirm the diagnosis is measuring the serum prolactin level (Option A). hCG (Option D) should be checked to rule out pregnancy in any woman with amenorrhea, but it would not explain the milky discharge and visual symptoms. LH (Option B) and FSH (Option C) are used to evaluate hypothalamic or ovarian failure but are not the primary diagnostic tests for galactorrhea. If prolactin levels are significantly elevated, an MRI of the sella turcica is then indicated. Thus, prolactin is the prioritized biochemical test
questions.learning: The combination of amenorrhea (absent periods) and galactorrhea (milky nipple discharge) is known as the amenorrhea-galactorrhea syndrome. This is most commonly caused by hyperprolactinemia.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which mutation is linked to the Philadelphia chromosome?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Reciprocal translocation

The mutation associated with the Philadelphia chromosome is a result of reciprocal translocation.

Fusion of BCR-ABL is created by a reciprocal (9;22)translocation (Philadelphia chromosome. This is detected by cytogenetics, fluorescent in situ hybridization (FISH), or polymerase chain reaction (PCR) and occurs in Chronic myelogenous leukaemia (CML). To form the abnormal chromosome, part of the BCR (breakpoint cluster region) gene of chromosome 22 fuses with part of the ABL gene (encodes a tyrosine kinase) of chromosome 9, directing the synthesis of a chimeric protein that has unregulated tyrosine kinase activity and drives cell proliferation.

The peak incidence of CML is in the fifth to sixth decade.

* Clinical features:

* Anemia weight loss, and anorexia.

* Splenomegaly

* Peripheral blood:

* Leukocytosis, exceeding 100,000 cells/mm3, which consists predominantly of neutrophils, band forms, metamyelocytes, myelocytes, eosinophils, and basophils.

* Blasts usually make up less than 5% of circulating cells.

* Bone Marrow:

* Markedly Hypercellular with maturing granulocytic precursors, with an elevated proportion of eosinophils and basophils.

* Low LAP score

Image – Interphase FISH showing (9;22) translocation.
questions.learning: Reciprocal translocation — The mutation associated with the Philadelphia chromosome is a result of reciprocal translocation. Fusion of BCR-ABL is created by a reciprocal (9;22)translocation (Philadelphia chromosome.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 45-year-old man presents to the emergency department with intense abdominal pain radiating to the back. Laboratory tests show markedly elevated serum amylase and lipase levels. In the management of this condition, which of the following interventions should be avoided?
options: Nil per oral to avoid pancreatic stimulation
Parenteral nutrition is preferred for 2-3 days over the nil per oral (NPO) approach
questions.explanation: The patient is suffering from acute pancreatitis, indicated by severe abdominal pain radiating to the back and elevated serum amylase and lipase levels. The mainstay of management in acute pancreatitis is aggressive fluid resuscitation, pain control, and supportive care. The preferred fluids for resuscitation are isotonic crystalloids, especially Ringer lactate or normal saline, as they effectively restore intravascular volume and correct fluid losses due to third spacing. In contrast, 5% dextrose should be avoided because it is not an effective volume expander and does not adequately replenish electrolytes or circulating volume. Nil per oral (NPO) is appropriate initially to rest the pancreas. Early enteral feeding is now recommended once the patient stabilizes, as it reduces complications. Although parenteral nutrition is not preferred routinely, it may be used when enteral feeding is not feasible. Thus, among the given options, administration of 5% dextrose is inappropriate in the management of acute pancreatitis
questions.learning: The patient is suffering from acute pancreatitis, indicated by severe abdominal pain radiating to the back and elevated serum amylase and lipase levels.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: The most common site of obstruction by a nasal polyp from the maxillary sinus is?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Middle meatus

The maxillary sinus opens into the middle meatus at the lower part of the infundibulum, in its medial wall and thus a nasal polyp will obstruct the middle meatus.

Infundibulum is the space limited medially by the uncinate process and frontal process of the maxilla, and laterally by the lamina papyracea.

Pearl PF1078: Structures opening into meatuses of nose

* Inferior meatus: Nasolacrimal duct, guarded by the valve of Hasner

* Middle meatus: Frontal sinus, maxillary sinus, anterior ethmoidal sinus. All these together form the osteo-meatal complex or Picadle’s circle.

* Superior meatus: Posterior ethmoidal sinus

* Sphenoethmoidal recess: Sphenoid sinus
questions.learning: Middle meatus — The maxillary sinus opens into the middle meatus at the lower part of the infundibulum, in its medial wall and thus a nasal polyp will obstruct the middle meatus.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text:
A patient comes to ED with fever and headache. On examination he has neck stiffness. CSF analysis was done and it shows the following findings. Most likely diagnosis is:

Opening pressure – Increased

Proteins- Mildly increased

Glucose – Normal

Lymphocytes – Increased.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Coxsackie

The given symptoms cluster of fever, vomiting, and neck stiffness is suggestive of meningitis. A CSF analysis showing increased opening pressure, lymphocytic pleocytosis, mildly increased protein, and normal glucose is suggestive of viral meningitis. Among the given options, Coxsackie (Option D) is the only viral cause of meningitis.

Other options:

Option A: Tuberculous meningitis shows lymphocytic pleocytosis with low glucose.

Option B: Bacterial meningitis shows neutrophilic pleocytosis with low glucose.

Option C: Fungal meningitis shows lymphocytic/neutrophilic pleocytosis with low glucose.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: The image shows changes in membrane potential during an action potential. The region marked between 4 to 5 is due to ________.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Efflux of K+

The region marked between 4 and 5 in the action potential curve indicates repolarization due to the efflux of K+ ions across the cell membrane.

The sequence of events during the action potential occurs in the following sequence.

1. Resting state: Both channels are closed.

2. Na+ channels open in response to depolarizing stimulus. Sodium enters the cell. The membrane reaches threshold potential.

3. The sodium influx causes the opening of more Na+ channels through a positive feedback mechanism. Rapid depolarization occurs.

4. Sodium conductance decreases.

5. Na+ channels close and K+ channels open. Due to K+ efflux, repolarization occurs.

6. Na+ channels are reset and are ready to respond to another depolarizing stimulus (relative refractory period). During this phase, the K+ channels remain open and slowly return to the closed state causing after-hyperpolarization.

7. Both channels are closed. The membrane returns to RMP.
questions.learning: Efflux of K+ — The region marked between 4 and 5 in the action potential curve indicates repolarization due to the efflux of K+ ions across the cell membrane.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Heart of sewage disposal plant:
questions.explanation: The aeration tank is called the “heart of a sewage disposal plant” because it is the main site of biological treatment. Here, activated sludge (microorganisms) breaks down organic matter in sewage using oxygen supplied by aeration. This process significantly reduces biochemical oxygen demand (BOD) and removes most of the pollutants. Why other options are incorrect: (A) Primary sedimentation tank:Removes suspended solids by settling, but no major biological treatment occurs. (C) Secondary sedimentation tank:Used for settling of activated sludge after aeration, not the main treatment step. (D) Sludge digestion tank:Handles sludge stabilization (anaerobic digestion), not primary sewage purification. Since the maximum purification occurs in the aeration tank, it is considered the heart of the sewage treatment plant
questions.learning: The aeration tank is called the “heart of a sewage disposal plant” because it is the main site of biological treatment. Here, activated sludge (microorganisms) breaks down organic matter in sewage using oxygen supplied by aeration.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: During epidural anesthesia, which of the following layers is least likely to be punctured?
questions.explanation: In epidural anesthesia, the goal is to place the local anesthetic into the potential space just outside the dural sac. Therefore, the Arachnoid mater is the layer least likely to be punctured; if the arachnoid is breached, the procedure becomes a spinal (subarachnoid) block rather than an epidural. During a standard midline approach, the needle passes through the skin, subcutaneous tissue, Supraspinatus ligament (Option C), interspinatus ligament, and finally the Ligamentum flavum (Option B) to reach the epidural space. The Infraspinatus (Option D) is a muscle of the rotator cuff in the shoulder and is entirely irrelevant to spinal or epidural anatomy. Successful epidural placement relies on the "loss of resistance" technique as the needle exits the dense ligamentum flavum. Accidental puncture of the dura/arachnoid is a recognized complication known as a "dural tap," which can lead to a significant post-dural puncture headache. Knowledge of these spinal layers is critical for safe regional anesthesia

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following is not true about P-glycoprotein?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Also known as MDR2

P-glycoprotein is also known as multidrug resistance protein 1 or MDR1 (not MDR2).  It is also denoted by cluster of differentiation 243 (CD243).

P-glycoprotein (P-gp) is one of the first members of the ATP-binding cassette (ABC) transporter, which acts as an efflux membrane transporter. It is responsible for limiting cellular uptake and the distribution of xenobiotics and toxic substances. It is associated with multidrug resistance (MDR).

• Increased P-gp expression: Reduces the absorption of drugs that are substrates for P-gp
• Decreased P-gp expression: Leads to supratherapeutic plasma concentrations and drug toxicity
questions.learning: Also known as MDR2 P-glycoprotein is also known as multidrug resistance protein 1 or MDR1 (not MDR2). It is also denoted by cluster of differentiation 243 (CD243).

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which chemotherapeutic drug is most likely to cause extrapyramidal symptoms such as acute dystonia, bradykinesia, and tremors in a patient receiving chemotherapy?
questions.explanation: Metoclopramide is a commonly used anti-emetic, particularly in patients undergoing chemotherapy. It acts primarily as a dopamine D₂-receptor antagonist. Because it readily crosses the blood–brain barrier, metoclopramide blocks dopamine receptors in the basal ganglia, which can lead to extrapyramidal side effects (EPS). These include acute dystonia, parkinsonism (bradykinesia, rigidity, tremors), and akathisia, and they occur more frequently in children and young adults. Ondansetron (Option A) is a 5-HT₃ (serotonin) receptor antagonist and does not interfere with dopaminergic pathways; therefore, it does not cause EPS. Meclizine (Option C) and scopolamine (Option D) are antihistaminic and anticholinergic agents, respectively, used mainly for motion sickness and vestibular disorders, and they are not associated with dystonic reactions. Acute dystonic reactions due to metoclopramide can be rapidly reversed with anticholinergic agents such as diphenhydramine or benztropine. With prolonged or high-dose use, metoclopramide carries a risk of tardive dyskinesia, which may be irreversible, hence the drug carries a black-box warning
questions.learning: Metoclopramide is a commonly used anti-emetic, particularly in patients undergoing chemotherapy. It acts primarily as a dopamine D₂-receptor antagonist.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Cough on scratching the external acoustic canal is due to?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Auricular branch of vagus

Cough on scratching the external acoustic canal is due to the auricular branch of the vagus nerve (Arnold's nerve).

Arnold's nerve supplies the concha and corresponding eminence on the medial surface. It also supplies the posterior wall and floor of the external auditory canal. Scratching or mechanical stimulation of the ear leads to activation of Arnold's nerve, which evokes reflex cough (ear-cough reflex/otorespiratory reflex).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Consider the following statements regarding inflammatory bowel disease: 1. Ulcerative colitis (UC) involves terminal ileum and rarely causes proctitis. 2. Cobblestone appearance of bowel is seen in Crohn’s disease. 3. Skip lesions are a characteristic of ulcerative colitis but never seen in Crohn’s disease. 4. Ulcerative colitis is more common in smokers than non-smokers. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 2 only

Crohn disease is characterized by transmural inflammation, skip lesions, and a cobblestone appearance, and can involve any part of the gastrointestinal tract from mouth to anus. Ulcerative colitis (UC) causes continuous mucosal inflammation, beginning in the rectum (proctitis) and extending proximally.

• 2. Cobblestone appearance of bowel is seen in Crohn’s disease ✔️: Cobblestone appearance is a classic feature of Crohn disease.

Why are the other statements incorrect?

• 1. Ulcerative colitis (UC) involves terminal ileum and rarely causes proctitis ❌: UC always involves the rectum and rarely involves the terminal ileum (except backwash ileitis in extensive disease).
• 3. Ulcerative colitis is more common in smokers than non-smokers ❌: Skip lesions are characteristic of Crohn disease, not UC.
• 4. Ulcerative colitis is more common in smokers than non-smokers ❌: Smoking increases the risk of Crohn disease, whereas it is protective against UC.
questions.learning: 2 only Crohn disease is characterized by transmural inflammation, skip lesions, and a cobblestone appearance, and can involve any part of the gastrointestinal tract from mouth to anus.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Identify the structure marked in the given image.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Cystic artery

In the given image the marked structure is the cystic artery.

The image below mentions the boundaries of Calot's triangle and cystic artery.

Calot's triangle is an important surgical landmark as the cystic artery usually can be found within its boundaries. The cystic artery should be identified while performing a cholecystectomy to avoid damage to the extrahepatic biliary system.

The boundaries of Calot’s triangle are: 3C's

* Medially – Common hepatic duct.

* Inferiorly – Cystic duct.

* Superior – Cystic artery.

The cystic artery is the main source of blood supply to the biliary system. After originating from the right hepatic artery, it passes posterior to the common hepatic duct and superior to the cystic duct at the hepatobiliary triangle. On reaching the superior aspect of the neck of the gallbladder, it divides into a superficial branch and a deep branch.

The image given below shows the cystic artery arising from the right hepatic artery within the Calot’s triangle.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which anatomical structure is located approximately 25 cm from the central incisor?
questions.explanation: According to many clinical/endoscopic sources (as in your key), the cricopharynx (upper esophageal sphincter) is located approximately 25 cm from the central incisors. It marks the junction of the pharynx and esophagus and acts as a functional sphincter preventing air entry during respiration and reflux during swallowing. It is also a key site evaluated in conditions like dysphagia and Zenker’s diverticulum. Why other options are incorrect: (B) Arch of Aorta: This produces a physiological constriction slightly lower, around 30 cm, not at 25 cm in this reference system. (C) Left principal bronchus: It crosses the esophagus at about 35 cm, causing another constriction, but is located further down. (D) Diaphragm: The esophageal hiatus is found at 40–45 cm, representing the lowest constriction near the gastroesophageal junction

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following muscles is not involved in the formation of the perineal body?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Internal anal sphincter muscle

The perineal body (central tendon of the perineum) is a fibromuscular node located between the urogenital triangle and anal triangle, anterior to the anus. It serves as an important point of attachment for several perineal muscles that support the pelvic floor and maintain pelvic organ stability.

Muscles attached to the perineal body include:

• Bulbospongiosus muscle
• Superficial transverse perineal muscle
• Deep transverse perineal muscle
• External anal sphincter
• Fibers of levator ani (especially pubococcygeus)

The internal anal sphincter is not attached to the perineal body because it is a smooth muscle continuation of the circular layer of the rectum and functions involuntarily.
questions.learning: Internal anal sphincter muscle — The perineal body (central tendon of the perineum) is a fibromuscular node located between the urogenital triangle and anal triangle, anterior to the anus.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: During the anthropometric evaluation, the height for age of a child is < - 2SD. This is most likely due to?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Chronic malnutrition

Low height for the age (height for age < -2SD) in children indicates chronic malnutrition and stunting.

Classification of nutritional status depending on the anthropometry (height/length for age):

Classification
Criteria

Moderately stunted (or) moderate chronic malnutrition

Height/length-for-age

< (–2 SD) and > (–3 SD)

Severely stunted (or) severe chronic malnutrition

Height/length-for-age

< (–3 SD)

Nutritional status is often assessed in terms of anthropometry:

• Low weight for height, or wasting, indicates acute malnutrition.
• High weight-for-height indicates overweight.
• Low height-for-age, or stunting, indicates chronic malnutrition. This is the best indicator of long-term nutritional status in the pediatric population.
• Low weight-for-age indicates acute or chronic malnutrition. It does not differentiate between wasting and stunting. Hence, it has limited clinical significance.

Mid-upper arm circumference (MUAC) is an age-independent parameter used for the screening of wasting in children. In children aged 6 months to 5 years, MUAC <11.5cm is classified as severe malnutrition.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A patient presents with respiratory depression suspected due to opioid overdose. What should be the next step in management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Naloxone

A patient with respiratory depression due to suspected opioid overdose requires immediate reversal of opioid effects.

Naloxone is the drug of choice because it is a pure opioid antagonist that rapidly reverses the effects of opioids at µ-opioid receptors, restoring respiratory drive and consciousness.

Key points about Naloxone:

• Given IV, IM, SC, or intranasal
• Rapid onset of action
• Used specifically for acute opioid overdose
• May require repeat dosing because its duration is shorter than many opioids

Why other options are incorrect:

• Naltrexone: Long-acting opioid antagonist used for maintenance therapy in opioid or alcohol dependence, not acute overdose.
• Buprenorphine: Partial opioid agonist used for opioid dependence treatment, not overdose reversal.
• Methadone: Long-acting opioid agonist used for maintenance therapy in opioid dependence.

Therefore, the immediate management is Naloxone.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Insect in ear can be killed by:
questions.explanation: When a live insect enters the external auditory canal, it can cause severe pain and distress due to its movements against the tympanic membrane. The immediate management priority is to kill or immobilize the insect before attempting removal. Instilling a few drops of oil (such as olive oil, mineral oil, or even baby oil) is the safest and most effective method. The oil suffocates the insect quickly by blocking its respiratory spiracles. Once dead, it can be easily removed by irrigation or forceps. Hydrogen peroxide (Option B) can cause bubbling and irritation that may provoke the insect to sting or bite. Water (Option C) may cause some insects to swell, making removal more difficult. Petrol (Option D) is highly toxic and corrosive to the delicate skin of the ear canal and should never be used. Therefore, oil is the standard clinical recommendation for safely killing an insect in the ear
questions.learning: When a live insect enters the external auditory canal, it can cause severe pain and distress due to its movements against the tympanic membrane. The immediate management priority is to kill or immobilize the insect before attempting removal.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: The patient complains of repeated episodes of crusting in the nose with occasional bleeding. She had undergone surgery for nasal obstruction four months back. On examination, the following finding is seen. Which surgery has the highest likelihood to result in this complication?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Submucosal resection

The given clinical vignette of a patient with complaints of repeated episodes of crusting in the nose with occasional bleeding and a history of nasal surgery for nasal obstruction is likely to have undergone correction of her DNS(Deviated Nasal Septum). The image is that of septal perforation; SMR (Submucosal resection ) has a higher likelihood of causing the same.

Septal perforation can occur after nasal surgery. Features depend on the size of the perforation. Smaller perforations can present with whistling while the larger perforations will present with epistaxis and crust formation. Therefore, septoplasty has become a more favored treatment of DNS than SMR due to its conservative approach.

Septoplasty is a conservative technique in the surgical correction of septal deformity. The key advantage is that it can be carried out as a daycare procedure, most of the bone and cartilage are retained, and complications are less. The deformed septum may corrected by various techniques like scoring the concave side, shaving, and wedge excision. Sometimes realignment by joining straight pieces of the septum outside the nose and replacing them can be done which is called extra-corporeal septoplasty.

The indications for an SMR are:

• DNS causing symptoms of nasal obstruction and recurrent headaches.
• DNS causing obstruction of paranasal sinuses and middle ear, resulting in recurrent sinusitis and otitis media.
• Recurrent epistaxis from a septal spur.
• As a part of septorhinoplasty, for cosmetic correction of external nasal deformities.
• As a preliminary step in hypophysectomy or vidian neurectomy.

It is contraindicated in children below 17 years of age, during acute respiratory infection, bleeding diathesis, untreated diabetes, or hypertension.

In this procedure, mucoperichondrial and mucoperiosteal flaps are raised on both sides of the septum. Bony and cartilaginous parts of the septum are excised. This is followed by extensive dissection of the septum removing all deformed bony and cartilaginous parts of the septum and preserving only a caudal and a dorsal strut of cartilage.

There is a greater chance of complications associated with SMR that include bleeding, septal hematoma, septal abscess, perforation, depression of the nasal bridge, retraction of the columella, and persistence of the deviation. The flapping of the nasal septum and toxic shock syndrome following SMR can also occur.

Conservative procedure

Can be done for adults and persons < 18 yrs if bilateral and severe

Other options:

Option A: FESS (Functional Endoscopic Sinus Surgery) is a minimally invasive procedure to enlarge nasal drainage pathways and improve sinus ventilation; rarely causes septal perforation.

Option C: Denker Approach is a surgical technique to access the maxillary sinus, pterygopalatine, and infratemporal fossae, used for large sinonasal tumors and extensive sinus pathology.

Option D: Endoscopic Surgical Treatment of Odontogenic Maxillary Sinusitis involves middle or inferior meatotomy; inferior meatotomy is preferred for foreign bodies or sinus floor cysts.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 28-year-old woman in her third trimester presents to the emergency department after a fainting episode while lying down. She reports improvement after sitting up. What is the most likely cause of her symptoms?
questions.explanation: This patient is experiencing Supine Hypotensive Syndrome, a common occurrence in late pregnancy. When a pregnant woman lies flat on her back, the heavy gravid uterus can compress the Inferior Vena Cava (IVC). This obstruction reduces venous return to the heart, leading to a sudden drop in cardiac output and systemic blood pressure, which causes the fainting episode (syncope). The symptoms are immediately relieved by sitting up or turning onto the left lateral side, which shifts the uterus off the IVC. SVC compression (Option B) affects the upper body and is not related to uterine weight. While the patient has hypotension (Option C), "IVC compression" is the specific anatomical explanation for the symptom in this clinical context. Motion sickness (Option D) involves nausea and vertigo related to movement, not position-dependent syncope. Pregnant women should be counseled to avoid sleeping in the supine position and to always use a wedge or pillow to maintain a lateral tilt to ensure optimal placental and maternal circulation
questions.learning: This patient is experiencing Supine Hypotensive Syndrome, a common occurrence in late pregnancy. When a pregnant woman lies flat on her back, the heavy gravid uterus can compress the Inferior Vena Cava (IVC).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following is the most commonly affected nerve after parotid surgery?
questions.explanation: The facial nerve (cranial nerve VII) is the most commonly affected nerve during parotid surgery. This is because it passes directly through the parotid gland, dividing it into superficial and deep lobes. Within the gland, it forms a complex branching pattern (temporal, zygomatic, buccal, marginal mandibular, cervical branches), making it highly vulnerable during surgical dissection. Even with careful identification and preservation, temporary or permanent facial weakness/paralysis may occur, affecting facial expressions. Hence, it is the most clinically significant and most commonly injured nerve in parotidectomy. Why other options are incorrect: (B) Auriculotemporal nerve: It lies near the gland and may be involved in Frey’s syndrome (gustatory sweating), but it is less commonly injured than the facial nerve. (C) Glossopharyngeal nerve: Located deeper and away from the parotid gland, so it is rarely affected. (D) Greater auricular nerve: It may be sacrificed during surgery causing sensory loss over the ear, but it is less commonly affected compared to the facial nerve, which is the primary nerve at risk
questions.learning: The facial nerve (cranial nerve VII) is the most commonly affected nerve during parotid surgery. This is because it passes directly through the parotid gland, dividing it into superficial and deep lobes.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which of the subsequent conditions is Bone Anchored Hearing Aid (BAHA) implemented?
questions.explanation: A Bone Anchored Hearing Aid (BAHA) is a specialized device that bypasses the external and middle ear by transmitting sound vibrations directly through the skull bone to the functioning inner ear (cochlea). It is primarily indicated for patients with significant conductive or mixed hearing loss where conventional hearing aids cannot be worn. Congenital external auditory atresia (Option C), where the ear canal is absent or closed, is a classic indication for BAHA because a traditional aid cannot be inserted. Standard sensorineural hearing loss (Option A) is typically managed with conventional aids or cochlear implants. Acoustic neuroma (Option B) usually requires surgery or radiosurgery. Otitis media (Option D) is generally managed medically or with ventilation tubes. While chronic otitis media with persistent discharge might eventually necessitate a BAHA, the structural anatomical absence of the canal makes it the most definitive implemented condition
questions.learning: A Bone Anchored Hearing Aid (BAHA) is a specialized device that bypasses the external and middle ear by transmitting sound vibrations directly through the skull bone to the functioning inner ear (cochlea).

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A 24-year-old pregnant woman is receiving lithium therapy for bipolar disorder. Discontinuation of lithium during pregnancy is advised to prevent the risk of which fetal congenital abnormality?
questions.explanation: Lithium is a highly effective mood stabilizer for bipolar disorder, but it is a known teratogen when taken during pregnancy, especially during the first trimester. The specific congenital heart defect associated with maternal lithium use is "Ebstein anomaly" (Option A). This condition involves the downward displacement of the tricuspid valve leaflets into the right ventricle, leading to "atrialization" of the ventricle and severe tricuspid regurgitation. VACTERL defects (Option B) are a cluster of anomalies (Vertebral, Anal, Cardiac, etc.) with multifactorial origins. Coarctation of the aorta (Option C) and supravalvular aortic stenosis (Option D, classic for Williams syndrome) are not specifically linked to lithium exposure. While the absolute risk of Ebstein anomaly from lithium is lower than previously thought, it is significantly higher than the baseline population risk. Pregnant women on lithium require a detailed fetal echocardiogram between 18–22 weeks to screen for cardiac malformations and a careful risk-benefit discussion regarding medication management during gestation. **************
questions.learning: Lithium is a highly effective mood stabilizer for bipolar disorder, but it is a known teratogen when taken during pregnancy, especially during the first trimester.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 17-year-old boy falls on an outstretched hand and now has pain and swelling at the base of the thumb. Which bone is most likely fractured?
questions.explanation: The scaphoid is the most commonly fractured carpal bone. The classic mechanism of injury is a fall on an outstretched hand with the wrist in extension. Clinical signs include pain and tenderness in the anatomical snuffbox, swelling at the base of the thumb, and pain with axial loading of the thumb. Lunate fractures (Option A) are less common and often associated with dislocations or Kienbock's disease. Pisiform (Option C) and trapezoid (Option D) fractures are rare carpal injuries that typically result from direct trauma rather than an indirect fall. Scaphoid fractures are notorious for their poor blood supply, specifically the retrograde flow to the proximal pole, which increases the risk of avascular necrosis and non-union if not properly managed. Initial X-rays may be negative, so a high index of clinical suspicion and follow-up imaging (MRI or repeat X-rays in 10–14 days) are often required
questions.learning: The scaphoid is the most commonly fractured carpal bone. The classic mechanism of injury is a fall on an outstretched hand with the wrist in extension.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: In a patient on mechanical ventilation and placed in prone position which of the following about PEEP is true?
options: Prevents atelectasis of lung and alveolar collapse
Increases venous return and thus maintains cardiac output
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Prevents atelectasis of lung and alveolar collapse

PEEP helps keep alveoli open and prevents atelectasis, especially beneficial in prone-positioned ventilated patients. It improves oxygenation by maintaining functional residual capacity, while the other options are incorrect: PEEP does not reduce CO₂, does not lower inspiratory pressures, and typically reduces venous return.
questions.learning: Prevents atelectasis of lung and alveolar collapse PEEP helps keep alveoli open and prevents atelectasis, especially beneficial in prone-positioned ventilated patients.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is the most common type of Guillian-Barre syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Acute inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy

Acute inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy (AIDP) is the most common type of GBS.

There are several types of Guillain–Barre syndrome, which are recognized by electrodiagnostic studies and pathological distinctions. These include:

A. Demyelinating

• Acute inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy (AIDP) - most common

B. Axonal

• Acute motor axonal neuropathy (AMAN)
• Acute motor–sensory axonal neuropathy (AMSAN)

C. Regional GBS syndromes

• Miller–Fisher syndrome (MFS)
• Pure sensory forms
• Ophthalmoplegia with anti-GQ1b antibodies as part of severe motor-sensory GBS
• GBS with severe bulbar and facial paralysis
• Acute pandysautonomia

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text:
Which of the following sodium transporters are present maximally in the early part of the PCT?

1. Na-K-ATPase
2. Na-glucose cotransporter
3. Na-H antiporter
4. Na-HCO3 symporter
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1, 2, 3

The sodium transporters present in the early part of PCT are Na-K-ATPase, Na+-glucose cotransporter (SGLT) and Na+-H+ antiporter.

Reabsorption of sodium in different parts of the nephron are:

• Proximal convoluted tubule (PCT):

• Nearly 60% of the filtered sodium is reabsorbed in the PCT. Solutes mainly absorbed in the proximal tubule are sodium, chloride, bicarbonate, phosphate, lactate, glucose, amino acids etc.
• Na+ is actively pumped from these cells into the interstitial space by Na-K ATPase in the basolateral membrane after travelling by cotransport or exchange via the tubular lumen into the tubular epithelial cells along its concentration and electrical gradients. It extrudes three Na+ in exchange for two K+ that are pumped into the cell.
• In early PCT, the main sodium channels used for reabsorption are Na+-glucose cotransporter (SGLT), Na+-H+ antiporter, Na+-amino acid cotransporter, Na+-phosphate cotransporter, etc.
• In distal PCT, due to high chloride concentration in the lumen, it favours NaCl reabsorption, driven by Cl− gradient.
• The total solute and water reabsorption are proportional to each other. Thus, the entire proximal tubule also reabsorbs nearly 60% of the filtered water (isosmotic reabsorption).

• Loop of Henle:

• The thin descending limb has no active transport of Na+ outside the lumen but the loop is permeable to water, making the tubular fluid hypertonic.
• A thick ascending limb reabsorbs nearly 30% of the Na+ by Na–2Cl–K cotransporter, an example of secondary active transport. This loop is impermeable to water. Since some of the solutes are reabsorbed and water is not reabsorbed, it dilutes the tubular fluid.

• Distal convoluted tubule: Approximately 7% of the filtered load of sodium chloride is reabsorbed in the early distal tubule. This occurs due to the presence of sodium chloride co-transporter. Even this segment dilutes the tubular fluid as it is impermeable to water.
• Cortical collecting tubule: The remaining 3% of the filtered Na+ is absorbed via ENaCs (epithelial sodium channels) in this duct.  This portion is regulated by aldosterone to maintain homeostasis in Na+ balance.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: What should be the minimum interval between the administration of two live vaccines?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 4 weeks

The minimum interval between the administration of two live vaccines is 4 weeks.

This is because decreasing the interval between two doses may interfere with the antibody response and protection. Thus, live vaccines can either be given on the same day according to the schedule or 4 weeks apart.

Note: In Park 27th ed. the minimum interval between two live vaccines is given as 3 weeks. However, several other standard sources including CDC and UNDP suggested an interval of 4 weeks. When both are given in options, it is recommended to mark 4 weeks as the correct answer.
questions.learning: 4 weeks The minimum interval between the administration of two live vaccines is 4 weeks. This is because decreasing the interval between two doses may interfere with the antibody response and protection.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which hormone is responsible for the development of the structure labeled as 1 in the given image?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Estrogen

The structure labeled as 1 in the given image is the lactiferous duct, which develops under the influence of estrogen.

Estrogen stimulates the hypertrophy and proliferation of the ductal system and the stroma. It also causes hypertrophy of the uterus during pregnancy and relaxes the pelvic ligaments and pubic symphysis to aid in parturition.

Progesterone (Option D) leads to lobular growth and alveolar budding and causes the alveolar cells to become secretory. It also inhibits uterine contractions and is thus responsible for maintaining pregnancy. It stimulates fallopian tube secretions, which provide nutrition to the developing morula and blastocyst.

Prolactin (Option C) a hormone from the anterior pituitary, stimulates the secretion of milk from the alveolar cells. Suckling stimulates this secretion. Prolactin levels are high in pregnancy. However, there is limited milk production prior to delivery because estrogen and progesterone inhibit this process. Thus, after delivery, as their levels fall, the lactogenic action of prolactin takes over.

Milk is secreted continuously into the alveoli but is only ejected into the ducts during suckling. When the baby suckles, oxytocin is released from the posterior pituitary. It leads to milk ejection due to the contraction of the myoepithelial cells that surround the alveoli. This process is known as the milk letdown reflex.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of the following is/are true about optic neuritis? I. Proportionate loss of colour vision and contrast to visual acuity II. 70% cases of multiple sclerosis are affected III. Treatment is done by oral steroids IV. Optic neuritis presents with normal fundus or disc edema
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Only IV

I. Proportionate loss of colour vision and contrast to visual acuity : FALSE

• In optic neuritis, colour vision loss is disproportionately severe compared to visual acuity
• Especially red desaturation

II. 70% cases of multiple sclerosis are affected :FALSE

• Optic neuritis is common in MS, but:

• \~20-25% present with optic neuritis as first manifestation
• \~50% of MS patients develop optic neuritis during lifetime

III. Treatment is done by oral steroids :FALSE

• Based on Optic Neuritis Treatment Trial (ONTT):

• IV methylprednisolone → speeds recovery
• Oral steroids alone are contraindicated (↑ recurrence risk)

IV. Optic neuritis presents with normal fundus or disc edema : TRUE

• Two forms:

• Retrobulbar neuritis → fundus normal (“patient sees nothing, doctor sees nothing”)
• Papillitis → disc edema present

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: In patients with underlying cardiac disease who require general anesthesia, which inhalational anesthetic agent is preferred because of its minimal cardiovascular effects and greater hemodynamic stability?
questions.explanation: Desflurane is considered the preferred inhalational anesthetic in this question because of its minimal myocardial depressant effect and ability to maintain cardiac output. It has very low blood-gas solubility, allowing rapid adjustment of anesthesia depth and better intraoperative control. These properties contribute to relatively stable hemodynamics in controlled settings, making it acceptable in patients with cardiac disease in many exam-based contexts. However, clinically, desflurane may cause sympathetic stimulation, leading to transient tachycardia and hypertension, especially with rapid increases in concentration. Despite this, some exam keys emphasize its minimal direct cardiac depression over these effects. Other options: (A) Halothane causes significant myocardial depression and sensitizes the heart to catecholamines, increasing arrhythmia risk. (B) Isoflurane produces vasodilation and may cause reflex tachycardia, increasing myocardial oxygen demand. (D) Sevoflurane provides excellent cardiovascular stability and is widely preferred in practice, but may show mild myocardial depression
questions.learning: Desflurane is considered the preferred inhalational anesthetic in this question because of its minimal myocardial depressant effect and ability to maintain cardiac output.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 24-year-old otherwise healthy woman presents with a 2-day history of dysuria, increased urinary frequency, and suprapubic discomfort. She has no fever, flank pain, vomiting, or vaginal discharge. Her vital signs are stable, and there is no history of recent antibiotic use or urinary tract abnormalities. She is diagnosed with an uncomplicated lower urinary tract infection, and empirical therapy is planned. Which of the following drugs should not be preferred as first-line empirical treatment in this case?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Ciprofloxacin

Uncomplicated acute cystitis in an otherwise healthy, non-pregnant woman is most commonly caused by Escherichia coli. Nitrofurantoin, fosfomycin, and cotrimoxazole (where local resistance is <20%) are the recommended first-line empirical therapies. Fluoroquinolones (e.g., ciprofloxacin) should not be preferred as first-line treatment because of increasing bacterial resistance, risk of collateral damage, and serious adverse effects. They should be reserved for complicated infections or when first-line agents cannot be used.

Why not the other options?

• A. Nitrofurantoin: First-line drug for uncomplicated cystitis; achieves high urinary concentrations but should not be used for pyelonephritis due to poor renal tissue penetration.
• B. Cotrimoxazole: First-line option if local E. coli resistance is <20% and there has been no recent use.
• D. Fosfomycin: First-line agent given as a single oral dose with excellent activity against common uropathogens, including many multidrug-resistant strains.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 65-year-old man has the following lesion over the face. He complains of bleeding while itching. Which of the following is seen in the lesion?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Rolled out edge

The given history with the image showing an ulcer over the face with pearly, rolled-out borders points to a diagnosis of basal cell carcinoma.

Basal cell carcinoma (BCC) is an epithelial tumor arising from basal cells. It is the most common type of skin cancer most commonly seen over the face, above the line joining corner of the mouth, and lobule of the ear. Risk factors for BCC include ultraviolet radiation (strongest risk factor), age 40-80 years with excessive sun exposure, light-skinned people, and exposure to arsenic compounds, coal tar, aromatic hydrocarbons, and infrared light. It is more common in males than females. It is also associated with syndromes such as xeroderma pigmentosum and Gorlin's syndrome.

Features of BCC include:

* Pearly nodule with rolled border

* Tortuous telangiectatic vessels

* Surface which can get ulcerated with raised and beaded edge, often with a central depression or umbilication

* Bleeding on minor trauma

BCC has various subtypes such as nodular (most common type), pigmented, nodulocystic, morphoeic, infiltrative, and fibroepithelioma of Pinkus.

It is locally aggressive and can erode the bone or facial sinuses. It rarely metastasizes via lymph nodes.

The occasional presence of melanin in the nodular variant of BCC (pigmented BCC) may lead to confusion with melanoma.

Diagnosis is confirmed by a wedge biopsy. X-ray or CT may be needed if there is a local invasion. Histology shows peripheral palisading of cells.

Treatment:

* Surgical: Wide excision (4-6 mm clearance) with a skin graft or flap or primary suturing

* Mohs' surgery for BCC close to the eyes, nose, or ear to preserve more tissue.

* Non-surgical: Radiotherapy, vismodegib and sonedegib.
questions.learning: Rolled out edge — The given history with the image showing an ulcer over the face with pearly, rolled-out borders points to a diagnosis of basal cell carcinoma.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: For the diagnosis of resistant hypertension, the patient should have uncontrolled hypertension despite taking three antihypertensive drugs. This should include at least one:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Diuretic

For the diagnosis of resistant hypertension, the patient should have uncontrolled hypertension despite taking three antihypertensive drugs, including at least one diuretic.

While a calcium channel blocker, beta blocker, or alpha-blocker can be part of the antihypertensive regimen, the inclusion of a diuretic is necessary for the diagnosis of resistant hypertension. The diuretic helps in addressing fluid retention which is often a significant contributor to hypertension.

Resistant hypertension is more common in patients aged >60 years than in younger patients. It may be related to nonadherence to therapy, obesity, and excessive alcohol intake.

In the absence of a specific identifiable cause, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists like spironolactone have been found to be most effective add-on drugs for the treatment of resistant hypertension.
questions.learning: Diuretic For the diagnosis of resistant hypertension, the patient should have uncontrolled hypertension despite taking three antihypertensive drugs, including at least one diuretic.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A 68-year-old homeless man is found unresponsive in a park during winter. Autopsy reveals a cold, pale body with erosive hemorrhagic lesions on gastric mucosa, especially near the fundus and absence of any significant trauma. Which finding is most supportive of hypothermia as the cause of death?
options: Dark brown postmortem staining on dependent parts
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Wischnewski spots on gastric mucosa

• Winter ; Cold, pale body
• Erosive hemorrhagic lesions in gastric mucosa (especially fundus)
• No significant trauma

Features suggestive of - Hypothermia.

❌Option A. Washerwoman skin on hands

• Can be seen with prolonged exposure to moisture (like drowning).
• Not specific for hypothermia.

❌Option B. Purple discoloration of nail beds

• That’s cyanosis. Very nonspecific.
• Can occur in many causes of death.

✅ Option C. Wischnewski spots on gastric mucosa

Wischnewski spots are:

• Dark brown/black hemorrhagic erosions in gastric mucosa
• Classically associated with hypothermia
• Mechanism : due to stress-induced hemorrhage + acid digestion of blood

❌Option D. Dark brown postmortem staining on dependent parts

That’s livor mortis. Completely nonspecific.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which one of the following parameters precisely defines grade 3 abruptio placentae?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Intrauterine fetal death

The Sher classification of abruptio placentae is based mainly on the clinical severity and fetal status:

• Grade 1 (mild): Minimal vaginal bleeding, no maternal or fetal distress.
• Grade 2 (moderate): More significant bleeding, maternal tachycardia, uterine tenderness, and fetal distress.
• Grade 3 (severe): Intrauterine fetal death (IUFD), often associated with significant concealed hemorrhage and maternal complications such as coagulopathy/DIC.

Therefore, IUFD precisely defines Grade 3 abruptio placentae.

Why not the other options?

• A. Moderate vaginal bleeding: More consistent with Grade 2.
• B. Maternal tachycardia: Usually indicates Grade 2 disease.
• C. Low fibrinogen: May occur in severe abruption due to DIC, but it is not the defining criterion for Grade 3.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: What is the Battle sign?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Mastoid ecchymosis

Battle sign refers to the retro auricular or mastoid ecchymosis that typically results from fracture of the middle cranial fossa following head trauma. It is prominent when there is a fracture of the petrous temporal bone.

An image showing Battle sign is shown below:

Pearl PF0033: Signs of base of skull fracture

Signs of Base of Skull Fracture

* Bilateral periorbital haematoma (raccoon eyes)

* Battle’s sign (bruising over mastoid)

* CSF rhinorrhoea or otorrhoea

* Haemotympanum or bleeding from ear
questions.learning: Mastoid ecchymosis Battle sign refers to the retro auricular or mastoid ecchymosis that typically results from fracture of the middle cranial fossa following head trauma.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: In a Firearm injury, blackening surrounding the gunshot entry wound is due to?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Smoke deposition

Blackening occurs due to the deposits of smoke over the epidermis which can be removed with a wet cloth. This can be seen up to around 15 cm of firing.

Other injuries related to firearms are:

• Burn injuries - occur due to flame released during the firing. It is seen in contact shot wounds or distances up to 5-8 cm. Singeing of hair is caused due to burns.
• Tattooing - occurs due to the deposition of unburnt powder particles. These are difficult to remove. They are also called stippling or peppering. This is seen up to 50 cm of firing
• Greasing and collaring - occur due to the deposition of the lubricant of the bullet in the tissues, during its penetration. It can be found in contact, near-shot, or distant shot wounds.

In a firm contact shot, the imprint of the muzzle of the gun is seen on the skin around the wound. The victim is within the range of flame, hence singeing of the hair will be present. Tattooing begins only when the muzzle-to-target distance is >1cm, like in a loose contact shot.

When the distance between the victim and the firing is 5-8cm, it is called a close shot. The victim is within the range of the flame, hence, features related to flame, smoke, and powder deposition will be seen. Singeing, burning, blackening and tattooing will be present.

When the distance between the victim and the firing is >50 cm, it is a distant shot. The victim lies outside the range of flame and powder deposition. Hence, features related to flame, smoke, and powder deposition are absent. Burning, blackening, and tattooing are absent.
questions.learning: Smoke deposition Blackening occurs due to the deposits of smoke over the epidermis which can be removed with a wet cloth. This can be seen up to around 15 cm of firing.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which pneumoconiosis is caused by exposure to cotton dust?
questions.explanation: Byssinosis is an occupational lung disease caused by the inhalation of dust from cotton, flax, or hemp. It is often called "Monday morning fever" because symptoms like chest tightness and dyspnea are typically most severe when workers return to the textile mill after a weekend break. Bagassosis (Option B) is a hypersensitivity pneumonitis caused by inhaling dust from moldy sugar cane fiber (bagasse). Anthracosis (Option C) is caused by the inhalation of coal dust or carbon particles and is commonly found in miners. Silicosis (Option D) is caused by inhaling crystalline silica dust in industries like stone cutting or sandblasting. Long-term chronic exposure to cotton dust can eventually lead to permanent, irreversible obstructive lung disease. Prevention focuses on industrial hygiene, including improved local exhaust ventilation, the use of personal protective masks, and regular medical screening of workers to detect early respiratory decline

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 35-year-old man presented with serial blood pressure recordings of above 140/90 mmHg. Which one of the following signs is not a clue for an underlying cause of hypertension?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Vitiligo

Vitiligo is not a typical clinical clue for secondary hypertension.

• A. Radio-femoral delay — Clue for secondary hypertension

• Suggests coarctation of the aorta, a secondary cause of hypertension.
• Femoral pulses are delayed and weaker compared with radial pulses.

• B. Enlarged kidneys — Clue

• May suggest polycystic kidney disease, an important renal cause of secondary hypertension.

• C. Bull neck and buffalo hump — Clue

• Characteristic of Cushing syndrome, which can cause secondary hypertension through excess cortisol.

• D. Vitiligo — Not a typical clue

• Vitiligo is associated with autoimmune disorders but is not a characteristic clinical clue to a specific secondary cause of hypertension.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A full-term neonate, delivered via an uncomplicated vaginal birth, is noted to have bullae and abrasions over the shoulder, knees, and legs shortly after delivery, as shown in the image. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Epidermolysis Bullosa

The above clinical scenario of the neonate having blisters and abrasions on the shoulder, buttocks, and knee after an uneventful vaginal delivery (due to minor handling/care)  points toward Epidermolysis bullosa.

Epidermolysis bullosa simplex (EBS) is a type of blistering disease. It occurs due to the mutation in the Keratin gene (KRT5 or KRT14) encoding for Keratin 5 or 14 expressed in the basal cell layer. This mutation causes the production of defective intermediate filaments. This makes epidermal basal cells fragile and subsequently causes blisters on physical pressure. The separation in EBS is within the epidermis (basal cell layer). The child is affected at birth, and caregivers present the baby with blisters on the hands, elbows, feet, and ankles. More blisters will appear as the baby starts crawling.

Option A: Erythema is superficial reddening of skin, which happens due to dilatation of capillaries secondary to an insult; it does not present as skin peeling in neonates.

Option C: Pustular melanosis are benign lesions seen predominantly in black neonates, contains neutrophils, and is present at birth as vesiculopustular eruption around the chin, neck, back, extremities, palms and soles.

Option D: Erythema toxicum is a self-limiting lesion that commonly occurs around day two of life and is a normal newborn phenomenon. It appears as firm, yellow-white, 1-2mm papules or pustules with surrounding erythema. They can be clustered or sparse and usually spare the palms and soles.

Pearl PF2200: Benign findings in a newborn

1. Erythema toxicum – small, white papules on an erythematous base that usually present on the face, trunk, and extremities. They contain eosinophils and may persist for a week.

2. Mongolian spots – Slate-blue, demarcated areas of pigmentation seen over the buttocks and back. This is also called dermal melanocytosis.

3. Pustular melanosis – Benign lesions seen predominantly in black neonates, contains neutrophils, and is present at birth as vesiculopustular eruption around the chin, neck, back, extremities, palms and soles.

4. Sebaceous Hyperplasia - White-Yellow papules on nose of a newborn due to hyperplastic sebaceous glands

5. Milia - Pearly opalescent white, epidermal inclusion cysts usually over the face.

6. Epstein Pearls - nests of epithelial cells, that appear as whitish/yellowish spots on hard palate. Usually, resolve by 3 months.

7. Cutis Marmorata - Transient lacy reticular vascular pattern of skin caused due to exaggerated physiologic vasomotor response on exposure to low environmental temperature.

8. Sucking Blisters - Solitary or scattered superficial bullae present at birth on the upper limbs of infants, which are caused by vigorous sucking on the affected part in-utero.

9. Salmon patch or naevus simplex - Small, ill-defined, pink-coloured macules commonly seen over glabella, eyelids, upper lip, and nuchal area, which develop due to vascular ectasia.

10. Harlequin colour change - A transient, well-demarcated colour change, with one half of the body displaying erythema and the other half pallor, usually occurring between two and five days of age.

11. Vaginal bleeding in the newborn at 2–3 days of age and enlargement and secretion of the breasts in both sexes.

12. Hymenal tags

13. Physiological phimosis

14. Conjunctival hemorrhage

15. Peeling of skin (especially in post terms)
questions.learning: Epidermolysis Bullosa — The above clinical scenario of the neonate having blisters and abrasions on the shoulder, buttocks, and knee after an uneventful vaginal delivery (due to minor handling/care) points toward Epidermolysis bullosa.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: If a single zygote divides between 9 and 12 days after fertilization, what type of twins are most likely to result?
questions.explanation: The classification of monozygotic twins depends entirely on the timing of zygote cleavage. When division occurs late, specifically between 9 and 12 days after fertilization, the amnion has already formed. Consequently, the twins will share a single placenta and a single amniotic sac, resulting in monochorionic monoamniotic (MoMo) twins. Cleavage before 3 days results in dichorionic diamniotic twins (Option A). Division between 4 and 8 days leads to monochorionic diamniotic twins (Option C), which is the most common type. If division occurs even later than 13 days, incomplete cleavage results in conjoined twins (Option B). MoMo pregnancies are high-risk due to the potential for umbilical cord entanglement and twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome. Understanding this embryological timeline is vital for obstetricians to provide appropriate prenatal monitoring and risk assessment. Since the amnion forms around day 8, a split occurring on day 9-12 inevitably forces the fetuses into a shared environment within the same amniotic cavity
questions.learning: The classification of monozygotic twins depends entirely on the timing of zygote cleavage. When division occurs late, specifically between 9 and 12 days after fertilization, the amnion has already formed.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A patient with a history of bone marrow transplant presented with a lesion in the lung. On microscopic examination, the lesion is shown below. What is the likely causative agent?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Aspergillosis

The given clinical scenario of lung lesion and the image showing septate hyphae with branching at acute angles is suggestive of aspergillosis.

Invasive aspergillosis occurs due to infection with Aspergillus species. It is often seen in immunocompromised patients. Most cases of invasive aspergillosis involve the lungs. The clinical features include fever, cough which may be productive, chest discomfort, hemoptysis, and shortness of breath. Voriconazole is the drug of choice.

Other manifestations include allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis where central bronchiectasis is usually seen. Aspergilloma and superficial infections like otomycosis or mycotic keratitis are the other presentations.

Histopathological examination of the tissue section shows characteristic dichotomous branching at an acute angle. The hyphae stain poorly with hematoxylin and eosin, so periodic acid–Schiff (PAS) stain is used.

Other methods for diagnosis include detection of galactomannan (Aspergillus cell-wall component) and culture isolation. Aspergillus fumigatus grows dark green colonies, while Aspergillus niger appears black. Yellow-green colonies are seen in case of Aspergillus flavus. Microscopic examination of colonies stained with lactophenol cotton blue would show septate hyphae and conidiophores.
questions.learning: Aspergillosis — The given clinical scenario of lung lesion and the image showing septate hyphae with branching at acute angles is suggestive of aspergillosis.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Peripheral chemoreceptors are most sensitive to?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hypoxia

Peripheral chemoreceptors are most sensitive to hypoxia.

Peripheral Chemoreceptors are located in the carotid bodies (at the bifurcation of the common carotid arteries) and aortic bodies (near the aortic arch). They are sensitive to changes in pO2, pCO2, and pH of the blood. In response to changes in these parameters, they send impulses to the medullary respiratory centers and modify the duration and frequency of respiratory cycles.

Peripheral chemoreceptors are most sensitive to a drop in partial pressure of oxygen (PaO₂) in arterial blood.

Mechanism:

Type I glomus cells in the carotid and aortic bodies have O2-sensitive K+ channels, which are inactivated in response to hypoxia. This reduces the K+ efflux, depolarizing the cell and causing Ca2+ inﬂux, via L-type voltage-gated calcium channels. The Ca2+ influx triggers action potentials and consequent excitation of the afferent nerve endings in the peripheral chemoreceptors.

Hypoxia (PaO₂ < 60 mmHg) strongly stimulates these receptors, leading to an increase in respiratory rate and depth to improve oxygenation.

Other Options:

Peripheral chemoreceptors also respond to hypercapnia (Option A) and acidosis (Option C). However, these are primarily detected by central chemoreceptors, located in the medulla, which monitor CO₂ levels in cerebrospinal fluid.

Alkalosis (Option D) causes a weaker response from peripheral chemoreceptors compared to hypoxia.
questions.learning: Hypoxia Peripheral chemoreceptors are most sensitive to hypoxia. Peripheral Chemoreceptors are located in the carotid bodies (at the bifurcation of the common carotid arteries) and aortic bodies (near the aortic arch).

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following statements is incorrect about rotavirus vaccine?
options: Available as monovalent and pentavalent vaccines
Not recommended after 6 months of age
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. It is a subunit vaccine

Rotavirus vaccine is not a subunit vaccine.

Rotavirus vaccines are oral, live attenuated vaccines and are of 3 types:

1. Rotarix (human monovalent) vaccine is administered in 2 oral doses:

• First dose: At 6 weeks, no later than 12 weeks (due to the risk of intussusception).
• Second dose: With a gap of 4 weeks from the first dose, to be given by 16 weeks and no later than 24 weeks.

2. RotaTeq (pentavalent bovine-human reassortant) vaccine is administered in 3 oral doses at 2, 4, and 6 months. The first dose is given between 6-12 weeks and subsequent doses within a 4-10 weeks gap. All the 3 doses should be given before 32 weeks.
3. Rotavac (monovalent liquid frozen) vaccine is administered in 3 oral doses, 4 weeks apart at 6,10 and 14 weeks. It should not be administered to children more than 8 months of age.

Option C: According to the MoHFW, the rotavirus virus vaccine can be given till the age of 1 year and the potential benefit from vaccination outweighs the risk of intussusception. However, per the CDC guidelines, the maximum age for all rotavirus vaccines is 8 months, 0 days. Since this is a recall question, the options appeared as such in the exam. Additionally, rotavirus is a live vaccine, making option 2 (which states that it is a subunit vaccine) the distinctly wrong statement and the better answer.
questions.learning: It is a subunit vaccine Rotavirus vaccine is not a subunit vaccine. Rotavirus vaccines are oral, live attenuated vaccines and are of 3 types: 1.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Who is responsible for handling the investigation in the case of a custodial death?
questions.explanation: Under the laws of India (specifically Section 176 of the CrPC), an inquest in the case of a custodial death—any death that occurs while a person is in police or judicial custody—must be conducted by a Judicial Magistrate. This mandatory legal requirement is designed to ensure an impartial, independent investigation into the cause and circumstances of the death, serving as a safeguard against potential human rights abuses or cover-ups. A Police inspector (Option A), Jail superintendent (Option B), or Superintendent of Police (Option C) are not legally authorized to lead this specific type of death inquiry, as they are part of the very system where the custody occurred. The Judicial Magistrate has the power to examine witnesses, record statements, and order a post-mortem examination by a medical board if necessary. This transparent process is a fundamental principle of justice and the rule of law, ensuring that the state is held accountable for the safety and lives of all individuals under its detention
questions.learning: Under the laws of India (specifically Section 176 of the CrPC), an inquest in the case of a custodial death—any death that occurs while a person is in police or judicial custody—must be conducted by a Judicial Magistrate.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A mother delivers in a rural area under the guidance of a skilled birth attendant. Incorrect regarding the care provided by the skilled birth attendant is:
options: Start breastfeeding as soon as possible
Clear eyes with a sterile swab
Bath to newborn with warm water
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Bath to newborn with warm water

A skilled birth attendant (SBA) provides essential newborn care focused on thermal protection, early breastfeeding, and infection prevention.

Immediate actions include early initiation of breastfeeding, covering the baby’s head and body, and gentle eye care with a clean/sterile swab if indicated.

Bathing the newborn immediately is contraindicated, as it increases the risk of hypothermia; bathing should be delayed for at least 24 hours (or until the baby is stable).
questions.learning: Bath to newborn with warm water — A skilled birth attendant (SBA) provides essential newborn care focused on thermal protection, early breastfeeding, and infection prevention.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: In a community of 5000, the crude birth rate is 25 per 1000 people. What is the number of pregnant females in this community?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 138

The number of pregnant females is 138.

Step 1: In the given question, the crude birth rate is 25 per 1000 people i.e 25 children are born from pregnant mothers for every 1000 people. Therefore there are 25 pregnant females per 1000 population.

Step 2: Since the total population is 5000, the total no of pregnant females = 25 x 5000/1000 = 125

Step 3: We should also consider the pregnancy wastage i.e 10% of total live births =10 x 125/100=12.5 (since some pregnancies may not result in live birth i.e abortions and stillbirths, a correction factor of 10% is to be added to avoid the underestimation of the number of pregnancies)

Step 4: Total pregnant females = total live birth + pregnancy wastage = 125+12.5=137.5 ,which is rounded off to 138.

Pearl PF1746: Fertility Indicators

Crude birth rate

* It is the simplest measure of fertility although its usage is unsatisfactory

* India, as per SRS bulletin 2018, had a birth rate of 20.0 per 1000 population

General Fertility Rate

* It is a better indicator of fertility than crude birth rate

* The demerit of this indicator is that not all women in the denominator are exposed to childbirth

Age-specific fertility rates is a more precise measure of fertility and is also a sensitive indicator of family planning achievement.

Total Fertility Rate

* It is the sum of all age-specific fertility rates multiplied by 5

* This measure gives the approximate magnitude of completed family size

Gross Reproductive Rate is the average number of girls that would be born to a woman if she experiences the current fertility pattern throughout her reproductive span, assuming no mortality.

Net Reproduction Rate

* It is a demographic indicator

* NRR of 1 is equivalent to approximately the 2 child norm

* If the NRR is less than 1, then the reproductive performance of the population is said to be inadequate
questions.learning: 138 The number of pregnant females is 138. Step 1: In the given question, the crude birth rate is 25 per 1000 people i.e 25 children are born from pregnant mothers for every 1000 people.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 54-year-old man was brought to the casualty with fever, headache, focal seizures. EEG shows focal temporal lobe spikes. CSF sample analysis shows 50 cells with 90% Lymphocytes and 10% Neutrophils. What would be the drug of choice for this condition?

Correct answer: B. Acyclovir

The clinical hallmark of encephalitis is the acute onset of fever and focal neurologic signs and with hemorrhagic necrosis especially the temporal lobe if there is HSV encephalitis. The most sensitive investigation is HSV DNA demonstration in CSF by PCR.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following stains is used for the detection of hemosiderin deposits?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Perl’s prussian blue

Perl's prussian blue stain is used to detect hemosiderin deposits.

Hemosiderin is a hemoglobin-derived granular pigment that is golden-yellow to brown. It accumulates in the tissues when there is a local or systemic excess of iron.

Iron is normally stored within cells in association with the protein apoferritin, forming ferritin micelles. Large aggregates of these micelles are hemosiderin deposits seen both in light and electron microscopy.

Image 1: Hemosiderin deposits in tissue

Image 2: Prussian blue staining of hemosiderin

*Note: Iron dispersed in the cytoplasm is seen in electron microscopy as ferritin micelles.
