questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The structure marked with the asterisk in the electron micrograph indicates _____________.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Secretory vesicles

The structure marked with the asterisk in the electron micrograph indicates presynaptic secretory vesicles. The structure marked with the arrowhead is postsynaptic density.

The secretory vesicles are synthesized by the neurons and are involved in electrochemical signalling in the brain and neuromuscular junctions.

On electron microscopy:

• Mitochondria appear as round or elliptical bodies of 0.5-2.0 micron long on an electron microscope, consisting of an outer and an inner mitochondrial membrane, cristae, and mitochondrial matrix.

• Golgi bodies (or Golgi apparatus) appear as stacks of flatenned membranous cisternae surrounded by clusters of vesicles.

• Ribosomes may be attached to the membrane of the rough endoplasmic reticulum (as shown in the image below), or else, they may exist as monosomes or as a chain of granular structures called polyribosomes associated with mRNA.
questions.learning: Secretory vesicles — The structure marked with the asterisk in the electron micrograph indicates presynaptic secretory vesicles. The structure marked with the arrowhead is postsynaptic density.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 45-year-old man is admitted with respiratory distress. CT imaging reveals a nasal polyp associated with fluid accumulation in a paranasal sinus. Obstruction of drainage from which structure is most likely responsible for this finding?
questions.explanation: The CT scan findings show a nasal polyp obstructing the drainage of the maxillary sinus. The maxillary sinus (Antrum of Highmore) is the largest paranasal sinus and drains into the middle meatus of the nose via the maxillary ostium. When a polyp grows in the middle meatus, it blocks this ostium, leading to secondary sinusitis and fluid accumulation. Regarding the distractors, the ethmoidal sinuses (Option A) are multiple small cells; the anterior ones drain to the middle meatus, but the large fluid collection shown is within the maxilla. The sphenoidal sinus (Option B) drains into the sphenoethmoidal recess. The frontal sinus (Option C) also drains to the middle meatus, but its obstruction would show fluid in the forehead region on CT. Thus, the anatomical location of the fluid collection confirms maxillary sinus involvement
questions.learning: The CT scan findings show a nasal polyp obstructing the drainage of the maxillary sinus. The maxillary sinus (Antrum of Highmore) is the largest paranasal sinus and drains into the middle meatus of the nose via the maxillary ostium.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of the following would be prescribed for simple myopic astigmatism?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. -1.00 DC X 180 degree

Among the above options, -1.00 DC × 180 degrees is the correct prescription for simple myopic astigmatism (SMA).

There are 3 components for prescription of glasses.

1. The first number is the refractive power of the spherical component. It is represented as convex (+) or concave (-) dioptre sphere (DS).

2. The second number denotes the power of the cylinder, represented as convex (+) or concave (-) dioptre cylinder (DC).

3. The above two components are followed by an x representing the axis (orientation) of the cylinder.

In the most common type of SMA - with-the-rule astigmatism - meridian A (represented by 90 degrees) is more curved than meridian B (represented by 180 degrees). The light rays refracting from B focus on the retina, whereas those refracting from A focus in front of the retina.

To correct this error, a negative cylindrical lens (DC) is used to focus the myopic rays of meridian A on the retina. This correction needs to occur at 90 degrees (meridian A). The axis of a cylindrical lens is perpendicular to the required correction and thus, the spectacles will have an axis of 180 degrees.

There is no spherical refractive error since the light rays from meridian B lies on the retina. Thus DS is 0.
questions.learning: -1.00 DC X 180 degree Among the above options, -1.00 DC × 180 degrees is the correct prescription for simple myopic astigmatism (SMA). There are 3 components for prescription of glasses.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: The greenish-black color of the first stool in the newborn is due to :
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Biliverdin

The greenish-black color of the first stool in the newborn is due to biliverdin.

Meconium is a dark, viscous material that is normally present in the intestine of the fetus and passed within 1st 48hour of life. Meconium appears after the 20th week and at term, it is uniformly distributed throughout the gut up to the rectum indicating the presence of intestinal peristalsis.

It is composed of various products of secretion, such as desquamated fetal cells, glycerophospholipids from the lungs, lanugo, scalp hair, vernix, and undigested products from swallowed amniotic fluid. The greenish-black color of meconium is due to the presence of bile pigments excreted by the biliary tract, especially biliverdin (pigment from the oxidation of bilirubin).

During intrauterine hypoxia, the relaxation of the anal sphincter due to vagal stimulation can lead to the passage of meconium into the amniotic fluid. Additionally, the release of arginine vasopressin (AVP) from the fetal pituitary gland due to intrauterine hypoxia can stimulate the colon muscles to contract, resulting in intraamniotic defecation. Meconium aspiration syndrome can occur when meconium is inhaled, as it is toxic to the lungs.

Other options:

Option A: Bilirubin is responsible for the yellow color of the stools.

Option D: Neonates do not harbor gut flora at birth.
questions.learning: Biliverdin — The greenish-black color of the first stool in the newborn is due to biliverdin. Meconium is a dark, viscous material that is normally present in the intestine of the fetus and passed within 1st 48hour of life.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Cardiovascular System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: Which of the following is responsible for the bradycardia seen in Cushing reflex?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Baroreceptor activation

In Cushing reflex, raised intracranial pressure causes cerebral ischemia, leading to sympathetic activation and severe hypertension. The resulting increase in arterial pressure stimulates baroreceptors, which trigger a reflex parasympathetic response, producing bradycardia.

A) Heart failure – Not the mechanism of reflex bradycardia here.

C) Cardiac conduction defect – Not involved in Cushing reflex.

D) Increased RVLM activity – Causes hypertension, not bradycardia.
questions.learning: Baroreceptor activation — In Cushing reflex, raised intracranial pressure causes cerebral ischemia, leading to sympathetic activation and severe hypertension.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient with CKD with refractory hypertension is brought to the casualty with dizziness. His BP was found to be 200/120mmHg. His BUN was 50mg/dl and creatinine was 3mg/dl. Potassium was 6mEq/L. Which of the following is an indication of emergency hemodialysis?
options: Severe acidosis with elevated BUN and creatinine
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Severe acidosis with elevated BUN and creatinine

Severe acidosis with elevated BUN and creatinine with symptoms like dizziness and altered mental status is an indication for hemodialysis.

The emergent indications of dialysis or renal replacement therapy can be remembered by the mnemonic - 'AEIOU' (vowels in the English alphabet). These include:

• Severe metabolic Acidosis ( pH < 7.1) with concomitant renal injury (Option D).
• Electrolyte abnormalities - Severe hyperkalemia (>6.5 mmol/L) or rapidly rising potassium levels (Option C).
• Intoxication - In cases of severe poisoning of toxic substances like methanol or ethylene glycol, and in cases of overdose with a dialyzable drug.
• Fluid Overload that is not responsive to diuretic therapy.
• Uremia - elevated BUN with signs and symptoms of uremia like bleeding, pericarditis, and altered mental status.
questions.learning: Severe acidosis with elevated BUN and creatinine Severe acidosis with elevated BUN and creatinine with symptoms like dizziness and altered mental status is an indication for hemodialysis.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 35-year-old male underwent surgery for an ileal perforation. Due to heavy contamination, only the sheath was closed, and the wound was left open. Daily wound washing was performed, and the wound was closed on postoperative day 5. By which mechanism does wound healing occur in this case?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Tertiary intention

Wound healing occurs by tertiary intention in this case. The wound is cleaned and left open for a few days. This allows soft tissues to drain and also ensures no infection is present before surgical closure can be done.

Wound closure is categorized into primary, secondary, or tertiary:

Primary closure is done for clean wounds with minimal tissue loss that are amenable to approximation of wound edges. Healing occurs by primary intention. Primary closure is ideally performed within 6 to 8 hrs of trauma, but wounds in vascular areas (e.g. face) may be delayed to up to 24 hours after trauma.

Secondary closure allows healing by secondary intention. The wound is left open to heal largely by the formation of granulation tissue and contraction. These wounds often have significant tissue loss precluding tension-free approximation of edges, with devitalized edges. Wound dressings are changed daily to aid in the formation of granulation tissue and subsequent contraction.

Tertiary closure, also known as delayed primary closure, results in a combination of healing by primary and secondary intention. The wound is thoroughly irrigated, debrided, and left open for 2 to 5 days before surgical closure. It is used for wounds that are grossly contaminated without significant tissue loss.
questions.learning: Tertiary intention Wound healing occurs by tertiary intention in this case. The wound is cleaned and left open for a few days.

questions.text: SARS CoV-2 diagnosis is done by all except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Southern blotting

SARS-CoV-2 diagnosis relies on detection of viral RNA or viral antigens/antibodies:

• RT-PCR / Real-time PCR: Detect viral RNA with high sensitivity; gold standard for diagnosis.
• Immunoassays: Detect viral antigens (rapid tests) or host antibodies against the virus.
• Southern blotting, however, detects DNA sequences and is not used for RNA viruses like SARS-CoV-2.

Why other options are incorrect:

D. Immunoassays: Widely used for serological testing or rapid antigen detection.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 5-year-old child presents with abdominal pain, irritability, and developmental delay. On examination, pallor and a bluish line along the gums are noted. Laboratory investigations show microcytic anemia, and peripheral blood smear reveals basophilic stippling of red blood cells. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of abdominal pain (painter's colic), irritability, and developmental delay in a child is highly suggestive of lead poisoning. The most specific physical finding is the Burtonian line (Burton's line), a stippled blue line on the gums caused by subepithelial granules of lead. Laboratory findings of microcytic anemia accompanied by basophilic stippling (punctate basophilia) on the peripheral smear are pathognomonic for this toxicity. Lead inhibits essential enzymes like ferrochelatase and ALA-dehydratase. Iron deficiency (Option A) lacks the gum line and basophilic stippling. Sideroblastic anemia (Option B) shows ringed sideroblasts in the bone marrow but not the neurological or gingival signs. Thalassemia minor (Option D) is often asymptomatic or mild and does not explain the developmental delay. Treatment requires removing the lead source and initiating chelation therapy
questions.learning: The clinical presentation of abdominal pain (painter's colic), irritability, and developmental delay in a child is highly suggestive of lead poisoning.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following is correct regarding oxytocin?
options: It can be given by oral route
It is secreted by anterior pituitary
In higher doses, it exerts diuretic like action
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. It is responsible for galactokinesis

Oxytocin is responsible for galactokinesis (milk ejection reflex).

Other options:

* It can not be given by oral route because it has emotional side effects.

* It is secreted by the posterior pituitary.

* It does not have diuretic-like action at higher doses.

WHO guidelines for active management of the third stage of labor (AMTSL) recommends oxytocin administration immediately (within 1 minute) after the delivery of the fetus.  Oxytocin 10 IU is given IM or IV. It should be given after the delivery of the fetus and before the delivery of the placenta.

Milk ejection by oxytocin follows a stimulation mechanism similar to uterine contraction in delivery (cervical dilatation).

The physiological actions of oxytocin are:

* Contraction of the pregnant uterus: Cervical dilatation transmits signals to the hypothalamus and stimulates the secretion of oxytocin, which acts on the smooth muscles of the uterus and contracts it.

* Milk ejection from breasts: Suckling reflex transmits signals to the hypothalamus which causes the release of oxytocin which acts on the myoepithelial cells of the breast. This results in ejection of milk.

The action of oxytocin is an example of positive feedback mechanism.

AMTSL  guidelines recommended by WHO :

* Immediate administration of prophylactic uterotonic (Oxytocin). Oxytocin 10 IU is given IM or IV.

* Controlled cord traction during placental delivery (in cesarean section and in vaginal birth where skilled birth attendants are present)

* Delayed cord clamping

* Postpartum abdominal uterine tonus assessment for early identification of uterine atony is recommended for all women. Continuous monitoring of uterine tone is done every 15 minutes for 2 hours. If uterine atony is detected, a fundal massage is performed.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A child presents with brown-colored urine and oliguria for the last 3 days. He has mild facial and pedal edema. His blood pressure is 126/90. He has 2+ proteinuria with >100 red cells/HPF and a few granular casts. His creatinine is 0.9, urea is 56. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. PSGN

A child presenting with acute onset (3 days) gross hematuria, hypertension, edema, oliguria, and mild to moderate proteinuria is suggestive of a nephritic syndrome picture. The only disease which causes this out of the given options is post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN).

PSGN is primarily caused by Group A β-hemolytic streptococcal infections in children aged 5 to 12 years. It is caused by immune complexes containing streptococcal antigens (M protein of cell wall) and specific antibodies. PSGN typically manifests as an acute nephritic syndrome, appearing either 1 to 2 weeks after streptococcal pharyngitis or 3 to 6 weeks after streptococcal pyoderma. The severity of kidney involvement can vary, ranging from asymptomatic microscopic hematuria with normal renal function to gross hematuria with acute renal failure. Edema, hypertension, and oliguria may be present depending on the extent of renal involvement.

Laboratory findings commonly include a significant decrease in serum C3 levels during the acute phase, with values returning to normal within 6 to 8 weeks. To confirm the diagnosis, evidence of a preceding streptococcal infection is necessary. The antistreptolysin O (ASO) titer often increases following pharyngitis, while the anti-deoxyribonuclease B level is a reliable indicator of cutaneous streptococcal infection.

Light microscopic examination reveals enlarged, hypercellular glomeruli with diffuse mesangial and endothelial proliferation, as well as leukocyte infiltration. Immunofluorescence analysis demonstrates granular deposits of IgG and complement C3 along the glomerular basement membrane (GBM) and in the mesangium. Electron microscopy primarily shows subepithelial humps, with subendothelial deposits observed in early stages of the disease.

Managing the acute effects of renal insufficiency (sodium restriction and diuretics) and hypertension is the mainstay. Antibiotic therapy with a 10-day course of penicillin is recommended to limit the spread of nephritogenic pathogens. But antibiotics do not alter the natural course of PSGN. Complete resolution of the hematuria and proteinuria in the majority of children occurs within 3–6 weeks of the onset of nephritis but 3–10% of children may have persistent microscopic hematuria, non-nephrotic proteinuria, or hypertension.

questions.learning: PSGN — A child presenting with acute onset (3 days) gross hematuria, hypertension, edema, oliguria, and mild to moderate proteinuria is suggestive of a nephritic syndrome picture.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 35-year-old carpenter presents with sudden anterior shoulder pain after lifting a heavy object overhead. He reports hearing a “pop” at the time of injury, followed by immediate swelling and bruising. Examination reveals a bulge in the mid–upper arm, and he has marked weakness in elbow flexion and forearm supination. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation described is a classic case of a long head of the biceps tendon rupture. The patient’s sudden "pop" sound during heavy overhead lifting and the subsequent formation of a visible bulge in the mid-upper arm—commonly referred to as the "Popeye deformity"—are pathognomonic. This muscle bulge occurs because the detached muscle belly retracts distally toward the elbow. The long head of the biceps is essential for elbow flexion and forearm supination, which explains the significant weakness the patient experiences. Triceps muscle rupture (Option B) would present with a bulge on the posterior aspect of the arm and weakness in elbow extension. A humerus fracture (Option C) would cause severe localized bone pain, instability, and usually a different radiographic appearance rather than an isolated muscle bulge. Tennis elbow (Option D), or lateral epicondylitis, involves chronic overuse pain at the lateral epicondyle rather than acute muscle deformity or flexion weakness

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A young patient presented with PND, dyspnea, and hemoptysis. However, the patient succumbed to her illness. On autopsy, the lungs showed hemosiderin-laden macrophages. In all of the following it can occur, except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Right heart failure

• Hemosiderin-laden macrophages (“heart failure cells”) result from chronic pulmonary congestion with RBC extravasation and breakdown.
• They are seen in left-sided heart failure, pulmonary venous obstruction, and volume overload states causing raised pulmonary capillary pressure.

These macrophages appear brown due to iron deposition. They indicate chronic pulmonary venous hypertension.

Analyzing Each Option

| Option | Causes Pulmonary Venous HTN? | Heart Failure Cells?

| ------ | ---------------------------- | --------------------

| A — Right heart failure | ❌ RHF → systemic venous congestion, NOT pulmonary | EXCEPT ✅

| B — Protein-losing enteropathy | ❌ No mechanism for pulmonary venous HTN | EXCEPT ✅

| C — Pulmonary venous obstruction | ✅ Directly raises pulmonary venous pressure | Yes ✅

| D — Volume overload | ✅ → Biventricular failure → pulmonary congestion | Yes ✅

The Controversy

This is genuinely controversial because both A and B are mechanistically correct "excepts."

Why A (Right heart failure) is the standard expected answer:

• Classic teaching: RHF causes systemic congestion (hepatomegaly, pedal edema, JVD), NOT pulmonary venous hypertension
• Therefore heart failure cells should NOT occur in isolated RHF
• Most Indian textbooks (Harsh Mohan, Robbins) frame it this way

Why B (Protein-losing enteropathy) could also be argued:

• PLE has absolutely no mechanism for pulmonary venous HTN
• It causes hypoalbuminemia → generalized edema, but not specifically pulmonary venous congestion
• Some argue B is a "cleaner" except than A

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A newborn male presents with urinary retention, lethargy, and a distended bladder. Antenatal ultrasonography revealed a characteristic “keyhole sign” along with a thickened bladder wall. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Posterior urethral valves (PUV) are congenital obstructing membranous folds in the male posterior urethra. The "keyhole sign" on antenatal ultrasound refers to a dilated bladder and a dilated posterior urethra, which is a classic finding for PUV. Postnatal symptoms include urinary retention, a palpable distended bladder, and lethargy. Hypospadias (Option A) involves an abnormal urethral opening on the ventral penis and does not cause high-grade internal obstruction. Vesicoureteral reflux (Option B) is the retrograde flow of urine; while it can occur secondary to PUV, it does not produce the "keyhole sign" independently. Neurogenic bladder (Option D) results from spinal or nerve defects and lacks the specific urethral membrane found in PUV. PUV is a leading cause of chronic kidney disease in male infants and requires urgent cystoscopic ablation
questions.learning: Posterior urethral valves (PUV) are congenital obstructing membranous folds in the male posterior urethra. The "keyhole sign" on antenatal ultrasound refers to a dilated bladder and a dilated posterior urethra, which is a classic finding for PUV.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: In which clinical situations is it essential to perform serial measurements of serum beta‑hCG (human chorionic gonadotropin) levels?
options: Pregnancy associated with Neural tube defects
questions.explanation: Serial monitoring of serum beta-hCG is the absolute standard of care for the follow-up of a molar pregnancy (gestational trophoblastic disease) . After surgical evacuation, hCG levels must be measured weekly until they become undetectable to ensure that no trophoblastic tissue remains. Persistent or rising levels indicate the development of gestational trophoblastic neoplasia (e.g., choriocarcinoma), which requires chemotherapy. In Down syndrome (Option A), hCG is measured as part of a one-time "quadruple screen," not for serial monitoring. Neural tube defects (Option B) are screened via alpha-fetoprotein. Rh-negative pregnancy (Option D) is managed by monitoring maternal antibody titers, not hCG. Therefore, because hCG is the definitive tumor marker for molar disease progression, its serial measurement is critical for patient survival and the detection of malignancy. Patients are typically advised to avoid pregnancy until hCG levels have remained normal for six months

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: General Physiology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A neurophysiology question states that the extracellular concentration of potassium is 5 mmol/L and the intracellular concentration is 50 mmol/L. Using a Nernst slope of 61 mV (at 37°C, monovalent ion, log10 form), what is the approximate equilibrium potential for potassium?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. -61 mV

The Nernst equation for a monovalent ion at 37°C is:

E = 61 log ([Ion]out / [Ion]in)

For potassium:

Eₖ = 61 log (5/50)

Eₖ = 61 log (0.1)

Eₖ = 61 × (−1)

Eₖ = −61 mV

A 10-fold higher intracellular K⁺ concentration gives a potassium equilibrium potential of approximately −61 mV.

Why not the others?

• A. +61 mV: Concentrations reversed (50 outside, 5 inside)
• C. +6.1 mV / D. −6.1 mV: Would result from a much smaller concentration gradient

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 19-year-old male presents with recurrent episodes of arthralgia, urethral discharge, and gonococcal infections. Culture of the synovial fluid from the knee grows Neisseria gonorrhoeae. Which of the following investigations is most appropriate to evaluate for an underlying immunodeficiency in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Late complement deficiency (C5-C9)

Recurrent or disseminated Neisseria infections strongly suggest a defect in the membrane attack complex (C5–C9), which is essential for killing Neisseria due to their thin cell wall. Late complement deficiency classically presents with repeated gonococcal or meningococcal infections. Testing for C5–C9 levels or CH50 is therefore the most appropriate investigation.

| Defect / Deficiency | Organism Susceptibility | Mechanism

| ------------------- | ----------------------- | ---------

| C5–C9 (MAC)
(terminal) | Neisseria spp. (especially N. meningitidis) | Failure of complement-mediated lysis

| C3 deficiency | Pyogenic infections (Strep, Staph, H. influenzae) | Impaired opsonization

| C1, C2, C4 (early) deficiency | SLE-like disease | Immune complex deposition
questions.learning: Late complement deficiency (C5-C9) Recurrent or disseminated Neisseria infections strongly suggest a defect in the membrane attack complex (C5–C9), which is essential for killing Neisseria due to their thin cell wall.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Cardiovascular System · Acute Coronary Syndrome Mi
questions.text: A 55-year-old man comes to the OPD due to recurrent episodes of retrosternal chest pain. The episodes occur during physical activity, usually when he climbs stairs or walks uphill, and resolve after he rests for a few minutes. He is prescribed sublingual nitroglycerin to take as needed when the chest pain occurs. This drug is most likely to relieve this patient's symptoms by causing which of the following hemodynamic changes?
options: Decrease in left ventricular end-diastolic volume
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Decrease in left ventricular end-diastolic volume

Sublingual nitroglycerin primarily causes venodilation, which reduces venous return (preload). This leads to a decrease in left ventricular end-diastolic volume (LVEDV), lowering myocardial wall stress and reducing oxygen demand, thereby relieving exertional (stable) angina.

A. Decrease in heart rate – Not a primary effect of nitrates; reflex tachycardia may occur.

C. Decrease in peripheral arteriolar resistance – Minor effect; arteriolar dilation is not the main mechanism.

D. Increase in coronary blood flow – Limited in stable angina; symptom relief is mainly from ↓ demand, not ↑ supply.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text:
A 30-year-old drowsy male was brought to the casualty. His pulse was 130/min, respiratory rate -30/min. His lab reports are given below. He showed improvement on nasogastric aspiration and administration of sodium bicarbonate, calcium gluconate, and 4-methyl pyrazole. What substance did he most likely consume?

ABG - metabolic acidosis

Total serum calcium - 6.8 mg/dL

Blood Urea – 100 mg/dl

Creatinine – 3.4 mg/dl

Urine analysis - Calcium oxalate crystals.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Ethylene glycol

The given scenario point towards ethylene glycol poisoning.

Ethylene glycol is converted to glyoxyaldehyde by alcohol dehydrogenase. Glyoxyaldehyde causes kidney damage.

Methanol is converted to formaldehyde by alcohol dehydrogenase. Formaldehyde causes retinal damage like blurring of vision/loss of vision.

The principles of treatment for both these conditions are the same. It predominantly involves using fomipezole or ethanol to inhibit the metabolic conversion of these relatively non-toxic alcohols to their toxic metabolites.
questions.learning: Ethylene glycol — The given scenario point towards ethylene glycol poisoning. Ethylene glycol is converted to glyoxyaldehyde by alcohol dehydrogenase.

questions.text: All of the following are true about Kleine-Levin syndrome (KLS), except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Anorexia

Kleine-Levin Syndrome (KLS), sometimes referred to as “Sleeping Beauty Syndrome,” is a rare sleep disorder characterized by recurrent episodes of:

• Hypersomnia (sleeping up to 18–20 hours a day),
• Hyperphagia (excessive eating),
• Hypersexuality, and
• Behavioral disinhibition.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 25-year-old female, with a previous history of chlamydia infection, now presents with low-grade fever and non-specific lower abdominal pain. Examination reveals mild diffuse lower abdominal tenderness on deep palpation, cervical motion tenderness, and a mucopurulent vaginal discharge. What is the long-term sequelae of this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Infertility

In the above clinical scenario fo apatient with previous history of chlamydia infection, now with low-grade fever, lower abdominal pain, lower abdominal tenderness on deep palpation, cervical motion tenderness, and a mucopurulent vaginal discharge points towards the diagnosis of pelvic inflammatory disease and the most important complication of it is infertility.

Pelvic Inflammatory disease involves inflammation of the upper genital tract including the fallopian tubes as well as the ovaries. The most common cause of PID in sexually active young females is sexually transmitted infections involving gonococci and chlamydia.

Pelvic inflammatory disease and salpingitis may lead to sterility. Other complications are tubo-ovarian abscesses (hydrosalpinx or pyosalpinx), chronic interstitial salpingitis, tubo ovarian cyst and ectopic pregnancies. Rarely peritonitis may develop with perihepatic inflammation (Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome). The patient presents with right upper quadrant pain and tenderness with abnormal liver function tests.

Risk factors of PID:

* Menstrual teenagers

* Multiple sexual partners

* Absence of contraceptive pills

* Previous history of PID

* IUCD users

Protective factors of PID:

* Barrier methods (condoms, diaphragm)

* Oral contraceptive pills

* Pregnancy

* Menopause

Criteria to diagnose PID:

Any one of the minimum criteria + 1 or more additional criteria are required for the clinical diagnosis of PID.

Minimum criteria

*

* Lower abdominal tenderness

* Adnexal tenderness

* Cervical motion tenderness.

Additional criteria

*

* Oral temperature >38.3 oC

* Mucopurulent cervical or vaginal discharge and cervical friability

* Presence of abundant WBC on saline microscopy of vaginal fluid

* Raised ESR or CRP

* Laboratory documentation of positive cervical infection with Gonorrhea or C.trachomatis.

The definitive diagnosis of PID is through:

* Histopathologic evidence of endometritis on biopsy.

* Imaging (TVS/MRI) evidence of thickened fluid-filled tubes i.e., tubo-ovarian abscess.

* Laparoscopic evidence of PID.

Treatment

* OPD management of PID:

* Inj.Ceftriaxone 250 mg IM single dose + Doxycycline 100 mg BD x 14 days + Metronidazole 500 mg BD x 14 days.

* Parenteral treatment for PID (in hospitalised:

* Inj Cefotetan 2g IV BD + Doxycycline 100 mg BD or

* Inj Cefoxitin 2g IV QID + Doxycycline 100 mg BD.

To minimize disease transmission, women should be instructed to abstain from sexual intercourse until therapy is completed, symptoms have resolved, and partners have been adequately treated.

Sexually transmitted: Gonococcus, Chlamydia, Mycoplasma, Trichomonas
Aerobes: Staphylococci , Streptococci ,E. coli

Anaerobes: Bacteroides fragilis, Peptococcus, Clostridium, Actinomyces (IUD)

Others: Tubercular salpingitis

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Exclusive breastfeeding is recommended for __________________.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 6 months

Exclusive breastfeeding is recommended for 6 months.

Breastfeeding should be started as soon as possible after birth. For an infant to be called exclusively breastfed, pre-lacteal feeds and even water are not to be given. However, giving vitamin drops, if indicated, is included under the definition of exclusive breastfeeding.

Complementary foods rich in iron and other micronutrients should be introduced at about 6 months of age. Breastfeeding should be continued for at least the first year and beyond, as long as the mother and child mutually agree.
questions.learning: 6 months Exclusive breastfeeding is recommended for 6 months. Breastfeeding should be started as soon as possible after birth.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 65-year-old woman presents with vaginal bleeding 10 years after attaining menopause and has no significant past medical history. What is the most common cause of postmenopausal bleeding in this patient?
questions.explanation: A 65-year-old woman with postmenopausal bleeding (PMB) must always be evaluated for malignancy. Although endometrial atrophy is the most common cause worldwide, it is not given in the options. In Indian exam context, the most important and commonly emphasized cause of PMB is carcinoma cervix. Cervical cancer is highly prevalent in India and often presents with: 1. Postmenopausal bleeding 2. Postcoital bleeding (most common presentation) 3. Foul-smelling discharge Because of its high incidence and clinical importance, examiners frequently consider it the most likely cause of PMB when atrophy is not listed. Why other options are incorrect: (B) Decubitus ulcer → Rare, associated with prolapse (C) Tubercular endometritis → Uncommon cause (D) Hormone replacement therapy → Recognized cause but less common than malignancy
questions.learning: A 65-year-old woman with postmenopausal bleeding (PMB) must always be evaluated for malignancy. Although endometrial atrophy is the most common cause worldwide, it is not given in the options.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A woman arrived at the hospital with edema, visual disturbances, and heart failure after consuming a food item purchased from a seller who has now been arrested for food adulteration. Which of the following is the most likely food adulterant used? Beta-oxalyl amino alanine (BOAA)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Sanguinarine

The clinical presentation of edema, visual disturbances, and heart failure after consuming a food item purchased from a seller who has now been arrested for food adulteration is suggestive of epidemic dropsy. Sanguinarine is the toxic compound responsible for this.

Sanguinarine causes Epidemic Dropsy.

* Contamination of mustard oil with argemone oil.

* Toxic compound: Sanguinarine

Mechanism of action : Sanguinarine interfers with the oxidation of pyruvic acid which in turn accumulates in the blood and causes symptoms.

Clinical presentation: The patient presents with sudden onset, non-inflammatory swelling of bilateral legs which is often associated with diarrhoea. Some patients can develop glaucoma. Dyspnea, cardiac failure and death can occur in later stages.

Tests to detect argemone oil:

* Nitric acid test

* Paper chromatography: most sensitive(can detect very low concentration of argemone oil)

Other options:

Option A: Aflatoxins are produced by certain fungi, such as Aspergillus flavus and Aspergillus parasiticus, are the most potent hepatotoxins. These fungi can contaminate food grains such as groundnut, maize, parboiled rice, sorghum, wheat, and tapioca. It is mainly due to improper storage. It can be prevented by proper storage after drying. Moisture content should be kept below 10%. They do not cause the symptoms described in the question.

Option C: Lathyrism is a paralyzing disease of humans and animals and Beta-oxalyl amino alanine (BOAA) is the toxic compound causing this disease. Gradual spastic paralysis of lower limbs is associated with the consumption of Khesari dal/Lathyrus sativus leading to neurolathyrism.

Option D: Rapidly developing ascites and jaundice is associated with the consumption of millets contaminated with weed seeds of Crotalaria/Jhunjhunia which contain a toxic pyrrolizidine alkaloid and produce symptoms of endemic ascites, that manifest as rapidly developing ascites and jaundice.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text:
A couple presents to the infertility clinic with a normal hysterosalpingogram and a semen analysis report with azoospermia. Which of the following is the next best test to differentiate between an obstructive and a testicular cause of azoospermia?

FSH- Follicle-stimulating hormone, LH- Luteinizing hormone
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Serum FSH levels

Serum FSH level is the next best test to differentiate between an obstructive and a testicular cause of azoospermia. FSH is the main hormone stimulating the production of sperm in the testis and has the highest specificity and sensitivity among hormonal assays while differentiating between obstructive and non-obstructive azoospermia.

The absence of sperm in semen is known as azoospermia. It can be due to:

• Pre-testicular azoospermia due to a hypothalamic or pituitary abnormality (hypogonadotropic-hypogonadism)
• Testicular failure or non-obstructive azoospermia
• Post-testicular obstruction implies normal spermatogenesis but failure to deliver the sperm into the ejaculate because of ductal obstruction.

The algorithm for differentiating the causes of normal semen volume azoospermia is as follows:

• A low FSH level indicates pituitary or hypothalamic failure
• A high FSH level denotes primary gonadal failure or testicular cause
• A normal FSH level could be due to either non-obstructive or obstructive azoospermia. A testicular biopsy is usually required in such people to provide a definitive diagnosis.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A researcher finds out a sensitive test to be positive for a person. For diagnosis, which of the following will hold true?
options: It confirms that the person does not have the disease
It suggests that if the disease is rare, the person surely has the disease
It confirms that the person has the disease if the disease is common
It is an expected finding in case the disease is prevalent
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. It confirms that the person has the disease if the disease is common

A sensitive test, if it is positive it confirms that the person has the disease if the disease is common.

The sensitivity of a screening test is the ability of the test to identify correctly those who have the disease. In other words, Sensitivity is the ability of a test to detect true positives (TP) out of total disease (TP+FN).

Sensitivity = TP/ TP+FN
questions.learning: It confirms that the person has the disease if the disease is common A sensitive test, if it is positive it confirms that the person has the disease if the disease is common.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is the best study design to demonstrate the relationship between cause and effect?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Cohort study

Cohort study is the best study design to demonstrate the relationship between cause and effect.

A cohort study is a type of analytical study, which progresses from cause to effect, as exposure has occurred but not disease. It is also known as forward-looking study, incidence study, prospective study, and longitudinal study.

A well-designed cohort study is considered the most reliable means of showing an association between a cause or suspected risk factor and subsequent disease (or effect) because it eliminates many of the problems of the case-control study.

Relative risk (RR) calculated using cohort study demonstrates the relationship between cause and effect. It is a direct measure of the strength of association between suspected cause and effect. The larger the RR, the greater the strength of the association between the suspected factor and disease.

The advantages of cohort study are the following:

• The incidence can be calculated.
• Several possible outcomes related to exposure can be studied simultaneously.
• Provides a direct estimate of relative risk.
• Dose-response ratios can be calculated.
• Bias like misclassification can be minimized.

Other options:

Option A: In a case-control study, the study begins from the outcome and goes retrospectively to find out the exposure among the cases and controls.

Option C: A cross-sectional study is a prevalence study which is more useful for the study of chronic diseases. It is more appropriate for the study of the distribution of a disease in a population than studying its etiology.

Option D: Clinical trials are research studies performed on people that are aimed at evaluating new tests and treatments and their effects on human health outcomes.
questions.learning: Cohort study Cohort study is the best study design to demonstrate the relationship between cause and effect. A cohort study is a type of analytical study, which progresses from cause to effect, as exposure has occurred but not disease.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A patient presents to the emergency department after a road traffic accident. Although his vital signs are stable, he is unable to speak. He has no other neurological deficits, can write normally, and comprehends spoken instructions, responding appropriately by nodding. Based on these findings, where is the most likely site of the brain lesion?
questions.explanation: The patient demonstrates symptoms of Broca’s aphasia, also known as expressive or non-fluent aphasia. Key features include the inability to produce speech despite knowing what to say and having intact comprehension. The preservation of handwriting abilities and the ability to follow spoken commands rule out more global cognitive deficits or sensory aphasias. Broca's area is located in the posterior part of the inferior frontal gyrus (Brodmann areas 44 and 45) of the dominant hemisphere. Wernicke's area (Option B) involvement would cause fluent but meaningless speech with poor comprehension. Lesions in the primary motor cortex (Option C) would typically cause physical paralysis (hemiplegia) rather than an isolated speech deficit. Brainstem lesions (Option D) usually result in multiple cranial nerve palsies or altered consciousness. Therefore, the clinical focus on motor speech production with preserved comprehension identifies Broca's area as the lesion site
questions.learning: The patient demonstrates symptoms of Broca’s aphasia, also known as expressive or non-fluent aphasia. Key features include the inability to produce speech despite knowing what to say and having intact comprehension.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: 'c' wave in JVP is seen in
options: Slow filling at end of diastole
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Iso-volumetric contraction

'c' waves are produced by bulging of the tricuspid valve into the right atrium during the Iso-volumetric contraction of the right ventricle.
questions.learning: Iso-volumetric contraction 'c' waves are produced by bulging of the tricuspid valve into the right atrium during the Iso-volumetric contraction of the right ventricle.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 24-year-old male presents to the outpatient clinic with fever, sore throat, rash, and generalized lymphadenopathy 10 days after unprotected sexual exposure. Acute retroviral syndrome is suspected. The clinician wants to make an early diagnosis before seroconversion occurs. Which test should be ordered first to identify HIV infection at this stage?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. HIV RNA PCR (NAT)

During acute HIV infection (acute retroviral syndrome), symptoms such as fever, sore throat, rash, and lymphadenopathy occur before seroconversion, when HIV antibodies are not yet detectable.

Earliest detectable marker:

• HIV RNA by PCR (Nucleic Acid Test – NAT) detects viral RNA within \~7–10 days after infection, making it the most sensitive test during the window period.

Sequence of HIV markers after infection:

1.  HIV RNA (PCR/NAT) – earliest detection

2.  p24 antigen

3.  HIV antibodies (ELISA/Western blot)
questions.learning: HIV RNA PCR (NAT) During acute HIV infection (acute retroviral syndrome), symptoms such as fever, sore throat, rash, and lymphadenopathy occur before seroconversion, when HIV antibodies are not yet detectable.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Which among the following is the pathological basis behind refeeding syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Hypophosphatemia

Refeeding syndrome is a potentially life-threatening metabolic complication that occurs when nutrition is rapidly reintroduced after prolonged starvation or severe malnutrition. The resulting insulin surge drives phosphate, potassium, and magnesium into cells, with hypophosphatemia being the hallmark and primary pathological abnormality.

• Hypophosphatemia is the cardinal biochemical feature of refeeding syndrome.
• Phosphate is rapidly utilized for ATP, 2,3-BPG, and phosphorylated intermediates during renewed carbohydrate metabolism, leading to profound depletion.

Why not the other options?

• A. Hypokalemia: Commonly occurs due to intracellular shift but is secondary, not the defining abnormality.
• B. Hypocalcemia: May occur occasionally but is not the characteristic feature.
• C. Hyponatremia: Can develop due to fluid retention but is not the pathological basis of refeeding syndrome.
questions.learning: Hypophosphatemia Refeeding syndrome is a potentially life-threatening metabolic complication that occurs when nutrition is rapidly reintroduced after prolonged starvation or severe malnutrition.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: After reaching an equilibrium state during exercising, it was found that the body was consuming oxygen at the rate of 1500 ml/min. Calculate the MET score if the baseline oxygen consumption at rest is 250 ml/min.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 6

The MET score in the given scenario is 6.

One metabolic equivalent (MET) is defined as the amount of oxygen consumed while sitting at rest.

Normally, one MET= 3.5 ml O2 /kg body weight/min

In the above question, the baseline O2 consumption at rest is given as 250 ml/min. According to the definition of one MET, we can deduce that the given 250ml/min is one MET.

O2 consumption at reaching equilibrium during exercise= 1500ml/min

MET score= O2 consumption during exercise/ one MET

= 1500/250

= 6

The MET concept represents a simple, practical, and easily understandable procedure for expressing the energy cost of physical activities as a multiple of the resting metabolic rate. If the MET score is low, it means that the activity requires less oxygen compared to an activity that has a higher MET score. Eg. Gardening requires around 3-7 METS compared to that jogging that may need around 9-11 METS. We can classify activities as light, moderate or heavy, depending on MET scores. It can also be used to identify the functional capacity of a patient.
questions.learning: 6 The MET score in the given scenario is 6. One metabolic equivalent (MET) is defined as the amount of oxygen consumed while sitting at rest.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which vitamin, when infused in supraphysiological doses, causes macular edema and macular cysts?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Vitamin B3

Macular cysts and edema may develop in patients due to the infusion of supraphysiological doses of vitamin B3 (niacin toxicity).

The toxic effects of niacin include:

• Flushing associated with skin dryness, itching, paresthesia, and headache is seen. These effects may be seen with even a low dose of 30mg/day. Pre-medication with aspirin alleviates these symptoms as these symptoms are mediated by prostaglandins.
• Macular edema and macular cysts
• Nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain.
• Hepatic toxicity presents as jaundice with elevated AST and ALT levels.
• Fulminant hepatitis requiring liver transplantation.
• Glucose intolerance
• Hyperuricemia

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A diabetic patient presents to you with visual acuity of 6/9 in one eye. Further investigations revealed pre-retinal hemorrhages with neovascularization at the optic disc. What is the next step in management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Pan-retinal photocoagulation

The clinical vignette is suggestive of proliferative diabetic retinopathy with high-risk characteristics and the next step in management is pan-retinal photocoagulation.

Diabetic retinopathy is used to describe retinal changes seen in diabetic patients. It is classified into the following types:

• Non-proliferative diabetic retinopathy (NPDR)
• Proliferative diabetic retinopathy (PDR)
• Diabetic maculopathy
• Advanced diabetic eye disease

Fundoscopy in NPDR reveals hard exudates, cotton-wool spots, and microaneurysms. Hard exudates are small, discrete yellowish, waxy areas with crenated margins.

Proliferative diabetic retinopathy is marked by NVD or NVE which is the hallmark of the condition. Condensation of connective tissue surrounding the newly formed vessels results in the formation of a fibrovascular epiretinal membrane. Vitreous detachment and hemorrhage may also occur. Preretinal hemorrhages are considered a high-risk characteristic. In addition, changes seen in NPDR may also be present.

The condition usually develops 25 years after the onset of the disease. Hence, it is more commonly seen in patients with type I diabetes.

The image below shows NVD.

PDR with high-risk characteristics is managed with pan-retinal photocoagulation. Laser treatment helps by inhibiting the release of vascular endothelial growth factors (VEGF). Anti-VEGFs are recommended before pan-retinal photocoagulation in patients with PDR.

Diabetic maculopathy can be classified as:

• Focal exudative maculopathy: Microaneursysms, hard exudates, and hemorrhages can be seen.
• Diffuse exudative maculopathy: Diffuse retinal edema with few hard exudates.
• Ischemic maculopathy: Microaneursysms, hemorrhages, few hard exudates. Fluorescein angiography reveals areas of non-perfusion.
• Mixed maculopathy: Features of both exudative and ischemic maculopathy.

An FFA image showing features of macular ischemia is given below.

Other options:

Option A: Focal laser photocoagulation is the treatment of choice for focal diabetic macular edema (DME) that does not involve the fovea.

Option C: Grid laser photocoagulation can be used in diffuse DME not responding to anti-VEGFs and intravitreal steroids.

Option D: Scleral buckling can be used in cases of advanced PDR with tractional retinal detachment.
questions.learning: Pan-retinal photocoagulation — The clinical vignette is suggestive of proliferative diabetic retinopathy with high-risk characteristics and the next step in management is pan-retinal photocoagulation.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: GI Hepatobiliary System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 42-year-old male patient presented with jaundice. His AST was 48 U, ALT was 51 U, ALP, GGT were normal. Ultrasound of liver was suggestive of cirrhosis. Viral markers were done and the following results were obtained. What is the next best step? Anti-HAV: Negative Anti-HBeAg: Negative Anti-HBcAg IgG: Positive Anti-HBcAg IgM: Negative HBsAg: Negative Anti-HbsAg: Positive Anti-HCV: Positive
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. RT-PCR for hepatitis C virus

Anti-HCV positivity indicates exposure to hepatitis C virus but does not confirm active infection.

The next step is to detect viral RNA using RT-PCR to determine whether there is ongoing viral replication.

• Anti-HAV negative → no evidence of hepatitis A infection.
• HBsAg negative with anti-HBs positive and anti-HBc IgG positive → past hepatitis B infection with immunity.
• Anti-HCV positive → prior exposure to hepatitis C.

Since hepatitis C antibodies can persist even after viral clearance, confirmation of active infection requires detection of HCV RNA.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 55-year-old man undergoing a routine health checkup is found to have hepatomegaly and an abnormally dark skin pigmentation despite minimal sun exposure. A liver biopsy has been performed, and the histological image is provided. Based on these findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The combination of hepatomegaly and an unusually dark complexion (often described as "bronze diabetes" when combined with pancreatic damage) is the classic clinical presentation of hemochromatosis. Hemochromatosis is an iron-overload disorder where excessive iron is deposited in various organs. The provided liver biopsy image shows hepatocytes filled with golden-brown granules, which are hemosiderin deposits. Wilson's disease (Option A) involves copper accumulation and would not cause a "tan". Autoimmune hepatitis (Option B) presents with lymphocytic infiltration rather than pigment deposits. Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency (Option C) is characterized by periodic acid-Schiff (PAS)-positive diastase-resistant globules in the liver. Because the clinical triad of liver enlargement and skin hyperpigmentation, matched with microscopic iron deposits, is specific to iron overload, hemochromatosis is the most likely diagnosis
questions.learning: The combination of hepatomegaly and an unusually dark complexion (often described as "bronze diabetes" when combined with pancreatic damage) is the classic clinical presentation of hemochromatosis.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Functional residual capacity is:
options: Volume that remains after forced expiration
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Expiratory reserve volume + residual volume

Functional Residual Capacity (FRC) is expiratory reserve volume + residual volume.

From the picture given below, (FRC = ERV + RV).

Lung Capacities:

The total lung capacity can be broken down into alternative capacities that help to define functioning lungs.

• The vital lung capacity refers to the maximum amount of air expired from the fully inflated lung or maximum inspiratory level.
• The inspiratory capacity is the maximum amount of air inspired from the end-expiratory level.
• The functional residual capacity represents the volume of the air remaining in the lungs after expiration of a normal breath.
questions.learning: Expiratory reserve volume + residual volume Functional Residual Capacity (FRC) is expiratory reserve volume + residual volume. From the picture given below, (FRC = ERV + RV).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A patient with a pituitary adenoma compressing the optic chiasma presents with visual field loss. Which specific visual field defect is most likely to be observed in this patient?
questions.explanation: The optic chiasm contains the crossing fibers originating from the nasal retina of both eyes. These nasal retinal fibers are responsible for detecting the temporal (outer) fields of vision. A pituitary adenoma typically enlarges and compresses the central portion of the chiasm from below. This pressure disrupts the crossing nasal fibers, leading to a loss of the temporal visual fields in both eyes, a condition known as bitemporal hemianopia. Homonymous hemianopia (Option C) and homonymous anopia (Option B) result from lesions in the optic tract or radiations, where corresponding halves of the visual field are lost (e.g., both right fields). Quadrantanopia (Option D) occurs with partial lesions of the optic radiations in the temporal or parietal lobes. Thus, bitemporal field loss is the classic sign of a chiasmal lesion
questions.learning: The optic chiasm contains the crossing fibers originating from the nasal retina of both eyes. These nasal retinal fibers are responsible for detecting the temporal (outer) fields of vision.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: If a patient tests positive for a disease, which of the following represents the probability of her actually having the disease?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Positive predictive value

Positive predictive value implies the probability of a person with a positive test, actually having the disease.

It is the ability of a test to detect true positive(TP) out of total positive(TP+FP) and it is directly proportional to the prevalence of a disease.

PPV= TP/TP+FP

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: The maternal use of which of the following hormones is most likely to cause hypospadias in a male child? (NEET PG 2016)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Diethylstilbestrol

Diethylstilbestrol (DES) is a synthetic estrogen that was historically used during pregnancy and is associated with congenital abnormalities of the reproductive tract.

Maternal exposure to DES during pregnancy can cause:

• Hypospadias and cryptorchidism in male offspring
• Vaginal clear cell adenocarcinoma in female offspring
• Uterine and cervical malformations
• Infertility and pregnancy complications

Hypospadias occurs due to abnormal fusion of the urethral folds during male genital development, which can result from estrogenic endocrine disruption during fetal life.

Why other options are incorrect:

• Tolbutamide → sulfonylurea used in diabetes
• Clomiphene → ovulation induction agent
• Clonazepam → benzodiazepine associated mainly with CNS depression/withdrawal effects
questions.learning: Diethylstilbestrol Diethylstilbestrol (DES) is a synthetic estrogen that was historically used during pregnancy and is associated with congenital abnormalities of the reproductive tract.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following elements is not considered a microelement (trace element) required in very small quantities for normal human health?
questions.explanation: In human nutrition, elements are classified based on the required daily intake. Calcium is classified as a macroelement (or macromineral) because the body requires it in large amounts (typically ) for bone structure, muscle contraction, and nerve signaling. In contrast, Copper (Option A), Zinc (Option B), and Selenium (Option D) are all microelements (trace elements). These are essential for health but are required only in minute quantities (typically ), usually acting as cofactors for specific enzymes. Other macroelements include sodium, potassium, and magnesium. Other microelements include iron, iodine, and manganese. Understanding this distinction is vital for clinical nutrition; macroelement deficiencies often manifest with structural or major electrolyte issues, while trace element deficiencies typically present with specific metabolic or enzymatic dysfunctions. Therefore, due to its high daily requirement and structural role in the skeleton, calcium is definitively not a trace element
questions.learning: In human nutrition, elements are classified based on the required daily intake. Calcium is classified as a macroelement (or macromineral) because the body requires it in large amounts (typically ) for bone structure, muscle contraction, and nerve signaling.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: During a routine pediatric examination, a 5-month-old infant is observed to actively look at the mother’s face and show interest and recognition while she talks. At what age is this social–visual milestone normally achieved?
questions.explanation: Recognizing the mother's face and responding with interest or anticipation is a significant social milestone normally achieved at 3 months of age. At this stage, the infant also demonstrates social engagement and may begin "cooing" in response to speech. Regarding the distractors, a social smile appears earlier, typically at 2 months (Option A). By 6 months (Option C), the infant progresses to recognizing strangers and developing "stranger anxiety". By 9 months (Option D), milestones include waving "bye-bye" and using pincer grasp. Since the behavior described involves the specific recognition and engagement with a primary caregiver (mother), 3 months is the standard developmental expectation. Correct assessment of these milestones is essential for the early detection of neurodevelopmental delays
questions.learning: Recognizing the mother's face and responding with interest or anticipation is a significant social milestone normally achieved at 3 months of age. At this stage, the infant also demonstrates social engagement and may begin "cooing" in response to speech.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A farmer presents with a painful snakebite on his right foot, showing two distinct fang marks along with swelling and bleeding at the site. What should be the first step in the management of this patient?
options: Sling or splint leading to immobilization
See the snake brought by a relative
questions.explanation: The first step in the immediate management of a snakebite in the field or upon arrival at a clinic is the immobilization of the affected limb using a sling or splint. This is critical to slow the systemic absorption of venom through the lymphatic system, which is accelerated by muscle movement. The patient should be kept calm and moved as little as possible. Polyvalent Anti-Snake Venom (ASV) (Option A) is the definitive treatment but is only administered once signs of systemic envenomation or severe local effects are confirmed. Venom suction (Option C), cutting the wound, or applying a tourniquet are obsolete and harmful practices that increase local tissue damage. Trying to see or identify the snake (Option D) often leads to dangerous delays or additional bites. Immobilization is the most effective first-aid measure to prevent the rapid spread of toxins until life-saving ASV can be safely administered
questions.learning: The first step in the immediate management of a snakebite in the field or upon arrival at a clinic is the immobilization of the affected limb using a sling or splint.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following is the drug of choice (DOC) for treating morning sickness in pregnant women?
questions.explanation: Pyridoxine (Vitamin B6) is the first-line pharmacological treatment for mild to moderate nausea and vomiting of pregnancy (morning sickness). It is often used alone or in a fixed-dose combination with the antihistamine doxylamine. This combination is the only FDA-approved medication specifically for this indication and has an excellent safety profile. Domperidone (Option B) and Metoclopramide (Option D) are prokinetic agents used as second-line therapy for more severe or refractory cases. Ondansetron (Option C), a serotonin antagonist, is highly effective for severe nausea but is generally reserved for patients who have failed first-line therapies, partly due to controversial data regarding a slight increase in the risk of oral clefts if used in the first trimester. Therefore, for initial drug therapy in uncomplicated morning sickness, Pyridoxine remains the gold standard
questions.learning: Pyridoxine (Vitamin B6) is the first-line pharmacological treatment for mild to moderate nausea and vomiting of pregnancy (morning sickness). It is often used alone or in a fixed-dose combination with the antihistamine doxylamine.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: Codman's triangle is seen in which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation: Codman's triangle is a pathognomonic radiological sign of an aggressive or malignant bone lesion. It appears when a rapidly growing tumor lifts the periosteum away from the bone cortex, leaving a triangular area of new subperiosteal bone at the margin of the lesion. This is most classically seen in Osteogenic sarcoma (Osteosarcoma), the most common primary malignant bone tumor in children. While it can occasionally be seen in aggressive osteomyelitis (Option A), the "sunburst" appearance and Codman's triangle are hallmarks of osteosarcoma. Aneurysmal bone cysts (Option B) typically show a "soap-bubble" appearance with an intact, though thinned, cortex. Chondrosarcomas (Option D) are cartilage-forming malignant tumors that may show "popcorn" calcifications rather than the specific periosteal reaction of Codman's triangle. Recognizing this sign is critical as it indicates a highly invasive process requiring urgent biopsy and staging to determine the appropriate oncological management

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which among the following is the false statement regarding statins?
options: Although HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors substantially reduce the risk of cardiovascular events, there is mild increase in lipoprotein a (Lpa) levels.
These drugs should not be stopped even in severe conditions like injury, surgery, etc.
They can be given with verapamil and other enzyme inhibitors.
With the long term use, there is slight increase in the incidence of type 2 diabetes mellitus.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. They can be given with verapamil and other enzyme inhibitors.

The false statement regarding statins is that they can be given with verapamil and other enzyme inhibitors.

Statins like atorvastatin and rosuvastatin are metabolized by the cytochrome 3A4 enzymes of the liver. Verapamil is a cytochrome 3A4 inhibitor and may interfere with statin degradation. This leads to an increase in serum statin levels. The most important feature of statin toxicity is myopathy. It can present as myalgia but can sometimes also lead to fatal rhabdomyolysis.

Statins are the most commonly used hypolipidemic drugs. Statins act by inhibiting the rate-limiting HMG-CoA reductase enzyme, which in turn inhibits cholesterol synthesis. They decrease levels of low-density lipoproteins (LDL) and triglycerides and increase the levels of high-density lipoproteins (HDL) in plasma.

Other options:

Option A: Lipoprotein (lp) a is an LDL molecule that has apolipoprotein b and an additional apolipoprotein a. Studies indicate that these molecules are atherogenic and may independently cause cardiovascular disease. Although HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors substantially reduce the risk of cardiovascular events, there is a mild increase in lipoprotein a levels.

Option B: Statins can be continued during surgery. These drugs have proved to decrease overall mortality due to cardiovascular events. Statins also influence inflammatory responses and can be safely used in trauma.

Option D: Chronic administration of high statin doses also leads to an increased incidence of type 2 diabetes mellitus.
questions.learning: They can be given with verapamil and other enzyme inhibitors. The false statement regarding statins is that they can be given with verapamil and other enzyme inhibitors.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which criteria is not included in the definition of severe NPDR?
questions.explanation: The international clinical grading for Severe Non-Proliferative Diabetic Retinopathy (NPDR) follows the "4-2-1 rule". A patient is classified as having severe NPDR if they meet any one of the following criteria: 1. More than 20 intraretinal hemorrhages in each of the four quadrants (Option B). 2. Definite venous beading in two or more quadrants (Option D). 3. Prominent Intra-Retinal Microvascular Abnormalities (IRMA) in one or more quadrants. Microaneurysms (Option A) are the earliest sign of NPDR and are present in all stages, but their specific count in all quadrants is not the primary diagnostic threshold for "severe" compared to the 4-2-1 rule. Venous looping (Option C) is a common vascular change in diabetes, but it is not one of the specific criteria used in the 4-2-1 rule to define the "severe" stage. Recognizing severe NPDR is critical because these patients have a very high risk of progressing to Proliferative Diabetic Retinopathy (PDR) within one year. Close monitoring and timely pan-retinal photocoagulation (PRP) can prevent severe vision loss in these high-risk individuals

questions.text: Which one of the following is not a feature in cerebral palsy?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Flaccid paralysis

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Giving TPN (total para-enteral nutrition) in a patient in ICU with metabolic syndrome predisposes to:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Hyperglycaemia

Concept: TPN (Total Parenteral Nutrition)  contains a high amount of glucose as its main energy source.

In patients with metabolic syndrome:

• There is insulin resistance
• Cells cannot utilize glucose efficiently

So when large amounts of glucose are infused via TPN, the result is: hyperglycaemia.

Complications of TPN

| Complication | Reason

| ------------ | ------

| Hyperglycaemia | High glucose infusion

| Infection | Central venous catheter

| Electrolyte imbalance | Rapid metabolic shifts

| Refeeding syndrome | Sudden feeding in malnourished patients

| Liver dysfunction | Long-term TPN

Why other options are wrong

B. Reactive hypoglycaemia

Occurs with excess insulin, not with TPN.

C. Hyperlipidaemia

TPN does contain lipids→ But:  not the primary component (glucose is)

Lipid rise is less immediate and less prominent (  As compared to glucose imbalance)

Compared to glucose imbalance, this is not the most expected/important complication.

D. Hyperuricemia

Not directly related to TPN.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient comes to the hospital with chest pain for the last 3 hours. Vitals are stable. ECG revealed ST depression and T wave inversion in anterior chest leads. Which of the following would be the most appropriate line of management in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Aspirin with heparin

Based on the given clinical scenario of a patient presenting with sudden onset of chest pain, with ECG findings of ST depression in the anterior chest leads and T wave inversion, the most likely diagnosis is a non-ST-segment elevation-acute coronary syndrome (NSTE-ACS).  The most appropriate line of management in this patient would be to administer aspirin with heparin.

Percutaneous coronary intervention is indicated after coronary angiography in high-risk patients.

Fibrinolytic therapy is not indicated in patients with NSTE-ACS.

Arrhythmia prophylaxis is generally not routinely recommended in all patients with NSTE-ACS.

Acute coronary syndrome is classified into 2 groups:

• ST-segment Elevation Myocardial Infarction (STEMI)
• NSTE-ACS

NSTE-ACS further includes:

• NSTEMI (myocyte necrosis present and cardiac troponins elevated)
• Unstable Angina (myocyte necrosis absent and cardiac troponins not elevated)

The diagnosis of NSTE-ACS is based on the following:

Severe chest discomfort with at least one of 3 features:

• Occurring at rest or minimal exertion and lasting for more than 10 minutes
• Recent onset
• Crescendo pattern

ECG showing:

• ST segment depression
• T wave inversion

Elevated cardiac troponins in case of NSTEMI.

Management of NSTE-ACS:

To provide relief of pain and discomfort, initial treatment includes bed rest, nitrates, beta blockers, and inhaled oxygen (only if arterial O2 saturation <90%).

Antithrombotic therapy consisting of antiplatelet and anticoagulant drugs:

• Dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT): Aspirin (162-325 mg) AND one ADP receptor inhibitor (Ticagrelor, clopidogrel or prasugrel)
• Anticoagulation: Enoxaparin, unfractionated heparin, fondaparinux or bivalirudin
• An early invasive strategy including diagnostic coronary angiography (within 2–72 hours of presentation) followed by revascularization (percutaneous coronary intervention/ coronary artery bypass grafting) is indicated for stabilized patients who are at high risk of coronary events (Based on TIMI, GRACE or HEART score).

questions.text: Which of the following is a water soluble contrast?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Iohexol

Iohexol is a nonionic, water-soluble radiographic contrast medium.

It is used to visualize the following structres:

• Arteries
• Veins

It can be used during computer tomography (CT scan) as well. It can be given orally, intravenously, or can be injected into the body cavity.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A girl is diagnosed with lead poisoning. Which of the following enzyme defects is the likely cause of her condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. ALA dehydratase

The enzyme defective in lead intoxication is ALA dehydratase.

The most common cause of lead poisoning in children is seen due to lead paint which was used in the older times.

It is toxic because it can substitute for calcium in many fundamental cellular processes. It crosses red blood cell membranes as well as the blood-brain barrier and enters the neuroglia cells which support brain function.

The fatal dose of lead acetate is 20 g. The fatal period is 1-2 days.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which labeling is not correctly matched in the below image?
questions.explanation: The axillary artery is divided into three parts by the pectoralis minor muscle, and each part gives off specific branches. Label A identifies the superior thoracic artery, which arises from the first part. Label B identifies the thoracoacromial artery, a major branch of the second part. Label D identifies the posterior circumflex humeral artery, which arises from the third part and passes through the quadrangular space. Label C is incorrectly matched if it fails to show the subscapular artery arising from the third part and dividing into the circumflex scapular and thoracodorsal arteries. The subscapular artery is the largest branch of the axillary artery and is vital for the collateral circulation around the scapula. Surgeons must accurately identify these vessels during axillary dissections for breast cancer or shoulder surgery to avoid hemorrhage. Mislabeling these branches complicates the understanding of the vascular supply to the upper limb and thoracic wall

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A young man presents to the emergency department with complaints of severe abdominal pain and 3 episodes of vomiting in the past 9 hours. He says that the pain radiates to the back and is partially relieved by bending forwards. The abdominal radiograph of the patient is given below which shows 'colon cut-off sign". What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Acute pancreatitis

The clinial scenario and thr image showing colon cut-off sign is seen in acute pancreatitis.

The colon cut-off sign refers to the abrupt termination of the gas filling of the colon on the left side. The inflammation of acute pancreatitis may extend to the phrenicocolic ligament via the transverse mesocolon. This causes functional spasm of the splenic flexure resulting in the colon cut-off sign.

Acute pancreatitis:

Causes of pancreatitis -

* Gallstones

* Alcoholism

* Post ERCP

* Abdominal trauma

* Following biliary, upper gastrointestinal or cardiothoracic surgery

* Ampullary tumor

* Drugs (corticosteroids, azathioprine, asparaginase, valproic acid, thiazides, estrogens)

* Hyperparathyroidism

* Hypercalcemia

* Pancreas divisum

* Autoimmune pancreatitis

* Hereditary pancreatitis

* Viral infections (mumps, coxsackie B)

* Malnutrition

* Scorpion bite

* Idiopathic

Signs and symptoms of pancreatitis-

Symptoms:

* Acute onset of epigastric pain, which is severe, constant, and refractory to usual doses of analgesics.

* Typically radiates to back

* Relieved in the sitting forward position

* Nausea, repeated vomiting, retching, and hiccups

Signs:

* Hypotension, tachycardia, and tachypnea

* Grey Turner sign: bluish discoloration of the flanks

* Cullen’s sign: bluish discoloration around the umbilicus

* Pleural effusion (left > right): dullness on percussion, decreased breath sounds

Grey turner sign is given below:

Cullen's sign is given below:

Laboratory findings in acute pancreatitis: Elevated serum amylase and serum lipase

* Serum amylase level lacks specificity.

* Serum amylase levels do not correlate with the severity of pancreatitis.

* Serum lipase is more specific, and it is more useful when the patient presents 24–48 hours later.

Other features include:

* Hyperglycemia

* Hypocalcemia, hypoalbuminemia

* Leukocytosis

* Elevated serum levels of hepatic enzymes like alanine aminotransferase (ALT).

* Azotemia, due to prerenal acute renal failure in case of severe fluid loss

Management of acute pancreatitis: It involves nil per oral orders, providing fluid replacement and pain control. Antibiotics are rarely required if the infection spreads.

Pearl PF1586: X-Ray Findings in Acute Pancreatitis

Radiographic findings of acute pancreatitis are non-specific.

Sentinel loop sign: Generalized or local ileus, with isolated dilation of a segment of the gut (sentinel loop) consisting of jejunum, transverse colon, or duodenum adjacent to the pancreas

Colon cut-off sign: Functional spasm at the splenic flexure due to the extension of inflammation to phrenicocolic ligament via transverse mesocolon.

Renal halo sign: Edema around the kidney due to the involvement of paranephric fat resulting in:

* Obliteration of psoas shadow

* Localised ground-glass appearance
