questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Dohlman's procedure is used for the treatment of which condition?
questions.explanation: Dohlman’s procedure is a specialized endoscopic surgical technique used to treat Zenker’s diverticulum (Option B), a pharyngeal pouch that occurs at Killian's dehiscence. The procedure involves using a double-lipped endoscope to visualize the common wall between the diverticulum and the esophagus. This wall, which contains the cricopharyngeus muscle, is then divided using electrocautery or a laser. This "stapling" or division converts the pouch and the esophagus into a single cavity, preventing food entrapment and relieving dysphagia. Meckel's diverticulum (Option A) is an intestinal anomaly requiring abdominal resection. Bochdalek hernia (Option C) is a congenital diaphragmatic hernia treated with abdominal or thoracic repair. Menetrier’s disease (Option D) is a rare hypertrophic gastropathy involving the stomach. Because Dohlman’s is an endoscopic approach to a pharyngeal pouch, Zenker’s diverticulum is the correct clinical association. It offers a shorter recovery time compared to open diverticulectomy
questions.learning: Dohlman’s procedure is a specialized endoscopic surgical technique used to treat Zenker’s diverticulum (Option B), a pharyngeal pouch that occurs at Killian's dehiscence.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 5-year-old child presented with a history of edema of the face which later progressed to generalised edema. Urine showed massive proteinuria and light microscopy was normal. Electron microscopy showed effacement of podocyte foot processes. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Minimal change disease

This case of nephrotic syndrome shows effacement of the podocyte foot processes which is characteristic of minimal change disease (MCD).

Minimal change disease is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome. It is seen in ages 2-6 years with a clinical picture of nephrotic syndrome, that is, heavy proteinuria, oedema, hypoalbuminemia and hyperlipidemia. They may be asymptomatic or can present with peripheral oedema.

A renal biopsy is not required for confirmation and treatment can be initiated if the child fits the standard clinical picture of nephrotic syndrome. Light microscopy shows normal glomeruli and electron microscopy shows effacement of podocyte foot processes.

They show excellent response to steroid therapy with prednisone or prednisolone. A daily dose of 60 mg/m2/day for 6 weeks, followed by a single dose of 40 mg/m2 on alternate days for the next 6 weeks is the standard treatment.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A 35-year-old man presents with epistaxis, bleeding gums, and multiple ecchymoses. Laboratory investigations show hemoglobin of 8.5 g/dL, a platelet count of 12,000/µL, and a total leukocyte count of 52,000/µL with 83% blasts that are CD33-positive on flow cytometry. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The patient presents with signs of bone marrow failure (anemia, severe thrombocytopenia causing bleeding) and a high white blood cell count (leukocytosis). The presence of 83% blasts is diagnostic of an acute leukemia (threshold is ). The critical differentiating factor is the flow cytometry result showing CD33+. CD33 is a myeloid-specific marker, confirming Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML). Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia (ALL) (Option B) would typically express B-cell (CD19, CD20) or T-cell markers. Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia (CLL) (Option C) involves mature-looking lymphocytes and lacks a high blast count. Myelodysplastic Syndrome (MDS) (Option D) features cytopenias and dysplasia but by definition has fewer than 20% blasts. AML is common in adults and requires urgent induction chemotherapy. The clinical picture of bleeding gums and nosebleeds often points toward the M3 subtype (APL) or monocytic subtypes, but CD33 positivity broadly confirms the myeloid lineage
questions.learning: The patient presents with signs of bone marrow failure (anemia, severe thrombocytopenia causing bleeding) and a high white blood cell count (leukocytosis).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Revised A young sheep farmer presents to the OPD with pain in the right upper part of the abdomen. On examination, there is tenderness and enlargement of the liver. Blood investigations show eosinophilia, elevated liver enzymes, and abdominal ultrasound is as below. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hydatid cyst

The clinical vignette along with the ultrasound image showing multiple septations and rosette or honeycomb appearance is diagnostic of active hydatid cyst.

Hydatid cyst:

Echinococcus granulosus is the most common causative agent in hydatid cysts, while Echinococcus multilocularis and Echinococcus ligartus account for a small number of cases.

The hydatid cyst usually develops three weeks after the infection. The cyst is surrounded by a fibrous capsule called the pericyst that is derived from the host tissue.

The cyst wall is composed of two layers, ectocyst (outer gelatinous membrane), and endocyst (inner germinal membrane). Ectocyst is a laminated membrane, which is acellular. It helps in the passage of nutrients. The endocyst helps in producing the laminated membrane and scoleces.

The brood capsules are cellular masses in the hydatid fluid which consists of scoleces. In a definitive host, these scoleces develop into adult tapeworm while in the intermediate hosts these develop into new hydatid cysts. The brood capsules are attached to the endocyst by a pedicle or stalk. The brood capsules may mature and detach from the mother cyst and become the daughter cysts, which are an exact replica of the mother cysts.

The freed brood capsules and scoleces present in the hydatid fluid are called hydatid sand.

The image attached below shows the C.S of hydatid cyst.

Investigations:

Computed tomography (CT) scan is the best imaging modality for hydatid cyst. It shows the presence of a space-occupying lesion with a smooth outline with septa.

CT scan has an accuracy of 98% in the detection of hydatid cysts and higher sensitivity to demonstrate the daughter cysts and extra-hepatic cysts.
The indirect hemagglutination test and enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) have a sensitivity of 80% overall and are the initial screening tests of choice.

Note:

* First/Initial imaging test: USG

* Best imaging test: CT scan

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: What are the effects of posterior lesions in a Brodmann's area 22 in a stroke patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Receptive Speech Function

A posterior lesion in Brodmann's area 22, which is located in the superior temporal gyrus, typically affects receptive speech function. It is the sensory speech area.

The patient will most likely have Wernicke’s aphasia due to the damage to Wernicke’s area - area 22.

In Wernicke's aphasia, there is difficulty in finding words leading to poorly understood content for the listener. These patients also find it difficult to repeat sentences and name things properly. It is a type of fluent aphasia in which the speech is easy and fluent but there are difficulties related to the output of language like paraphasia (substitution of similar-sounding, non-words, or incorrect words). The speech is full of jargon and neologisms (non-existent words) that make little sense.

Other options:

Option A: Auditory Function is primarily mediated by Brodmann area 41, which is located in the primary auditory cortex within the superior temporal gyrus.

Option C: Expressive Speech Function is associated with Brodmann areas 44 and 45 (Broca's area), which are involved in language production and speech articulation. Lesions here can cause difficulty in producing coherent speech (Broca's aphasia).
Option D: Visual function primarily associated with Brodmann areas 17, 18, and 19 (the primary and secondary visual cortices).
questions.learning: Receptive Speech Function — A posterior lesion in Brodmann's area 22, which is located in the superior temporal gyrus, typically affects receptive speech function.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Which of the following mechanism is involved in X-ray production?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Bremsstrahlung radiation

Bremsstrahlung (“braking”) radiation is the principal mechanism of X-ray production. It occurs when high-speed electrons from the cathode are decelerated or deflected by the electric field of the tungsten target nucleus (anode), causing loss of kinetic energy that is emitted as X-ray photons. It accounts for approximately 85–90% of diagnostic X-rays.

The remaining 10–15% of X-rays are produced by characteristic radiation, which results from electron transitions between atomic shells after inner-shell ionization.

Why not the other options?

• A. Photoelectric effect: Interaction of X-rays with matter causing complete absorption of the photon; responsible for image contrast, not X-ray production.
• B. Compton effect: Scattering of X-rays by outer-shell electrons; a major source of image degradation and radiation exposure, not production.
• C. Pair production: Occurs only with high-energy photons (>1.02 MeV) and is not involved in diagnostic X-ray generation.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: What is the most likely diagnosis for this condition?
questions.explanation: The clinical triad of miosis (constricted pupil), mild ptosis (drooping eyelid), and anhidrosis (loss of sweating) on one side of the face is diagnostic of Horner syndrome. This syndrome results from a lesion in the sympathetic nerve pathway from the hypothalamus to the eye. The pupil remains small in dim lighting (dilation lag) because the sympathetic dilator muscle is paralyzed. Adie's tonic pupil (Option A) presents with a dilated pupil that reacts slowly to light. A blind eye (Option C) would show an afferent pupillary defect but not ptosis or anhidrosis. An Argyll Robertson pupil (Option D) is characterized by bilateral small pupils that accommodate but do not react to light, often associated with neurosyphilis. Because the patient exhibits the complete classic triad of sympathetic failure, Horner syndrome is the definitive diagnosis. Further investigation is required to locate the lesion along the first, second, or third-order neurons
questions.learning: The clinical triad of miosis (constricted pupil), mild ptosis (drooping eyelid), and anhidrosis (loss of sweating) on one side of the face is diagnostic of Horner syndrome.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which statement regarding a primary healthcare center (PHC) is incorrect?
options: There is 1 PHC per 30,000 population in plain areas.
Type A PHC conducts fewer than 20 deliveries per month.
Provides maternal and child health care, family planning, and MTP.
questions.explanation: The statement that a PHC is the first referral unit (FRU) is incorrect. In India’s public health infrastructure, the Community Health Center (CHC) is designated as the First Referral Unit, as it provides specialist services, blood storage, and emergency obstetric care that a PHC cannot. All other statements are true: there is indeed 1 PHC per 30,000 population in plain areas (and 1 per 20,000 in hilly/tribal areas) (Option A). PHCs are categorized by their delivery load, with Type A centers conducting fewer than 20 deliveries per month (Option B). PHCs serve as the primary hub for maternal and child health (MCH), family planning, and Medical Termination of Pregnancy (MTP) services (Option C). Therefore, the designation of "First Referral Unit" applies to the CHC level, not the PHC

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A patient underwent total laryngectomy for laryngeal cancer. Identify the modality of voice production in this patient shown in the image given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Tracheoesophageal prosthesis

The modality of voice production shown in the given image is a tracheoesophageal voice prosthesis.

In a tracheoesophageal prosthesis, the exhaled air from the trachea is diverted to the esophagus through a device that connects the trachea and esophagus. It has a one-way valve, which prevents food from entering into the trachea. A variety of tracheoesophageal prostheses are available including the provox, Blom-Singer, and Panje devices.

Other options:

Option A: Electrolarynx is a vibrating device that produces a low-pitched sound in the hypopharynx. It is then articulated by the palate, tongue, and teeth.

Option B: Chicago implant is a hearing aid.

Option D: In oesophageal speech, the patient is trained to swallow air and slowly release it into the pharynx. 6-10 words can be spoken in a rough manner before re-swallowing the air.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following is not amphipathic?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Triglycerides

Triglycerides are not amphipathic.

Amphipathic substances are those which have both a hydrophilic or polar region and a hydrophobic or nonpolar region.

Phosphoglycerols or glycerol-based phospholipids have a hydrophilic head which is a phosphate group with alcohol attached to it and a hydrophobic tail containing fatty acids or fatty acid-based hydrocarbons. Therefore, they are amphipathic.

Sphingolipids, like all membrane-based lipids, are amphipathic molecules having hydrophobic and hydrophilic properties.

Glycolipids are amphipathic molecules consisting of a hydrophilic oligosaccharide chain attached to a hydrophobic lipid that anchors the glycolipid in cell membranes.

But lipids like triacylglycerol and cholesteryl esters are termed neutral lipids and thus are not amphipathic.

Cholesterol is amphipathic.
questions.learning: Triglycerides Triglycerides are not amphipathic. Amphipathic substances are those which have both a hydrophilic or polar region and a hydrophobic or nonpolar region.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: At what CD count does Kaposi's sarcoma typically present?
questions.explanation: Kaposi's sarcoma (KS) is an AIDS-defining illness caused by Human Herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8). In patients with HIV, it typically presents when the immune system is significantly compromised, characterized by a CD4 count below 200 cells/mm³. While it can occasionally occur at higher CD4 counts, the risk and severity increase dramatically as the count drops below this threshold. KS manifests as violaceous, non-blanching macules, plaques, or nodules on the skin, mucous membranes, or internal organs. Higher CD4 ranges like 200-350 (Option B) or (Option D) are associated with lower risks for most opportunistic infections and malignancies. The introduction of Highly Active Antiretroviral Therapy (HAART) has significantly reduced the incidence of KS by allowing patients to maintain higher CD4 counts and suppress HIV viral loads. Treatment of KS in HIV patients primarily focuses on immune reconstitution through HAART, though local therapies or systemic chemotherapy may be required for extensive disease
questions.learning: Kaposi's sarcoma (KS) is an AIDS-defining illness caused by Human Herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8). In patients with HIV, it typically presents when the immune system is significantly compromised, characterized by a CD4 count below 200 cells/mm³.

questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Autoclave

Cold sterilization refers to sterilization methods that do not use high temperatures and are suitable for heat-sensitive materials. Cold methods are used for heat-labile instruments (e.g., endoscopes, plastics).

Cold sterilization methods:

• Plasma sterilization → uses hydrogen peroxide plasma
• Gamma rays → ionizing radiation used for disposable medical equipment
• UV rays → used for surface disinfection (limited penetration)

Not a cold sterilization method:

• Autoclave → uses moist heat under pressure (121°C), hence a heat sterilization method

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: An 8-year-old child with a known history of generalized tonic–clonic seizures presents with continuous convulsions lasting longer than 45 minutes. What is the most appropriate management in this situation?
questions.explanation: A seizure lasting more than 5 minutes (or 45 minutes in this extreme case) is defined as status epilepticus, a medical emergency. The standardized management algorithm for status epilepticus involves two stages. The first-line (emergent) treatment is a fast-acting benzodiazepine, with intravenous Lorazepam (or Diazepam/Midazolam) being the drug of choice to stop the active seizure. Once the acute seizure is controlled, the second-line (urgent) treatment involves giving a long-acting anticonvulsant to prevent recurrence, with Levetiracetam, Fosphenytoin, or Valproate being standard options. Valproate and Gabapentin (Option B) are not the initial status protocol. Carbamazepine (Option C) is used for focal seizures and is not indicated in the acute management of status. Starting with levetiracetam (Option D) is incorrect as its onset is too slow for emergency termination of an ongoing convulsion. Rapid intervention is critical to prevent neuronal damage and systemic complications from prolonged status
questions.learning: A seizure lasting more than 5 minutes (or 45 minutes in this extreme case) is defined as status epilepticus, a medical emergency. The standardized management algorithm for status epilepticus involves two stages.

questions.text: A patient recently underwent LASIK surgery for his myopia. He is now complaining of headaches and eye pain. Identify the test being performed on him.

This type of tonometer is unaffected by the corneal thickness and it is the tonometer of choice in post-Lasik patients.

Option A: Pachymetry is used to measure the corneal thickness.
The below image is of pachymetry.

Option C: Auto Refractotemetry is a computerized refractometer that is used to find out the error of refraction. This gives rapid information about the kind of refractive error in terms of sphere, cylinder with axis and inter pupillary distance.
Option D: A-Scan ultrasonography is a useful diagnostic tool for intraocular evaluation especially in the setting of opaque media. The report of the A scan is displayed as a unidimensional display of spikes along a baseline where the distance between the spikes gives the indirect measurement of the tissues. A-scan is used to measure

• The axial length of the eyeball for Intraocular lens (IOL) power calculation

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following are correct regarding activities under the Weekly Iron and Folic Acid Supplementation (WIFS) programme? 1. Administration of supervised weekly iron-folic acid supplements of 100 mg elemental iron and 500 μg folic acid. 2. Administration of supervised weekly iron-folic acid supplements of 60 mg elemental iron and 0.5 mg folic acid. 3. Biannual deworming with albendazole. 4. Annual deworming with albendazole. Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1 and 3

The Weekly Iron and Folic Acid Supplementation (WIFS) Programme is a Government of India initiative aimed at reducing the burden of iron deficiency anemia among adolescents (10–19 years) through weekly iron-folic acid supplementation and biannual deworming.

Why is B correct?

• 1. Administration of supervised weekly iron-folic acid supplements of 100 mg elemental iron and 500 μg folic acid. ✅

• WIFS recommends one tablet containing 100 mg elemental iron and 500 μg (0.5 mg) folic acid once weekly.

• 2. Administration of supervised weekly iron-folic acid supplements of 60 mg elemental iron and 0.5 mg folic acid. ❌

• 60 mg elemental iron is recommended for pregnant women under ANC programs, not under WIFS.

• 3. Biannual deworming with albendazole. ✅

• Albendazole 400 mg is administered twice yearly (every 6 months) to reduce helminthic infestation and improve iron absorption.

• 4. Annual deworming with albendazole. ❌

• WIFS recommends biannual, not annual, deworming.

questions.text: Which is the first organ to putrefy?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Brain

Among the given options, the first organ to putrefy is the brain.

The order of organ putrefaction (from first to last):

1. Larynx and trachea
2. Stomach, intestine, spleen
3. Liver and lungs
4. Brain
5. Heart
6. Kidney and the bladder
7. Prostate and uterus
8. Skin, muscle, tendons
9. Bones

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A patient presented with jaw swelling and weight loss. Suspecting a malignancy, the submandibular gland was resected. Which is the most likely nerve to be damaged during submandibular gland resection?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Lingual nerve

The most likely nerve to be damaged during submandibular gland resection is the lingual nerve.

It loops around the submandibular duct and hence is susceptible to injury during submandibular gland resection.

Course:

The lingual nerve arises from the posterior trunk of the mandibular nerve (V3 branch of the trigeminal nerve). The lingual nerve descends between the tensor veli palatini muscle and the lateral pterygoid muscle, where it is joined by the chorda tympani nerve. It then descends across the medial pterygoid muscle to enter the oral cavity. As the lingual nerve enters the floor of the oral cavity, it lies on the deep portion of the submandibular gland. It then passes into the tongue on the hyoglossus muscle where it is attached to the submandibular ganglion.

The submandibular duct lies between the lingual and hypoglossal nerves, superficial to the hyoglossus muscle. As the duct reaches the anterior border of the hyoglossus, it is crossed by the lingual nerve and lies in close proximity to the nerve. Hence lingual nerve injury is the most common.

Injury:

The lingual nerve is at risk to be injured during submandibular gland resection because dissection of the submandibular duct from the nerve is required. Also, it is connected to the submandibular ganglion which will lead to the nerve being exposed within the operating field.

The manifestations of lingual nerve injury depend on whether the lesion is proximal or distal to where it is joined by the chorda tympani nerve.

• Proximal injury: There is loss of sensation from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, gingivae, oral mucosa, lower lip, and chin.
• Distal injury: In addition to features of proximal injury, secretion from the salivary glands below the oral fissure and taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue is also lost.

Note:

The cranial nerves that are at risk during submandibular gland resection include:

• The marginal mandibular branch of the facial nerve
• Lingual nerve
• Hypoglossal nerve

Other options:

Option A: Nerve to mylohyoid is a branch of the inferior alveolar nerve and lies in the mylohyoid groove inferior to the mandibular foramen, hence the risk of injury is less.

Option B: Inferior alveolar nerve enters the mandibular canal via the mandibular foramen, hence is unlikely to be injured during submandibular gland excision.

Option D: Hypoglossal nerve injury is less common than lingual nerve injury as it only lies below and parallels to the submandibular duct.
questions.learning: Lingual nerve — The most likely nerve to be damaged during submandibular gland resection is the lingual nerve. It loops around the submandibular duct and hence is susceptible to injury during submandibular gland resection.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: What is the clinical term used to describe a 24-year-old man who exhibits an excessive and uncontrollable desire for sexual intercourse?
questions.explanation: The medical and psychiatric term for an excessive or uncontrollable sexual drive in a male is satyriasis (Option A). This condition is characterized by a persistent and abnormally high frequency of sexual urges or activity. Nymphomania (Option C) is the corresponding term historically used to describe the same condition in females. Frotteurism (Option B) is a paraphilic disorder where an individual derives sexual pleasure from rubbing against non-consenting people in crowded places. Masochism (Option D) refers to deriving pleasure from experiencing pain or humiliation. Because the question specifically identifies a 24-year-old man with an excessive craving for intercourse, satyriasis is the only gender-appropriate and clinically accurate term. In modern diagnostics, these conditions are often categorized under hypersexual disorder or compulsive sexual behavior disorder
questions.learning: The medical and psychiatric term for an excessive or uncontrollable sexual drive in a male is satyriasis (Option A). This condition is characterized by a persistent and abnormally high frequency of sexual urges or activity.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 30-year-old female presents with redness and pain in the eye. Examination revealed an IOP of 38 mm of Hg, aqueous flare, and corneal precipitates. Which of the following drugs must be avoided in her?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Prostaglandin analogs

The given clinical vignette is suggestive of anterior uveitis with a raised intraocular pressure. Among the given options, latanoprost is the least suited for use in this patient as it can result in worsening of the anterior uveitis.

Latanoprost is a PGF 2 alpha analog that acts by increasing the uveoscleral outflow and thereby lowers the intraocular pressure. Latanoprost is a prodrug and gets activated during its passage through the cornea. It acts by stimulating the prostanoid receptors on the ciliary muscles. This leads to the release of matrix metalloproteinases, which act to increases the uveoscleral outflow. It should be used with caution in those with uveitis, iritis, cystoid macular edema, and herpes simplex keratitis.

Topical prostaglandins like latanoprost, travoprost, bimatoprost, and tafluprost are now used as first-line agents to lower IOP.  The most common ocular side effects are conjunctival hyperemia, eyelash thickening, iris hyperpigmentation, and loss of periorbital fat (bimatoprost). The systemic side effects are uncommon and include occasional headache, malaise, myalgia, skin rash, and mild upper respiratory infections.
questions.learning: Prostaglandin analogs — The given clinical vignette is suggestive of anterior uveitis with a raised intraocular pressure. Among the given options, latanoprost is the least suited for use in this patient as it can result in worsening of the anterior uveitis.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Hemoglobin with iron in ferric form is _______
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Methemoglobin

Hemoglobin with iron in ferric form is methemoglobin.

Hemoglobin structure:

* Each consists of a tetramer of globin polypeptide chains: a pair of α-like chains and a pair of β-like chains.

* HbA (α2β2): Major adult hemoglobin

* HbF (α2γ2): Fetal Hemoglobin

* HbA2 (α2δ2): Minor adult hemoglobin

* Each globin chain enfolds a single heme moiety, consisting of a protoporphyrin IX ring complexed with a single iron atom in the ferrous state (Fe2+).

* Each heme moiety can bind a single oxygen molecule.

* The hemoglobin tetramer is highly soluble, but individual globin chains are insoluble.

* Unpaired globin precipitates, forming inclusions that damage the cell and can trigger apoptosis.

Methemoglobin is formed when hemoglobin is oxidized to contain iron in the ferric [Fe3+] rather than the normal ferrous [Fe2+] state. The presence of iron in the ferric state results shift of the oxygen-dissociation curve to the left. This shift leads to increased affinity of the ferrous iron for oxygen and thus impaired oxygen release to the tissue.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: The most common cause of seizures in a 2-year- old child is febrile seizures, which typically occur between 6 months and 5 years of age and are associated with a rapid rise in body temperature due to infection.
questions.explanation: In the pediatric population between the ages of 6 months and 5 years, febrile seizures are the most common cause of convulsive episodes (Option C). These are seizures triggered by a rapid rise in body temperature, usually associated with common childhood viral infections, in the absence of an intracranial infection or metabolic imbalance. While head trauma (Option A), severe malnutrition (Option B), and underlying neurological deficits (Option D) are important causes of symptomatic seizures, they are statistically much less frequent than simple febrile convulsions in this specific age group. Most febrile seizures are generalized, brief, and carry an excellent prognosis without the need for long-term antiepileptic therapy. Clinicians must focus on ruling out meningitis and managing the underlying fever. Therefore, given the 2-year-old age mark, febrile seizures remain the most prevalent etiology

questions.text: What dose of folic acid is recommended for a woman who wants to become pregnant but has a history of pregnancy complicated with a neural tube defect?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 4 mg/day

In a pregnancy complicated with a history of neural tube defect, 4 mg/day of folic acid is recommended.

Supplementation with folic acid is standard practice before and during pregnancy to reduce the incidence of neural tube defects and for as long as a woman is breastfeeding.

Option A: In a normal pregnancy, folic acid is given at a dose of 400-500 mcg/day.

Options B and C: In adults with conditions having a high cell turnover like hemolytic anemia, supplementation of folic acid at a dose of 1-2 mg/day is recommended.

In hyperhomocysteinemia, folic acid is given at a dose of 1 mg/day.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A child presents to the OPD with a mild cold. On examination, he is found to have adenoid facies. What is the treatment of choice?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Adenoidectomy with coblation

Adenoid facies is a characteristic look seen in chronic adenoiditis. The treatment of choice in chronic adenoiditis is adenoidectomy with coblation.

Clinical features:

* Nasal obstruction is the most common symptom. This leads to mouth breathing. Nasal obstruction also interferes with feeding or suckling in a child. As respiration and feeding cannot take place simultaneously, a child with adenoid enlargement fails to thrive.

* Nasal discharge, sinusitis, and epistaxis.

* Bilateral conductive hearing loss and serous otitis media due to eustachian tube obstruction.

* Rhinolalia clausa - hyponasal voice.

* Adenoid facies - elongated face with a dull expression, pinched up nose, absent nasolabial crease, open mouth, prominent and crowded upper teeth.

* Sleep apnoea - chronic cases lead to hypoxemia and pulmonary vasoconstriction. This consequently leads to pulmonary hypertension and cor pulmonale.

* Aprosexia - lack of concentration.

Management:

Definitive management is adenoidectomy. The treatment of choice is coblation adenoidectomy because it removes the tissue and prevents hemorrhage via radiofrequency ablation while curettage and microdebridement needs further cauterisation to control bleeding points. Older methods of classical adenoidectomy via mouth has been replaced by these newer techniques as the older methods were blind procedure
questions.learning: Adenoidectomy with coblation Adenoid facies is a characteristic look seen in chronic adenoiditis. The treatment of choice in chronic adenoiditis is adenoidectomy with coblation.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A patient of schizophrenia was started on olanzapine therapy a few months ago. It was effective in controlling the symptoms, but the patient stopped taking this drug. What can be the most likely reason?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Weight gain

This patient's cessation of olanzapine is most likely due to its well known side effect of weight gain.

Olanzapine is an atypical antipsychotic that blocks both serotonin (5HT2A) and dopamine (D2) receptors. Olanzapine and other atypical antipsychotics are efficacious in reducing negative symptoms (flattening affect and social withdrawal) of schizophrenia.

Olanzapine is a weak dopamine antagonist and therefore has fewer extrapyramidal side effects such as akathesia, dystonia and tadrive dyskinesia (Options B, C and D). However, because of the serotonin blockade, Olanzapine is prone to higher metabolic side effects such as weight gain and glucose intolerance.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: During surgical excision of the left submandibular gland, the hypoglossal nerve is accidentally injured. As a result of this nerve damage, which specific functional deficit is most likely to be observed in the patient?
options: Deviated tongue to the contralateral side
Deviated tongue to the same side
Loss of taste in the posterior one-third of the tongue
questions.explanation: The hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) provides motor innervation to the intrinsic and extrinsic muscles of the tongue, most notably the genioglossus. The genioglossus muscle is responsible for protruding the tongue. In a healthy state, both muscles work together to push the tongue straight out. When one hypoglossal nerve is injured (as in this submandibular surgery complication), the genioglossus on the ipsilateral (same) side becomes paralyzed. Consequently, when the patient attempts to protrude their tongue, the unopposed action of the intact genioglossus on the healthy side pushes the tongue toward the side of the lesion. Deviation to the contralateral side (Option A) is not seen in lower motor neuron hypoglossal injuries. Total inability to protrude (Option C) would require bilateral injury. Loss of taste (Option D) is a function of the glossopharyngeal (posterior 1/3) and facial nerves (anterior 2/3), not the hypoglossal. Therefore, ipsilateral tongue deviation is the definitive sign
questions.learning: The hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) provides motor innervation to the intrinsic and extrinsic muscles of the tongue, most notably the genioglossus. The genioglossus muscle is responsible for protruding the tongue.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text:
A 35-year-old female patient presents with complaints of nasal obstruction and post-nasal drip. There is a past history of FESS for failed conservative management 5 years ago. Uncinectomy and maxillary ostium dilation was done during the previous FESS. A DNE done now shows patent ostia and mucosal edema of the maxillary sinus lining. What is the next best step in management?

FESS- Functional endoscopic sinus surgery.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Steroid irrigation and antihistamines

The history of nasal obstruction and post-nasal drip and endoscopy showing mucosal edema is suggestive of acute rhinosinusitis. The next best step in management is symptomatic treatment with nasal steroid irrigation, decongestants, and antihistamines, regardless of the patient's past history of FESS operation.

Acute viral rhinosinusitis causes mucosal edema which causes obstruction of the sinus ostia. There is also reduced mucociliary transport in the sinuses resulting in stasis of secretions within the sinuses causing headache, facial pain, congestion, nasal obstruction or discharge, post-nasal drip, and hyposmia or anosmia.

If the sinuses remain obstructed or the mucociliary transport system does not return to normal, a bacterial infection can ensue, causing fever, purulent discharge, and persistent or worsening symptoms beyond 10 days.

In the case of bacterial sinusitis, antibiotics like amoxicillin and macrolides (erythromycin) are used for a short course (Option B).

Procedures like antral lavage and surgery (Option A) are done in cases not responding to medical therapy.

Biological therapy (Option D) is not used in the treatment of sinusitis.
questions.learning: Steroid irrigation and antihistamines — The history of nasal obstruction and post-nasal drip and endoscopy showing mucosal edema is suggestive of acute rhinosinusitis.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Increased LH: FSH ratio is seen in
questions.explanation: An increased LH:FSH ratio (typically greater than 2:1 or 3:1) is a classic biochemical finding in Polycystic Ovarian Disease (PCOD) or Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS). This hormonal imbalance occurs because increased GnRH pulse frequency leads to preferential LH secretion, which stimulates the ovarian theca cells to produce excessive androgens. In premature menopause (Option A) and Turner's syndrome (Option D), both LH and FSH are significantly elevated due to primary ovarian failure, but FSH is characteristically higher than LH. Sheehan syndrome (Option B) involves panhypopituitarism, leading to low levels of both gonadotropins. While the LH:FSH ratio is no longer part of the formal Rotterdam diagnostic criteria for PCOS, it remains a valuable clinical marker that supports the diagnosis in patients presenting with oligo-ovulation, hyperandrogenism, and polycystic morphology on ultrasound. This shift in gonadotropin balance is fundamental to the pathophysiology of the condition
questions.learning: An increased LH:FSH ratio (typically greater than 2:1 or 3:1) is a classic biochemical finding in Polycystic Ovarian Disease (PCOD) or Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: What is the optimum pressure for VAC?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. -100 to 130 mm of Hg

The optimum pressure for Vacuum-Assisted Closure therapy is between -100 to 130 mm Hg, with -125 mm Hg being the most commonly used setting.

(promote effective wound healing)

At around −125 mmHg, VAC therapy improves local blood flow, promotes granulation tissue formation, removes exudate and bacteria and causes wound contraction.
questions.learning: -100 to 130 mm of Hg The optimum pressure for Vacuum-Assisted Closure therapy is between -100 to 130 mm Hg, with -125 mm Hg being the most commonly used setting.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A female patient presents to you with six weeks of amenorrhea, associated with abdominal pain and vaginal bleeding with normal blood pressure. Investigations revealed beta-hCG to be 1400 mIU/mL. An ultrasound scan was done which showed a trilaminar endometrium with normal adnexa. What is the next best step in the management of this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Repeat beta-hCG after 48 hours

The given clinical vignette points to the possibility of diagnosis of either an abortion or ectopic pregnancy. The next best step in the management of this patient is to repeat beta-hCG after 48 hours for diagnosis.

The causes of bleeding in early pregnancy include abortion, ectopic pregnancy, and hydatidiform mole. The characteristic ultrasound finding of a molar pregnancy is snowstorm appearance and so it can be excluded.

A transvaginal ultrasound is done initially in such presentations to locate the gestational sac. If neither intrauterine nor extrauterine pregnancy can be confirmed, it is termed pregnancy of unknown location till definite diagnosis.

A cut-off of ≥1500 mIU/mL for β-hCG levels, known as the discriminatory level is used to aid in diagnosis. Serial monitoring of hCG can be used to assess fetal well-being in cases of threatened abortion. If the initial level is below this cut-off, the gestational sac location usually cannot be identified. In such situations, serial β-hCG levels are measured, and the pattern is assessed. If the value is above the discriminatory level, and an intrauterine pregnancy or abortion cannot be confirmed, then ectopic pregnancy has to be suspected.

The doubling time of hCG during early pregnancy is 1.4-2 days. Failure to double the hCG value along with an empty uterus at 48 hours is highly suggestive of ectopic pregnancy. A trilaminar endometrial pattern can be seen in ectopic pregnancy along with an adnexal mass separate from the ovary.

Once the diagnosis of ectopic pregnancy is confirmed, administration of methotrexate in single or multiple doses can be considered. A dilatation and curettage can be used to confirm the diagnosis.

Other options:

Option C: Measurement of progesterone cannot be used as a reliable diagnostic test. In general, values <5ng/mL point to a nonliving intrauterine or ectopic pregnancy.

Option D: Laparoscopy is the surgery of choice in hemodynamically stable patients for ectopic pregnancy.
questions.learning: Repeat beta-hCG after 48 hours — The given clinical vignette points to the possibility of diagnosis of either an abortion or ectopic pregnancy. The next best step in the management of this patient is to repeat beta-hCG after 48 hours for diagnosis.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 55-year-old man presents with sudden, painless loss of vision in his left eye that lasted a few minutes, after which his vision spontaneously returned. Based on this clinical presentation, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical description of sudden, painless, transient loss of vision ("like a curtain coming down") that resolves within minutes is the classic definition of Amaurosis fugax. It is typically caused by a transient embolic event originating from an atherosclerotic carotid artery. The provided fundus image confirms this by showing a Hollenhorst plaque—a bright, refractile cholesterol embolus lodged at a retinal arterial bifurcation. Central Retinal Artery Occlusion (CRAO) (Option B) causes permanent painless vision loss and characteristically shows a "cherry-red spot" on the macula. Central Retinal Vein Occlusion (CRVO) (Option C) presents with blurred vision and a "blood and thunder" fundus (diffuse hemorrhages). Hypertensive retinopathy (Option D) involves progressive changes like silver-wiring and hemorrhages but not sudden transient blindness. Amaurosis fugax is a critical warning sign for an impending stroke (TIA). Management requires urgent carotid Doppler ultrasound and systemic evaluation for cardiovascular risk factors, including antiplatelet therapy and potential carotid endarterectomy
questions.learning: The clinical description of sudden, painless, transient loss of vision ("like a curtain coming down") that resolves within minutes is the classic definition of Amaurosis fugax.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is a technology-based surveillance system used for tuberculosis (TB) control in India?
questions.explanation: Nikshay is the unified ICT (Information and Communication Technology) platform for tuberculosis (TB) surveillance and case management under India's National TB Elimination Programme (NTEP). It allows health officials to track TB patients from diagnosis through treatment completion across both public and private sectors. The platform facilitates real-time notification, monitors treatment adherence, and manages Direct Benefit Transfers (DBT) to patients for nutritional support. Nischay (Option B) is a brand of home pregnancy test kits and not related to TB. Dots99 (Option C) refers to a specific adherence monitoring tool using toll-free missed calls on medication packaging but is not the overarching surveillance system. DOTS (Option D) stands for "Directly Observed Treatment, Short-course," which is the standardized clinical management strategy rather than a digital surveillance application. Nikshay's comprehensive database is vital for evaluating program performance and achieving the national goal of eliminating TB by 2025 through data-driven public health actions
questions.learning: Nikshay is the unified ICT (Information and Communication Technology) platform for tuberculosis (TB) surveillance and case management under India's National TB Elimination Programme (NTEP).

questions.text: In children diagnosed with congenital heart disease, NADA's criteria include all the following, except?

Increased troponin-T is not included in NADA’s criteria.

Nada’s criteria is used to diagnose congenital heart disease in children. The presence of 1 major or 2 minor criteria indicates congenital heart disease.

Minor criteria

Systolic murmur  grade 3 or more

Any diastolic murmur (Option A)

Cyanosis

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Warthin's tumor is also called?
questions.explanation: Warthin's tumor is a benign salivary gland tumor, most commonly found in the parotid gland. It is also known as an Adenolymphoma (specifically papillary cystadenoma lymphomatosum). The name refers to its characteristic histological appearance: glandular (adenomatous) spaces lined by a double layer of oncocytic cells, set within a dense stroma of lymphoid tissue (lymphoma-like), often with germinal centers. Pleomorphic adenoma (Option B) is the most common overall salivary gland tumor and is known as a "benign mixed tumor." Mucoepidermoid carcinoma (Option C) is the most common malignant salivary gland tumor. Acinic cell carcinoma (Option D) is another low-grade malignant tumor. Warthin's tumor is unique because it is strongly associated with smoking and is the most common salivary gland tumor to present bilaterally or multicentrically. It characteristically appears as a slow-growing, soft, fluctuating mass at the lower pole of the parotid
questions.learning: Warthin's tumor is a benign salivary gland tumor, most commonly found in the parotid gland. It is also known as an Adenolymphoma (specifically papillary cystadenoma lymphomatosum).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presents with recurrent episodes of headache, palpitations, and profuse sweating, along with transient spikes in blood pressure. Investigations show elevated 24-hour urinary metanephrine levels. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: A pheochromocytoma is a rare, catecholamine-secreting tumor of the adrenal medulla chromaffin cells. It classically presents with the triad of "paroxysmal" symptoms: pounding headache, palpitations (tachycardia), and profuse diaphoresis (sweating). These "spells" are caused by the episodic release of epinephrine and norepinephrine. Between episodes, the blood pressure may be normal, but transient, severe elevations during spells are characteristic. The definitive diagnostic test is the measurement of catecholamine metabolites—metanephrines and vanillylmandelic acid (VMA)—in the blood or a 24-hour urine sample, which would be significantly elevated. Addison's disease (Option A) is adrenal insufficiency, which causes hypotension and hyperpigmentation. Renal artery stenosis (Option B) cause persistent, secondary hypertension but not episodic sweat/palpitation spells. Hyperthyroidism (Option D) can cause palpitations and sweating, but the symptoms are usually continuous, and metanephrines would be normal. Therefore, the combination of paroxysmal "5 Ps" (Pressure, Pain, Palpitations, Perspiration, Pallor) and elevated urinary metanephrines is diagnostic of pheochromocytoma
questions.learning: A pheochromocytoma is a rare, catecholamine-secreting tumor of the adrenal medulla chromaffin cells. It classically presents with the triad of "paroxysmal" symptoms: pounding headache, palpitations (tachycardia), and profuse diaphoresis (sweating).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: The respiratory motor neuron associated with origin of respiratory cycle is located in:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Posterior medulla oblongata

The dorsal respiratory group (DRG), located in the posterior (dorsal) medulla oblongata within the nucleus tractus solitarius (NTS), is classically regarded as the inspiratory centre responsible for initiating the normal respiratory cycle. It generates the inspiratory drive during quiet breathing and receives afferent input from peripheral chemoreceptors and pulmonary stretch receptors via the glossopharyngeal and vagus nerves.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A farmer, recently bitten by fleas in a storage area, presents with high fever, painful inguinal lymphadenopathy, vomiting, diarrhea, and hypotension. Smears from the lymph node discharge show bacteria with bipolar staining. Which staining method should be used to help confirm the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The patient’s history of flea bites and the clinical triad of high fever, painful lymphadenopathy (buboes), and systemic shock (hypotension) is pathognomonic for Bubonic Plague, caused by Yersinia pestis. A hallmark microbiological feature of Yersinia is its bipolar staining, where the ends of the bacilli stain more intensely, giving them a "safety-pin" appearance. Wayson's stain is the specific diagnostic technique used to demonstrate this bipolar staining pattern in clinical samples. Neisser and Albert's stains (Options A and C) are used to visualize the metachromatic granules of Corynebacterium diphtheriae. McFadyean's stain (Option D) is a specialized polychrome methylene blue stain used to detect the capsules of Bacillus anthracis. Therefore, because Wayson's stain is specifically designed for the rapid identification of the "safety-pin" morphology of the plague bacilli, it is the definitive choice for this farmer's diagnosis
questions.learning: The patient’s history of flea bites and the clinical triad of high fever, painful lymphadenopathy (buboes), and systemic shock (hypotension) is pathognomonic for Bubonic Plague, caused by Yersinia pestis.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following symptoms represent storage (irritative) symptoms seen in patients with benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH)? 1. Urgency 2. Enuresis 3. Hesitancy 4. Frequency 5. Dribbling
questions.explanation: Lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS) in BPH are divided into Storage and Voiding symptoms. Storage symptoms (also called Irritative symptoms) relate to the bladder's ability to hold urine. These include Frequency (4), Urgency (1), Nocturia, and Enuresis (2). Hesitancy (3) and terminal dribbling (5) are classic "Voiding" (Obstructive) symptoms, as they occur during or at the end of the urinary act due to the enlarged prostate blocking the urethra. Therefore, only options 1, 2, and 4 correctly represent the storage phase of bladder function. Storage symptoms are often the most bothersome to patients, as they interfere with sleep and daily activities. Recognizing this distinction is clinically important because treatment with alpha-blockers helps with voiding, while anticholinergics or beta-3 agonists are often added specifically to target these irritative storage symptoms. Thus, Option D is the correct grouping
questions.learning: Lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS) in BPH are divided into Storage and Voiding symptoms. Storage symptoms (also called Irritative symptoms) relate to the bladder's ability to hold urine.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: What is the mechanism of action of dicumarol?
options: Inhibits vitamin K dependant clotting factors
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Inhibits vitamin K dependant clotting factors

The mechanism of action of Dicumarol is by inhibiting the synthesis of Vit K-dependent clotting factors in the liver.

Dicumarol and warfarin competitively inhibit the gamma-carboxylation system due to structural similarity with vitamin K. Therefore, they can act as anticoagulants used for therapeutic purposes.

Vitamin K epoxide is reduced to the quinone form by epoxide reductase, which is sensitive to inhibition by warfarin and dicoumarol.

Other options:

Option A: Heparin is a powerful-acting anticoagulant that acts indirectly by activating plasma antithrombin III. The heparin-AT III complex then binds to clotting factors of the intrinsic and common pathways (Xa, IIa, IXa, XIa, Xlla, and XIIIa) and inactivates them.

Option C: Drugs like tranexamic acid inhibit plasminogen activation and dissolution of the clot, and are used to check fibrinolysis-associated bleeding.

Option D: Rivaroxaban and apixaban are active direct inhibitors of activated factor Xa which has become available for prophylaxis and treatment of DVT.

2) Direct thrombin inhibitors (DTI)

Parenteral DTI

Bivalent DTI- Lepirudin, Desirudin, Bivalirudin

3) Indirect thrombin inhibitors

4) Direct Oral Factor Xa Inhibitors
Rivaroxaban, Apixaban, Edoxaban, Betrixaban

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which electrolyte abnormality will lead to cardiac arrhythmia in the case of severe vomiting?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hypokalemia

The electrolyte imbalance most likely to cause arrhythmia in the setting of severe vomiting is hypokalemia.

Persistent vomiting results in loss of hydrochloric acid leading to the development of metabolic alkalosis (due to loss of H+) and hypochloremia (due to loss of Cl-). The kidneys try to compensate for alkalosis by secreting Na+ and HCO3-. However, the loss of sodium stimulates the secretion of aldosterone via the RAAS pathway. The aldosterone causes active reabsorption of sodium in exchange for K+ and H+ ions.

Loss of potassium ions leads to the development of hypokalemia. Loss of H+ ions in urine lowers the urinary pH resulting in aciduria. It is called paradoxical aciduria, since the body initially lost H+ ions due to loss of HCl, and instead of compensating that loss, the body is losing more H+ ions through urine.

Potassium plays a crucial role in cardiac electrical activity, maintaining the resting membrane potential and ensuring proper action potential conduction. Severe hypokalemia disrupts this balance, making the heart more susceptible to arrhythmias, including life-threatening ventricular tachyarrhythmias.

In patients with severe diarrhea, a net loss of bicarbonates (intestinal secretions) leads to metabolic acidosis.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A protein is fixed in formalin and embedded in paraffin wax. Which of the following methods is the most appropriate means for identification?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Immunohistochemistry

Immunohistochemistry (IHC) is the preferred technique for detecting and localizing specific proteins (antigens) in formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded (FFPE) tissue. It uses antigen-specific antibodies to identify protein expression while preserving tissue architecture, making it invaluable for tumor diagnosis, classification, and prognostic marker assessment.

• Immunohistochemistry is specifically designed for protein detection in FFPE tissue sections and allows visualization of protein expression within the histological context.

Why not the other options?

• A. Western blot: Detects proteins but requires fresh/frozen tissue lysates and does not preserve tissue architecture.
• C. Flow cytometry: Analyzes proteins on live cells or cell suspensions; not suitable for paraffin-embedded tissue.
• D. In situ hybridization: Detects DNA or RNA (nucleic acids), not proteins.
questions.learning: Immunohistochemistry Immunohistochemistry (IHC) is the preferred technique for detecting and localizing specific proteins (antigens) in formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded (FFPE) tissue.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A pregnant woman presents to the emergency department after being scratched by a stray dog, resulting in minor superficial abrasions without bleeding. What is the appropriate management or treatment in this situation?
options: No treatment as she is pregnant now
Local wound cleaning and rabies vaccine
Local wound cleaning, Rabies vaccines, and immunoglobulins
questions.explanation: This patient sustained a Category II rabies exposure (minor scratches without bleeding). According to WHO and national guidelines, Category II exposures require "local wound cleaning" with soap and water followed by the administration of the "rabies vaccine". Crucially, pregnancy (Option A) is not a contraindication to rabies post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP), as the vaccine is inactivated and life-saving. Local cleaning alone (Option B) is insufficient as it does not address the risk of viral entry. Immunoglobulins (Option D) are only required for Category III exposures (single or multiple transdermal bites or scratches with bleeding). Rabies is 100% fatal once symptoms develop; therefore, PEP must never be delayed or withheld regardless of the patient's physiological state. The intradermal or intramuscular vaccine schedule should be followed strictly to ensure protective antibody titers are achieved
questions.learning: This patient sustained a Category II rabies exposure (minor scratches without bleeding). According to WHO and national guidelines, Category II exposures require "local wound cleaning" with soap and water followed by the administration of the "rabies vaccine".

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: What is the best diagnostic test for evaluating endometrial pathology?
questions.explanation: Hysteroscopy-guided endometrial biopsy is considered the gold standard for evaluating endometrial pathology because it allows for direct visualization of the uterine cavity. This enables the clinician to identify and perform targeted sampling of suspicious areas, such as polyps, submucosal fibroids, or localized carcinomas, which significantly increases diagnostic accuracy. Pipelle biopsy (Option A) is a minimally invasive office procedure that is effective for detecting diffuse disease but can easily miss focal lesions. Dilatation and curettage (Option C) is a "blind" procedure that has a higher risk of sampling error for localized pathologies. Transvaginal sonography (Option D) is an excellent non-invasive screening tool to measure endometrial thickness but cannot provide a definitive histological diagnosis. Therefore, the ability to "see and sample" makes hysteroscopy-guided biopsy the superior diagnostic choice for suspected uterine abnormalities
questions.learning: Hysteroscopy-guided endometrial biopsy is considered the gold standard for evaluating endometrial pathology because it allows for direct visualization of the uterine cavity.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A young air-hostess presented to the outpatient department with dilated veins on her left leg (image). According to the CEAP classification for varicose veins, what will be the C stage in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. C2A

The image above shows dilated, tortuous veins of the lower limb. In asymptomatic patients, they are classified as C2A according to the Clinical-Etiology-Anatomy-Pathophysiology (CEAP) classification for chronic venous disorders.

Varicose veins are characterized by the tortuous dilatation of subcutaneous veins resulting from venous insufficiency. Patients have heaviness, burning, and aching over the affected area or whole limb, which increases throughout the day or on prolonged standing. Compression and elevation can relieve the symptoms.

Diagnosed by duplex ultrasound and is treated by modalities such as compression, laser ablation, radiofrequency ablation, endovenous glue, ultrasound-guided foam sclerotherapy, and open surgery.

Image A shows tortuous dilated veins (C2), Image B is atrophie blanche (C4b), and Image C shows fan-shaped telangiectasia (C4c).

The images below show C5 and C6 - healed and active venous ulcers respectively.
questions.learning: C2A — The image above shows dilated, tortuous veins of the lower limb. In asymptomatic patients, they are classified as C2A according to the Clinical-Etiology-Anatomy-Pathophysiology (CEAP) classification for chronic venous disorders.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 50-year-old woman presents with abnormal uterine bleeding for two months. What is the next line of management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Endometrial sampling

The next line of management in a 50-year-old woman with abnormal uterine bleeding is endometrial sampling.

Indications for endometrial sampling:

• Any female > 45 years with abnormal uterine bleeding
• A female of age < 45 years having exposure to excessive estrogen such as in PCOD, severe obesity, tamoxifen treatment
• Women with failed medical management and persistent bleeding
• Transvaginal ultrasound findings >12 mm in premenopausal women and > 4 mm in postmenopausal women.

Endometrial sampling may be done by either curettage or aspiration biopsy by pipelle or vibra aspirator.

Note: Transvaginal ultrasound is a better first-line investigation to assess AUB. Since TVS is not included in the options, endometrial sampling is the next best answer. Assessing the reason for AUB and ruling out malignancy in the postmenopausal age group are the initial steps before prescribing any treatment.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: In a woman who has sustained third- and fourth- degree burns over her back, what is the correct sequence of management steps that should be followed during treatment?
options: Resuscitation - debridement - allograft or auto- graft
questions.explanation: Resuscitation - debridement - allograft or autograft The management of severe burns (third and fourth degree) follows a critical surgical hierarchy. The absolute first step is always Resuscitation (Option B) to maintain hemodynamic stability and prevent burn shock using the Parkland formula. Once the patient is stabilized, the next priority is Debridement, which involves the removal of dead, necrotic tissue (eschar) to prevent infection. Finally, the open wound must be covered to prevent fluid loss and promote healing, typically using an allograft (temporary donor skin) or an autograft (the patient's own skin). Options A, C, and D are incorrect because reconstruction cannot occur before debridement, and debridement should not precede hemodynamic stabilization. Following this sequential path—Resuscitation, Debridement, and Grafting—is the established standard of care in burn centers to ensure patient survival and maximize functional outcomes after such severe injuries.
questions.learning: Resuscitation - debridement - allograft or autograft The management of severe burns (third and fourth degree) follows a critical surgical hierarchy. The absolute first step is always Resuscitation (Option B) to maintain hemodynamic stability and prevent…

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 22-year-old woman presents for emergency contraception within a few hours of unprotected sexual intercourse and prefers a single-dose option rather than multiple pills. What would be the most appropriate recommendation in this case?
questions.explanation: For emergency contraception (EC) following unprotected intercourse, Levonorgestrel 1.5 mg is the most appropriate single-pill regimen. This progestin-only pill is highly effective when taken within 72 hours and fulfills the patient's preference for a single dose. It also avoids the high risk of nausea and vomiting associated with estrogen-containing pills. Levonorgestrel 0.75 mg (Option A) requires two doses taken 12 hours apart, which is less convenient. The combination regimen (Option B), known as the Yuzpe regimen, is less effective and has more side effects. Desogestrel 3 mg (Option D) is a daily contraceptive and is not a standard drug for emergency use. While the copper IUD is the most effective EC method, among oral options, the 1.5 mg single-dose levonorgestrel is the clinical standard

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A neonate is brought to the hospital with complaints of projectile non-bilious vomiting after feeding. On examination, the child seems lethargic and dehydrated and abdominal examination reveals visible gastric peristalsis. A barium meal was done and the image is given below. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Congenital hypertrophic pyloric stenosis

The clinical scenario of projectile non- bilious vomiting with the string sign in barium meal is suggestive of Congenital Hypertrophic Pyloric Stenosis

Congenital Hypertrophic Pyloric Stenosis:

* It is common between 2 and 8 weeks of age.

* Hypertrophy of the circular muscle of the Pylorus results in constriction and obstruction of the gastric outlet.

* First-born male infants are at the highest risk.

* Infants usually present with projectile, non-bilious vomiting.

* Clinically, an olive-shaped mass is palpable in the right upper quadrant or epigastrium. When the infant is given a test feed, visible peristalsis is usually observed moving from left to right(not from right to left), followed by projectile vomiting.

Metabolic abnormality:

* Infants with hypertrophic pyloric stenosis develop a characteristic metabolic abnormality i.e Hypokalemic hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis with paradoxical aciduria.

* Persistent vomiting results in loss of hydrochloric acid leading to the development of metabolic alkalosis (due to loss of H+) and hypochloremia (due to loss of Cl-).

* Kidneys try to compensate alkalosis by secreting Na+ and HCO3-. However, loss of sodium stimulates the secretion of aldosterone through the RAAS pathway.

* The aldosterone causes active reabsorption of sodium in exchange for K+ and H+ ions.

* Loss of potassium ions leads to the development of hypokalemia.

* Loss of H+ ions in urine lowers the urinary pH resulting in aciduria. It is called paradoxical aciduria, since the body initially lost H+ ions due to loss of HCl, and instead of compensating that loss, the body is losing more H+ ions through urine.

Management:

* The child should be rehydrated and the metabolic abnormality has to be corrected before proceeding to surgery.

* The Ramstedt pyloromyotomy remains the standard surgical procedure for its treatment.

Note:

String sign in Radiology is seen:

* Crohn’s disease – String sign of Kantor

* Tuberculosis

* Hypertrophic Pyloric stenosis

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A patient with a history of trauma presents with hearing loss, and a high-resolution CT (HRCT) scan is performed. Which of the following structures is not typically visualized on HRCT?
questions.explanation: High-Resolution Computed Tomography (HRCT) of the temporal bone is the gold standard for visualizing the bony architecture of the middle and inner ear. It provides excellent detail of the bony labyrinth, including the 2.5 turns of the cochlea (Option A), the vestibule (Option B), and the semicircular canals (Option C). HRCT is highly effective at identifying temporal bone fractures or ossicular chain disruptions. However, HRCT uses X-rays and is primarily limited to visualizing bone and air spaces; it does not have the soft-tissue resolution to visualize microscopic structures like the Organ of Corti, which is the sensory neuroepithelium within the cochlear duct. To visualize fine soft-tissue details, fluids, or nerves (like the vestibulocochlear nerve), Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) is the required modality. Therefore, while HRCT is essential after trauma, it cannot directly confirm damage to the delicate sensory hair cells of the inner ear
questions.learning: High-Resolution Computed Tomography (HRCT) of the temporal bone is the gold standard for visualizing the bony architecture of the middle and inner ear.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 55-year-old lady presents with third degree uterine prolapse. Which of the following is the best management for her?
options: Vaginal hysterectomy with pelvic floor repair
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Vaginal hysterectomy with pelvic floor repair

In the clinal scenario of a 55-year-old woman with third-degree uterine prolapse, the ideal management is vaginal hysterectomy with pelvic floor repair.

Uterine prolapse is the descent of the uterus from its normal position which usually occurs due to laxity of ligaments that offer support, seen often due to childbirth, aging, or trauma. The uterine descent is clinically categorized into:

• First degree:  the external os remains above the vaginal introitus
• Second degree: The external os protrudes below the vaginal introitus but the uterine body remains inside the vagina
• Third degree (Syn: Complete prolapse): The uterine, cervix, body, and fundus descend to lie outside the introitus
• Procidentia involves prolapse of the uterus with the entire vagina everted.

The patient usually presents with a sense of heaviness in the pelvic region with lower back discomfort. Based on the structures involved the patient can additionally have urinary symptoms (like incontinence and urgency), bowel disturbances (constipation and tenesmus), or sexual discomfort during intercourse.

Symptomatic uterine prolapse is managed surgically with different procedures based on the profile of the patient. Conservative management is done for old asymptomatic women with mild degree prolapse.

A vaginal hysterectomy is recommended for patients who satisfy the following criteria:

• >40 years of age
• Have completed their families
• Do not wish to preserve menstrual and child-bearing function

Other options:

Option A: Fothergill repair or Manchester operation is a procedure done to preserve the reproductive function and vaginal prolapse with supravaginal cervix elongation. It initially involves preliminary curettage with low amputation of the cervix. After Mackenrodt's ligament is plicated,  anterior colporrhaphy and colpoperineorrhaphy are performed.

Option B: Sling operation (Purandare's operation) is indicated in congenital or nulliparous prolapse without cystocele. The procedure involves the extraperitoneal passage of rectus sheath strips joined to the anterior surface of the cervix by silk sutures.

Option D: Shirodkar procedure is a type of abdominal sling surgery done in young women to retain menstrual and reproductive function. It involves using a sling to fix the cervix to the lumbosacral fascia.
questions.learning: Vaginal hysterectomy with pelvic floor repair — In the clinal scenario of a 55-year-old woman with third-degree uterine prolapse, the ideal management is vaginal hysterectomy with pelvic floor repair.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A male patient presented to the OPD with a rash on his trunk. On examination, there is an eschar in the trunk region. Regional lymphadenopathy can also be noted. He reports that he recently experienced a mite bite during a camping trip in that area. What is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Scrub typhus

The most likely cause of eschar and lymphadenopathy following a mite bite on the trunk region is scrub typhus.

Scrub typhus is a bacterial infection transmitted through the bite of infected mites found in areas with heavy vegetation. The characteristic eschar (a black, necrotic lesion) at the site of the mite bite, along with regional lymphadenopathy, is a hallmark feature of scrub typhus.

Option (b): Endemic typhus - Endemic typhus, caused by Rickettsia typhi, typically presents with fever, rash, and headache but does not commonly result in eschar formation.

Option (c): Epidemic typhus - Epidemic typhus, caused by Rickettsia prowazekii, is transmitted by body lice and typically presents with fever, rash, and severe systemic symptoms but does not cause eschar formation.

Option (d): Rocky Mountain Spotted Fever - Rocky Mountain Spotted Fever, caused by Rickettsia rickettsii and transmitted by ticks, may present with rash and systemic symptoms but does not commonly produce eschar at the site of the tick bite.
questions.learning: Scrub typhus — The most likely cause of eschar and lymphadenopathy following a mite bite on the trunk region is scrub typhus. Scrub typhus is a bacterial infection transmitted through the bite of infected mites found in areas with heavy vegetation.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A Rh-negative mother delivered an Rh-positive baby and Coomb's test was positive for the baby. What is the mechanism of hypersensitivity seen in this scenario?
options: CD4+ T cell mediated cytokine release
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity

The pathophysiological mechanism underlying transfusion reactions or erythroblastosis fetalis as seen in this scenario is a type of type II hypersensitivity reaction and is due to antibody-dependant cellular toxicity.

Other options:

Option C: Antigen-antibody immune complex deposition is responsible for immune-complex mediated (type III) hypersensitivity reaction. These complexes circulate in the body and deposit in various sites (vessel walls, renal glomeruli, joints) to cause inflammation.

Option D: CD4+T cell-mediated cytokine release is responsible for T cell-mediated (type IV) hypersensitivity reaction.

Pearl PF0792: Mechanisms of Hypersensitivity Reactions

Type

Immune Mechanisms

Histopathological lesions

Prototypical Disorders

Production of IgE antibody →immediate release of vasoactive amines from mast cells

Antibody-mediated (type II)hypersensitivity

Immune complex-mediated (type III) hypersensitivity

(2) T-cell-mediated cytotoxicity

Contact dermatitis; multiple sclerosis; type 1 diabetes; tuberculosis

Pearl PF0793: Types of Type II Antibody-Mediated Hypersentivity

Antibodies that react with antigens present on cell surfaces or in the extracellular matrix cause disease by destroying these cells, triggering inflammation, or interfering with normal functions

• Myasthenia gravis (against acetylcholine receptor)

• Graves’ disease (against TSH receptor)

• Pemphigus vulgaris (against epidermal cadherin)

• Pernicious anemia (against intrinsic factor)

• Insulin resistant diabetes (against insulin receptor)

Antibodies can coat (opsonize) cells, with or without complement proteins, and target these cells for phagocytosis

• Transfusion reactions

• Erythroblastosis fetalis

• Autoimmune hemolytic anemia

• Autoimmune thrombocytopenic purpura

Antibodies may deposit in tissues or blood vessels, and elicit an acute inflammatory reaction by activating complement

• Goodpasture syndrome

• Vasculitis due to ANCA

• Acute rheumatic fever

• Vascular rejection in organ grafts

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following is not true about of proteoglycans?
options: Made of amino acids and sugars
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Holds less water

Proteoglycans can hold large amounts of water, and not less.

Proteoglycans are made of a central protein core with O-linked glycosaminoglycan side-chains. They hold large quantities of water and occupy space.

They provide the ground substance of connective tissue.

Chondroitin sulfate is a glycosaminoglycan that is bound to a protein to form chondroitin sulfate proteoglycan. It is present in the extracellular matrix. Hyaluronic acid and heparin are examples of glycosaminoglycans.

All of the other statements regarding proteoglycans are true.
questions.learning: Holds less water Proteoglycans can hold large amounts of water, and not less. Proteoglycans are made of a central protein core with O-linked glycosaminoglycan side-chains.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: The number of births per 1,000 women in the reproductive age group is called?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. General fertility rate

Number of live births per 1000 women in the reproductive age group (15 - 49 years) in a given year is called the general fertility rate

* GFR = Number of live births in an area in a year x 1000/Mid-year population of women in reproductive age in the same area in the same year.

* It is a better indicator of fertility than crude birth rate

* The demerit of this indicator is that not all women in the denominator are exposed to childbirth

Pearl PF1746: Fertility Indicators

Crude birth rate

* It is the simplest measure of fertility although its usage is unsatisfactory

* India, as per SRS bulletin 2018, had a birth rate of 20.0 per 1000 population

General Fertility Rate

* It is a better indicator of fertility than crude birth rate

* The demerit of this indicator is that not all women in the denominator are exposed to childbirth

Age-specific fertility rates is a more precise measure of fertility and is also a sensitive indicator of family planning achievement.

Total Fertility Rate

* It is the sum of all age-specific fertility rates multiplied by 5

* This measure gives the approximate magnitude of completed family size

Gross Reproductive Rate is the average number of girls that would be born to a woman if she experiences the current fertility pattern throughout her reproductive span, assuming no mortality.

Net Reproduction Rate

* It is a demographic indicator

* NRR of 1 is equivalent to approximately the 2 child norm

* If the NRR is less than 1, then the reproductive performance of the population is said to be inadequate
