questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which class of enzymes uses molecular oxygen as the hydrogen acceptor, resulting in the formation of water?
questions.explanation: In the mitochondrial electron transport chain, Cytochrome c oxidase (Complex IV) is the terminal enzyme responsible for the final reduction of oxygen. It transfers electrons to molecular oxygen, which then combines with hydrogen ions (protons) to generate water. This is the fundamental oxygen-consuming step of aerobic respiration. Catalase (Option A) breaks down hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen, but does not use molecular oxygen as a hydrogen recipient. Superoxide dismutase (Option B) converts superoxide radicals into oxygen and hydrogen peroxide. Pyruvate dehydrogenase (Option D) is a mitochondrial enzyme that links glycolysis to the TCA cycle but is not part of the respiratory chain's oxygen reduction. Inhibition of cytochrome c oxidase by poisons like cyanide or carbon monoxide is lethal because it completely halts ATP production. Understanding this specific role of Complex IV is essential for grasping how the body utilizes inhaled oxygen to drive cellular energy production
questions.learning: In the mitochondrial electron transport chain, Cytochrome c oxidase (Complex IV) is the terminal enzyme responsible for the final reduction of oxygen.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following is the most commonly seen tumor in the retroperitoneal space?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Liposarcoma

Liposarcoma is the most commonly seen tumor in retroperitoneal space.

Retroperitoneal tumors can be benign or malignant. Malignant retroperitoneal tumors may be mesodermal (75%), neuroectodermal (24%), or embryonic remnant (1%) in origin. Rarely it can be urologic or metastatic also. The order of frequency of primary retroperitoneal malignancy is as follows:

• Liposarcoma
• Leiomyosarcoma
• Rhabdomyosarcoma
• Fibrosarcoma
• Malignant nerve sheath tumors

Liposarcoma is composed of three histologic varieties (listed in order of decreasing frequency):

• Well-differentiated and undifferentiated liposarcoma
• Pleomorphic liposarcoma
• Myxoid/round cell liposarcoma

Among the three subtypes, pleomorphic liposarcoma is the most malignant and often metastasizes, while the well-differentiated is the least malignant. Myxoid liposarcoma has intermediate malignant behavior.

Diagnosis is confirmed by contrast-enhanced CT with CT of the chest to look for metastases.

Surgery is the main modality of treatment. Wide excision with complete en bloc dissection is done. Post-operative radiotherapy and chemotherapy are used as adjuvant methods. Radiotherapy is given at a dose of 5000 cGY, it can be external beam or intra-operative radiotherapy. Chemotherapeutic agents used are mesna, adriamycin, ifosfamide and dacarbazine (MAID regimen).
questions.learning: Liposarcoma Liposarcoma is the most commonly seen tumor in retroperitoneal space. Retroperitoneal tumors can be benign or malignant.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: At what level does the spinal cord end in adults?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. L1-L2

The distal termination of the spinal cord is the lower border of L1 in adults.

Because the spinal cord ends at L1, lower nerve roots course some distance before exiting the intervertebral foramina. These lower spinal nerves form the cauda equina.

Note:

In children, the spinal cord ends at L3 and moves up with age.
questions.learning: L1-L2 — The distal termination of the spinal cord is the lower border of L1 in adults. Because the spinal cord ends at L1, lower nerve roots course some distance before exiting the intervertebral foramina.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A patient underwent a hysterectomy and was given morphine in the post-operative period and in the ward for pain. She now presents with respiratory depression and pin point pupils. What is the drug used to treat this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Naloxone

The drug of choice for the reversal of respiratory depression is naloxone. Naloxone is a competitive antagonist at μ-opioid receptors and rapidly reverses the effects of opioid toxicity when administered.

Opioid overdose symptoms:

• Triad of coma, respiratory depression, and pinpoint pupils (miosis).
• Hypotension, bradycardia
• Shallow breathing
• Hypothermia

Naloxone is a pure opioid antagonist which reverses all effects, except sedation. Naloxone is also used for reversing neonatal asphyxia due to opioid usage in labor.

Other options

Option B - Meperidine (pethidine) is a mu-opioid receptor (MOR) agonist. It has a strong analgesic effect on the central nervous system. It is mainly used as an analgesic but can also be used in post-anesthetic shivering. It has a greater ability to enter the CNS and produce analgesia at lower systemic concentrations compared to morphine. Therefore, constipation, urinary retention, and nausea are less frequent compared to morphine.

Meperidine can cross the placenta and cause significant respiratory depression in the fetus. In patients or addicts who are tolerant to the depressant effects of meperidine, large doses repeated at short intervals may produce an excitatory syndrome that includes hallucinations, tremors, muscle twitches, etc.

Option C -Atropine is an anticholinergic drug. It acts through reversible, competitive inhibition of the postsynaptic muscarinic acetylcholine receptors. It is indicated in the treatment of organophosphate/muscarinic poisoning, in bradycardia, and to reduce salivary secretions.

The adverse effects of atropine are due to the antimuscarinic effects, including xerostomia, blurring of vision, photophobia, tachycardia, flushing, warm, dry skin, constipation, urinary retention, anhidrosis, delirium, and coma. Intoxication with atropine results in all the above symptoms along with convulsions, and circulatory collapse due to respiratory failure. Death may occur secondary to respiratory paralysis.

Option D - Buprenorphine is a partial μ agonist and an antagonist at δ and κ receptors. It is used as an analgesic and in the management of opioid dependence.
questions.learning: Naloxone — The drug of choice for the reversal of respiratory depression is naloxone. Naloxone is a competitive antagonist at μ-opioid receptors and rapidly reverses the effects of opioid toxicity when administered.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Broca’s area is situated in the __________.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Inferior frontal gyrus

Broca’s area is situated in the inferior frontal gyrus.

Broca’s motor speech area (44,45) is located in the inferior frontal gyrus.

Wernicke’s area (22) is located in the superior temporal gyrus.
questions.learning: Inferior frontal gyrus Broca’s area is situated in the inferior frontal gyrus. Broca’s motor speech area (44,45) is located in the inferior frontal gyrus.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: An exclusively breastfed 3-month-old baby was brought with complaints of lethargy, vomiting and diarrhoea. Further examination confirmed the presence of jaundice, hypotonia and hepatomegaly. Ocular examination revealed a bilateral cataract that resembled a drop of oil. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Galactosemia

The clinical scenario of an exclusively breastfed infant presenting with vomiting, diarrhea, jaundice, hypotonia, hepatomegaly and bilateral oil drop cataract is suggestive of classical galactosemia.

Classical galactosemia is an autosomal recessive disorder. The enzyme deficient here is galactose-1-phosphate uridyl transferase (GALT). Normally, newborns receive up to 40% of their calorie intake as lactose (glucose + galactose). Without GALT, the infant cannot metabolize galactose 1-phosphate, which accumulates and causes injury to the kidney, liver, and brain.

Clinical features include vomiting, hypoglycemia, hepatomegaly, jaundice, congenital cataracts, aminoaciduria, and failure to thrive. There is an increased incidence of Escherichia coli neonatal sepsis. Long-term complications include speech delays, learning impairment, motor dysfunction, and hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (in females).

Diagnosis: The presence of galactose in urine (positive Benedict's test), elevated blood galactose level, and elevated erythrocyte galactose-1-phosphate level help in confirming the diagnosis.

Treatment is a galactose-free diet. Supportive therapy and the prevention of complications are important.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Acrodermatitis enteropathica is an autosomal recessive metabolic disorder which affects the absorption of which one of the following micronutrients?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Zinc

Acrodermatitis enteropathica is a rare autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutations in the SLC39A4 gene, resulting in defective intestinal absorption of zinc. Zinc deficiency leads to characteristic skin lesions, alopecia, diarrhea, and impaired immunity.

Symptoms usually begin after weaning from breast milk, as breast milk contains highly bioavailable zinc. Lifelong oral zinc supplementation results in dramatic clinical improvement.

Why not the other options?

• A. Iodine: Deficiency causes goiter and hypothyroidism, not acrodermatitis enteropathica.
• C. Iron: Deficiency causes microcytic hypochromic anemia.
• D. Selenium: Deficiency is associated with cardiomyopathy (Keshan disease) and myopathy, not the characteristic dermatitis of acrodermatitis enteropathica.
questions.learning: Zinc Acrodermatitis enteropathica is a rare autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutations in the SLC39A4 gene, resulting in defective intestinal absorption of zinc.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A primigravida in labor at 5 cm cervical dilatation suddenly develops severe fetal bradycardia. On vaginal examination, cord prolapse is detected and the cord is still pulsating. What should be the immediate next step in management?
options: Fill the bladder and put back the cord
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Trendelenburg, push the head up

Cord prolapse occurs when the umbilical cord descends before the fetal presenting part, leading to cord compression and fetal hypoxia. Immediate Action Is Needed. Cord compression leads to:

Cord compression

↓

Reduced fetal oxygen supply

↓

Fetal bradycardia

↓

Fetal hypoxia

↓

Risk of fetal death

Therefore immediate decompression of the cord is essential.

Initial emergency measures include:

| Step | Purpose

| ---- | -------

| Trendelenburg or knee-chest position | Reduce cord compression

| Manual elevation of presenting part | Relieve pressure on cord

| Avoid handling the cord | Prevent vasospasm

| Oxygen to mother | Improve fetal oxygenation

After stabilization: Emergency cesarean section is performed.
questions.learning: Trendelenburg, push the head up Cord prolapse occurs when the umbilical cord descends before the fetal presenting part, leading to cord compression and fetal hypoxia.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Identify the device
questions.explanation: The image displays a Lippes Loop, which is a classic first-generation, non-medicated (inert) intrauterine device (IUD). It is characterized by its distinctive double-S shaped plastic frame made of polyethylene, often impregnated with barium sulfate for radiopacity. Mirena (Option A) is a T-shaped hormonal IUD that releases levonorgestrel. Copper T (Option C) is a T-shaped device wrapped with copper wire, which is the most common medicated IUD used today. Progestasert (Option D) was an older T-shaped device that released progesterone. The Lippes Loop was once widely used globally but has largely been replaced in modern practice by more effective copper-bearing or hormone-releasing T-shaped devices. It worked primarily by causing a sterile inflammatory response in the endometrium that was toxic to sperm and prevented implantation. Identifying these historical devices is a common requirement in medical licensing examinations
questions.learning: The image displays a Lippes Loop, which is a classic first-generation, non-medicated (inert) intrauterine device (IUD). It is characterized by its distinctive double-S shaped plastic frame made of polyethylene, often impregnated with barium sulfate for…

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: The clinical feature of physiological edema in pregnancy:
options: Is present on both lower limbs and abdomen
Is associated with cardiac or renal pathology
Is usually of moderate or severe grade
Disappears or markedly reduces on rest
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Disappears or markedly reduces on rest

Physiological edema is common in late pregnancy due to venous stasis from uterine compression of the inferior vena cava and pelvic veins, along with increased plasma volume. It is typically bilateral, mild, confined to the lower limbs, and improves with rest or leg elevation.

Why not the other options?

• A. Is present on both lower limbs and abdomen: Physiological edema is usually limited to the feet and ankles; generalized edema involving the abdomen is abnormal.
• B. Is associated with cardiac or renal pathology: Physiological edema occurs without underlying cardiac or renal disease.
• C. Is usually of moderate or severe grade: It is generally mild.
questions.learning: Disappears or markedly reduces on rest Physiological edema is common in late pregnancy due to venous stasis from uterine compression of the inferior vena cava and pelvic veins, along with increased plasma volume.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text:
Identify the true statement regarding split skin and full-thickness skin grafts:

1. Primary contracture is more with split skin grafts
2. Secondary contracture is more with split skin grafts
3. Primary contracture is more with full-thickness grafts
4. Secondary contracture is more with full-thickness grafts
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 2,3

Statements 2 and 3 are correct.

Split skin grafts (Thiersch grafts) are partial-thickness skin grafts consisting of the epidermis and a part of the dermis. Whereas, full-thickness grafts (Wolfe grafts) consist of the epidermis along with the entire dermis, with portions of the sweat glands, sebaceous glands, and hair follicles.

Primary contracture of the skin graft occurs due to passive recoil of the elastin fibers of the dermis. It occurs soon after the graft has been harvested.

• Since full-thickness grafts have more dermis (implying more elastin fibers), they undergo more primary contracture.
• Whereas, split skin grafts have less dermis, therefore, undergo less primary contracture.

Secondary contracture of the skin graft occurs due to the pull of myofibroblasts. It occurs over time, when the transplanted graft starts healing.

1. Full-thickness grafts have more ability to resist the pull of myofibroblasts, hence they have less secondary contracture.
2. Whereas, split skin grafts yield to the pull and develop more secondary contractures.

Primary contracture
Secondary contracture

Elastic recoil
Pull of myofibroblasts

Less in split-skin grafts
More in split-skin grafts

More in full-thickness grafts
Less in full-thickness grafts

Advantages of split over full-thickness skin graft:

• Large grafts can be harvested.
• In the case of thinner split-thickness grafts, the donor site heals more rapidly and can be reused in severe cases such as burns.
• Uptake is good. Meshing can be done, i.e. small splits are done in graft, allowing exudates to drain out, thus improving graft take up.
• Meshing also allows the graft to expand.

Advantages of full-thickness over split skin graft:

• It has a lesser degree of post-graft contraction
• Best cosmetic appearance as they include the highest number of skin appendage elements.
questions.learning: 2,3 Statements 2 and 3 are correct. Split skin grafts (Thiersch grafts) are partial-thickness skin grafts consisting of the epidermis and a part of the dermis.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which element acts as the cofactor for the enzyme glutathione peroxidase?
questions.explanation: Glutathione peroxidase is a vital antioxidant enzyme that protects cells from oxidative damage by catalyzing the reduction of hydrogen peroxide and lipid hydroperoxides. Its structural and functional integrity depends on selenium, which is incorporated into the enzyme as the amino acid selenocysteine at the active site. Manganese (Option A) is a cofactor for mitochondrial superoxide dismutase (Mn-SOD). Copper (Option C) and Zinc are cofactors for the cytosolic version of superoxide dismutase (CuZn-SOD) and are also essential for cytochrome c oxidase. Magnesium (Option D) is a ubiquitous cofactor for almost all enzymes utilizing ATP, such as hexokinase. Selenium deficiency can lead to Keshan disease (a cardiomyopathy), primarily because of the resulting impairment in glutathione peroxidase activity and increased oxidative stress. This biochemical relationship highlights the importance of trace elements in the body's endogenous defense mechanisms against reactive oxygen species, a frequent theme in biochemistry and nutritional science examinations
questions.learning: Glutathione peroxidase is a vital antioxidant enzyme that protects cells from oxidative damage by catalyzing the reduction of hydrogen peroxide and lipid hydroperoxides.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: One of the diabetic employees is stabbed in the middle of his palm. After three days, he develops swelling and severe pain and is unable to extend his middle and ring fingers, suspecting a buildup of pus in one of the palmar spaces. Infections of the:

* The ring and middle fingers spread into the mid-palmar space

* Index finger to thenar space

* Little finger spread to ulnar bursa and midpalmar space.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following statements is not true regarding Marjolin's ulcer?
options: It is seen in sites of chronic wounds or scars.
It can progress to squamous cell carcinoma.
It is radioresistant due to avascularity
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. It rapidly progresses to malignancy

The incorrect statement regarding Marjolin's ulcer is that it rapidly progresses to malignancy.

Marjolin’s ulcer refers to a rare form of cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma . It originates from areas of scarring or chronic wounds.

It progresses to full-fledged SCC gradually. The progression is gradual and slow. It has a long latency period of around 30 years. Since the ulcer occurs in scarred tissue without nerves and vessels, it is painless and radioresistant

Clinical signs of the tumour include:

* Ulceration

* Nodule formation

* An abrupt increase in size

* Everted or rolled wound margins

* Overgrowth of granulation tissue

* Tendency to bleed on manipulation

For the diagnosis, an edge-wedge biopsy can be done. MRI of the part and the regional node area is done to confirm the diagnosis. Treatment involves wide local excision, and in case of a large ulcer, amputation is required.

An image of Marjolin's ulcer is below:

Pearl PF0158: Marjolin’s Ulcer

* Low-grade cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma arising from

* Long-standing ulcer like venous ulcer

* Post-burn scar

* Chronic osteomyelitis

* Post-radiation ulcer.

* Slow progression to malignancy (SCC) since it is relatively avascular.

* Painless due to the absence of nerves in scar tissue.

* No secondary deposits since there are no lymphatics in scar tissue.

* Radioresistant due to avascularity.
questions.learning: It rapidly progresses to malignancy — The incorrect statement regarding Marjolin's ulcer is that it rapidly progresses to malignancy. Marjolin’s ulcer refers to a rare form of cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma .

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presents with chronic small bowel diarrhea. Duodenal biopsy reveals villous atrophy, and laboratory tests are positive for anti-endomysial antibodies and IgA tissue transglutaminase (TTG) antibodies. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical and laboratory triad of persistent small bowel diarrhea, villous atrophy on biopsy, and positive IgA tissue transglutaminase (TTG) and anti-endomysial antibodies is pathognomonic for Celiac sprue (Celiac disease) . This is an autoimmune-mediated enteropathy triggered by gluten ingestion in genetically susceptible individuals. Short bowel syndrome (Option A) results from the physical loss of intestinal length, typically after surgery. Whipple's disease (Option B) involves infection with Tropheryma whipplei and shows PAS-positive macrophages on biopsy. Tropical sprue (Option C) also causes villous atrophy and malabsorption but is associated with travel to endemic regions and is not linked to these specific autoantibodies. Because the TTG and endomysial antibodies are highly specific for gluten-sensitive enteropathy, Celiac sprue is the definitive diagnosis. Management requires a lifelong, strict gluten-free diet to allow the intestinal villi to recover and prevent long-term complications like lymphoma or osteoporosis
questions.learning: The clinical and laboratory triad of persistent small bowel diarrhea, villous atrophy on biopsy, and positive IgA tissue transglutaminase (TTG) and anti-endomysial antibodies is pathognomonic for Celiac sprue (Celiac disease) .

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 2-year-old previously unimmunized girl is brought with poor feeding and fever for 6 days. On day 4 of fever, her mother noticed a maculopapular reddish rash starting from the face and spreading over the neck, chest, arms and trunk over the next one day and she has developed extensive mouth ulcers. The child has a mid-arm circumference of 11 cm but no edema. As per IMNCI, she will be classified as:
options: Measles with eye or mouth complications
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Severe complicated measles

The child has typical measles:

• Fever followed by a maculopapular rash beginning on the face and spreading downward
• Extensive oral/mouth ulcers, indicating a severe mouth complication
• Poor feeding

As per IMNCI, measles with severe mouth complications is classified as severe complicated measles.

The MUAC of 11 cm indicates severe acute malnutrition (SAM), but the clinical classification being tested here is the measles classification, and the severe oral complication places the child in the severe category.

Why not the other options?

• A. Measles with eye or mouth complications: Used for less severe eye/mouth complications such as corneal ulceration or mouth ulcers without severe features.
• B. Measles: Used when there are no complications.
• D. Measles with severe acute malnutrition: Although MUAC 11 cm indicates SAM, the prominent severe measles complication determines the classification asked here.
questions.learning: Severe complicated measles — The child has typical measles: • Fever followed by a maculopapular rash beginning on the face and spreading downward • Extensive oral/mouth ulcers, indicating a severe mouth complication • Poor feeding As per IMNCI, measles…

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A patient presented with dysuria and pain in the back. His lumbar spine X-ray shows the below finding. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Hyperparathyroidism

The given clinical scenario and X-ray showing diffuse calcification of both kidneys are suggestive of nephrocalcinosis which is seen in hyperparathyroidism.

Nephrocalcinosis is the deposition of calcium in the kidney parenchyma or tubules which is seen in conditions causing hypercalcemia like hyperparathyroidism.

Clinical features of hyperparathyroidism:

• Bones:

• Pathological fractures
• Subperiosteal bone resorption - 2nd and 3rd digits, most common in the radial aspect
• Salt and pepper skull
• Osteitis fibrosa cystica or VonReckling Hausen’s disease of bone

• Stones

• Multiple and recurrent renal stones - most common
• Nephrocalcinosis

• Abdominal groans - colicky due to pancreatitis
• Psychiatric overtones - raised PTH causing CNS depression and psychiatric symptoms
• Band keratopathy
• Features of hypercalcemia -

• Vomiting
• Confusion
• ECG changes: increased PR interval, shortened QT interval

Investigations done in primary hyperparathyroidism:

• Ultrasonography of the neck is a safe and widely used technique for the localization of abnormal parathyroid glands.
• Nuclear medicine scanning with radiolabeled Sestamibi is also a widely used technique. Sestamibi accumulates in parathyroid adenomas. This radionuclide is concentrated in the thyroid and parathyroid tissue but usually washes out of normal thyroid tissue in under an hour. It persists in abnormal parathyroid tissue.
• Dual-energy radiographic absorptiometry is a useful tool to demonstrate skeletal involvement in primary hyperparathyroidism.
questions.learning: Hyperparathyroidism — The given clinical scenario and X-ray showing diffuse calcification of both kidneys are suggestive of nephrocalcinosis which is seen in hyperparathyroidism.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: According to the latest 2024 updates in NIS, what are the correct fractional doses of IPV vaccines?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 6 weeks, 14 weeks and 9 months

According to the latest 2024 updates in NIS, the correct fractional doses of IPV vaccines is given at 6 weeks, 14 weeks and 9 months.

In January 2023, updates were made to the National Immunization Schedule (NIS), which included the addition of a third dose of fractional IPV to be administered at 9 months of age.

According to the National Immunization Schedule (NIS) in India, the fractional Inactivated Polio Vaccine (f IPV) is administered in three fractional doses. The first dose is given at 6 weeks of age, the second dose is administered at 14 weeks, and the third dose is administered at 9 months. Each fractional dose consists of 0.1 ml of IPV, delivered intradermally. This schedule is designed to enhance immunity against poliovirus in infants.

The adoption of fractional dosing in the NIS aims to optimise vaccine utilisation while maintaining effective immunisation coverage. Studies have indicated that three fractional doses of IPV can elicit an immune response comparable to that of a full-dose regimen, especially when administered at the recommended intervals. This approach not only ensures adequate protection for children but also contributes to the global effort to eradicate polio by making efficient use of available vaccine resources.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 20-year-old male patient presents to the emergency department with swelling at the base of the thumb after falling on an outstretched hand while playing football. Which of the following is most likely to be to be injured?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Scaphoid

The history of falls on the outstretched hand and swelling at the base of the thumb suggests the diagnosis of a scaphoid fracture.

The scaphoid is the most commonly fractured carpal bone. Mechanism of injury is:

* Axial compression directly on the bone

* Hyperextending the wrist joint

Such mechanisms are commonly seen when a person falls onto an outstretched hand.

Clinical features:

* Pain is typically felt along the radial side of the wrist. Proximal to the metacarpal of the thumb.

* An important feature is focal tenderness, which is usually detected at specific points:

* Just below Lister’s tubercle

* Over the volar prominence near the distal wrist crease

* Swelling is not specific. It may or may not be present.

The most common complications include nonunion, avascular necrosis (osteonecrosis) of the proximal fracture segment, and osteoarthritis.

Diagnostic sign- precisely localized tenderness in the anatomical snuff box.

X-ray of the wrist is taken but it has a high false-negative rate. Hence empiric splinting or MRI is recommended as the next step in such cases where clinical suspicion exists but X-ray findings are normal. Undisplaced fractures are managed by immobilization in a scaphoid cast applied in a glass-holding position. Reduction with compression screw is preferred for displaced fractures.
questions.learning: Scaphoid — The history of falls on the outstretched hand and swelling at the base of the thumb suggests the diagnosis of a scaphoid fracture. The scaphoid is the most commonly fractured carpal bone.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following graphs represents normal response to OGTT?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Graph D

The graph representing normal response to oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT) is graph D.

Oral glucose tolerance test is routinely used to diagnose gestational diabetes mellitus. It is performed by giving a bolus of glucose (75g) to the patient, and measuring blood glucose at intervals of time to assess the tolerance and response of the islets of pancreas to glucose. 5 measurements of glucose is noted in blood and urine at half hour intervals.

Indications:

• Patients with symptoms suggestive of diabetes mellitus, but with fasting blood glucose value being borderline (between 100-126 mg/dl).
• Excessive weight gain during pregnancy, a past history of big baby (more than 4 kg) or a past history of miscarriage.
• To rule out benign renal glucosuria.

Glucose Tolerance Curve (GTC) is the graph plotted by taking plasma glucose measurements on Y-axis and plotting against time, on the X-axis.

Graph D: Normal: This is the normal response seen in a healthy individual. It is characterized by a peak glucose value reached within 1 hour, following which glucose levels reach the base value. The levels don't cross the renal threshold at any point of time.

Graph A and Graph B: Diabetes mellitus: The graph will peak after 1-1.5 hours and does not return to fasting level within 2.5 hours. The highest value exceeds the renal threshold.

Depending on severity, the graph can show mild, moderate, and severe diabetic curve.

Graph C: Lag curve: The fasting blood glucose is normal here, but the curve rapidly rises in 1/2 to 1 hour and exceeds the renal threshold. There is a rapid and complete return to normal value in a few minutes. This is seen in hyperthyroidism, early diabetes, and sometimes during pregnancy.
questions.learning: Graph D — The graph representing normal response to oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT) is graph D. Oral glucose tolerance test is routinely used to diagnose gestational diabetes mellitus.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 30-year-old woman presents with persistent hypertension, chest pain and cramping in her legs, particularly during exertion. A chest radiograph was taken, which reveals the condition, as shown in the image below. What is the likely underlying cause of her hypertension?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Coarctation of aorta

This clinical scenario and the image showing the figure of 3 sign point towards coarctation of aorta as the cause of hypertension in this patient.

The figure of 3 sign refers to the indentation of the aorta at the coarctation site. There is pre and post-stenotic dilatation along with left paramediastinal shadow, as shown below.

Other chest X-ray features in coarctation of the aorta are dilated left subclavian artery, dilated ascending aorta and notching of ribs 4-8 due to rib erosion by dilated collateral vessels.
questions.learning: Coarctation of aorta — This clinical scenario and the image showing the figure of 3 sign point towards coarctation of aorta as the cause of hypertension in this patient.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 22-year-old man with recurrent bleeding undergoes a CECT scan showing several findings. Which of the following statements is true?
options: Bleeding is from the adjacent invading blood vessels
questions.explanation: The clinical scenario of a 22-year-old male with recurrent epistaxis (bleeding) and a mass on CECT is characteristic of Juvenile Nasopharyngeal Angiofibroma (JNA). A fundamental and dangerous pathological feature of JNA is that its tumor vessels lack a muscular coat (tunica media), which means they lack the ability to contract. This absence of contractility explains why even minor trauma to the tumor results in profuse, life-threatening hemorrhage that is difficult to stop. JNA is characteristically benign but locally aggressive and typically has a pseudo-capsule, making Option D false. The tumor does not usually outgrow its supply; it is highly vascular (Option A). The bleeding comes from the tumor's own abnormal vessels, not just invaded ones (Option C). Because of this hemorrhage risk, preoperative embolization of the feeding vessels (e.g., maxillary artery) is mandatory before surgical excision. JNA is a classic medical licensing topic due to these unique vascular properties
questions.learning: The clinical scenario of a 22-year-old male with recurrent epistaxis (bleeding) and a mass on CECT is characteristic of Juvenile Nasopharyngeal Angiofibroma (JNA).

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following drugs acts by inhibiting the catechol-O-methyltransferase enzyme?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Tolcapone

Tolcapone acts by inhibiting the catechol-O-methyltransferase enzyme and is used in the management of Parkinson's disease.

Parkinsons disease arises as a result of the loss of dopaminergic neurons in the striatum. Therefore the mainstay of treatment in this disease is to increase dopamine in this area.

Important drugs used in the treatment of Parkinson's disease are

1. Levodopa is a prodrug. It crosses the blood-brain barrier. In the brain, levodopa is converted to dopamine by decarboxylation in dopaminergic neurons in the striatum.

Levodopa therapy significantly improves the signs and symptoms of Parkinson's disease. But the major problem with levodopa is the wearing-off phenomenon. Each dose of levodopa improves the symptoms for a period of 1–2 h, but rigidity and akinesia return rapidly after the effect of the drug reduces. Increasing the dose and frequency of administration can improve this situation, but the patients often develop dyskinesias, excessive and abnormal involuntary movements. In the later stages of the disease, patients may fluctuate rapidly between being “off,” having no beneficial effects from their medications, and being “on” having some beneficial effects but along with side effects.

2. Carbidopa- is a peripheral decarboxylase inhibitor. Levodopa if administered alone will undergo decarboxylation by the decarboxylases present in the intestinal mucosa and other peripheral sites. This will lead to decreased concentration of the drug reaching the brain. In order to prevent this levodopa is always given with carbidopa.

3. Catechol-O-methyl transferase (COMT) inhibitors- The addition of carbidopa to the levodopa prevents the peripheral decarboxylation of the drug. However, levodopa can now be methylated by catechol-O-methyl transferases and inactivate it. This is prevented by COMT inhibitors tolcapone and entacapone.

4. Selective monoamine oxidase B (MAO-B) inhibitors- Dopamine in the striatum is predominantly metabolized by the MAO-B enzyme. Inhibiting this enzyme will increase the dopamine concentrations in these neurons. Eg. selegiline and rasagiline.

5. Dopamine receptor agonists- They act at the dopamine receptors and help in the improvement of the symptoms. Rotigotine acts on D1 and D2 receptors, whereas ropinirole and pramipexole both act on the D2 and D3 receptors. Apomorphine acts on D4 and mildly on D2, D3, and D5 receptors. It also has adrenergic action.

6. Muscarinic receptor antagonists- these are used as adjuncts to dopamine therapy. Eg. trihexyphenidyl and benztropine. Diphenhydramine, an antihistamine is also used.

7. Amantadine is an antiviral agent used for the prophylaxis and treatment of influenza A. It has antiparkinsonian activity. It alters dopamine release in the striatum, has anticholinergic properties, and blocks-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptors. It can be used in mild diseases.
questions.learning: Tolcapone Tolcapone acts by inhibiting the catechol-O-methyltransferase enzyme and is used in the management of Parkinson's disease. Parkinsons disease arises as a result of the loss of dopaminergic neurons in the striatum.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: The Hallpike (Dix–Hallpike) maneuver is used to evaluate which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation: The Dix-Hallpike maneuver is a diagnostic clinical test specifically used to assess vestibular function, specifically to confirm a diagnosis of Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo (BPPV). It involves moving the patient from a sitting to a supine position with the head turned 45 degrees to one side and extended 20 degrees back. A positive test is indicated by the elicitation of vertigo and a characteristic rotatory nystagmus, which signifies that loose calcium carbonate crystals (otoconia) have entered the posterior semicircular canal. Audiometry (Option B) and cochlear function tests (Option C) assess hearing thresholds rather than balance. Corneal tests (Option D) evaluate cranial nerve function (V and VII) or ocular health. The Hallpike maneuver is the gold standard bedside test for differentiating positional vertigo from other balance disorders. Thus, it is a primary tool for evaluating the peripheral vestibular apparatus
questions.learning: The Dix-Hallpike maneuver is a diagnostic clinical test specifically used to assess vestibular function, specifically to confirm a diagnosis of Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo (BPPV).

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following are causes of GnRH dependent precocious puberty? 1. Constitutional 2. Tubercular encephalitis 3. McCune-Albright syndrome 4. Primary hypothyroidism Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1, 2 and 4

GnRH-dependent (central) precocious puberty (CPP) results from premature activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal (HPG) axis.

Why are the statements correct/incorrect?

• 1. Constitutional (idiopathic): Correct. This is the most common cause, especially in girls.
• 2. Tubercular encephalitis/CNS infection: Correct. CNS infections can damage hypothalamic pathways and trigger central precocious puberty.
• 3. McCune–Albright syndrome: Incorrect. It is GnRH-independent (peripheral) due to autonomous estrogen production.
• 4. Primary hypothyroidism: Although classically categorized as GnRH-independent, severe longstanding hypothyroidism can present with precocious puberty (Van Wyk–Grumbach syndrome).
questions.learning: 1, 2 and 4 GnRH-dependent (central) precocious puberty (CPP) results from premature activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal (HPG) axis. Why are the statements correct/incorrect? • 1.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: At what point in time is the population assessed for calculation of crude death rate?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1st July

Crude death rate is a mortality indicator, which uses the mid-year population as its denominator. The mid year population is always attributed as population on 1st July of any year.

Pearl PF0954: Crude Death Rate

Crude death rate:

* The crude death rate is the simplest measure of mortality.

* It is the number of deaths (from all causes) per 1000 estimated mid-year population in one year, in a given place.

* Crude death rate =  (Number of deaths per year)/(Mid-year population) x 1000

* Disadvantage: lacks comparability for communities with populations that differ in age, sex, race, etc.

* Currently, the crude death rate in India is 6.3.

Note: Crude death rate according to SRS in the year 2018 is 6.2
questions.learning: 1st July Crude death rate is a mortality indicator, which uses the mid-year population as its denominator. The mid year population is always attributed as population on 1st July of any year.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A female patient with a known case of thyroid malignancy was found to show high levels of serum calcitonin. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Medullary thyroid carcinoma

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC). Histopathology shows the presence of amyloid deposits that are derived from the altered calcitonin molecules.

Medullary thyroid carcinoma is a tumor of parafollicular or C cells of the thyroid gland. They are derived from the neural crest cells of the ultimobranchial bodies.

Most of the MTCs occur sporadically. However, around a quarter of the cancers are associated with familial MTC, MEN2A, and MEN2B.

Patients with sporadic MTC present at an older age, whereas patients with familial MTC usually present at a younger age. Features of MTC include:

* Painful neck mass with cervical lymphadenopathy

* Dysphagia, dysphonia or dyspnea if locally invaded

* Diarrhoea due to increased intestinal motility by serotonin

* Cushingoid habitus due to ectopic ACTH production

* Metastasis is blood-borne

* Microscopically, they consist of sheets of neoplastic cells separated by collagen and amyloid stroma

It is diagnosed by careful family history, physical examination, raised calcitonin, CEA levels, and fine-needle aspiration biopsy of the mass.

Total thyroidectomy with central neck node dissection is the treatment of choice in MTC patients. External beam radiotherapy can be used in patients with unresectable tumors. Targeted therapy can be considered using vandetanib, sorafenib, sunitinib, and cabozantinib.

Prophylactic total thyroidectomy should be considered within 5years of age in MEN2A mutation and within 1year of age in MEN2B mutation.

Surgical management of MTC is as follows:

Extent of cancer
Surgery done

MTC without LN involvement

Total thyroidectomy + Central neck dissection (prophylactic)

MTC + level VI LN involved

Total thyroidectomy + Central neck dissection (therapeutic) + Modified radical neck dissection (prophylactic)

MTC + other LNs involved

Total thyroidectomy + Central neck dissection + Modified radical neck dissection (therapeutic)
questions.learning: Medullary thyroid carcinoma — The given clinical scenario is suggestive of medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC). Histopathology shows the presence of amyloid deposits that are derived from the altered calcitonin molecules.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A patient presents to the hospital with a history of high fever and chills. On examination, a maculopapular rash was observed over the neck, with a positive tourniquet test. What is the probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Dengue haemorrhagic fever

The clinical features are suggestive of dengue haemorrhagic fever.

Dengue, also known as break-bone fever, manifests after an incubation period of 3-14 days. Dengue fever is an acute febrile illness with two or more of the following manifestations: headache, retroorbital pain, myalgia, arthralgia, and rash.

Dengue haemorrhagic fever, or dengue shock syndrome, can occur in individuals with preexisting non-neutralising heterologous dengue antibodies caused by previous infection with a different serotype of the virus or passively acquired maternal antibodies in children. Initially, symptoms simulate normal dengue; however, the patient’s condition worsens.

The virus–antibody complexes are formed within a few days of the second dengue infection, and the non-neutralising enhancing antibodies promote infection of higher numbers of mononuclear cells followed by the release of cytokines, vasoactive mediators, and procoagulants, leading to the disseminated intravascular coagulation seen in the haemorrhagic fever syndrome.

The most important pathology of dengue haemorrhagic fever is increased vascular permeability with plasma leakage into the interstitial spaces associated with increased levels of vasoactive cytokines, which can lead to life-threatening shock in some patients. The clinical criteria of dengue haemorrhagic fever are dengue fever with haemorrhagic tendencies evidenced by one b more of the following:

* Positive tourniquet test

* Petechiae, ecchymoses or purpura

* Bleeding from the mucosa, gastrointestinal tract, injection sites or other sites

* Thrombocytopenia, a more than 20% drop in haematocrit following volume replacement treatment compared to baseline

* Signs of plasma leakage (pleural effusion, ascites, hypoproteinaemia)

Dengue shock syndrome is characterised by all the above criteria for dengue haemorrhagic fever with evidence of circulatory failure manifested by rapid, weak pulse and narrow pulse pressure or hypotension for age, cold, clammy skin and restlessness.

Other options:

Option B: Quartan fever, which occurs on the first and fourth days, is typically associated with Plasmodium malariae infection.

Option C: The disease can present as classical filariasis or occult filariasis. Clinical features include:

* Classical filariasis – Fever, lymphangitis, lymphadenitis, lymphedema, lymphangiovarix, hydrocele, lymphorrhagia, elephantiasis

* Occult filariasis – Massive eosinophilia, hepatosplenomegaly, dyspnoea, arthritis, glomerulonephritis, etc.

Option D: Chikungunya fever is due to infection with the chikungunya virus, spread by mosquitos. The Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus mosquitoes are the most common vectors. It presents as an acute onset of fever, arthralgia, and myalgia with other flu symptoms such as headache, loss of appetite, and nausea. A progressive maculopapular rash develops, which is more pronounced on the trunk.
questions.learning: Dengue haemorrhagic fever — The clinical features are suggestive of dengue haemorrhagic fever. Dengue, also known as break-bone fever, manifests after an incubation period of 3-14 days.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 52-year-old patient underwent a lumpectomy and was found to have low-grade DCIS with 2 mm clear margins. What is the next step in management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Radiotherapy

Ductal Carcinoma In Situ (DCIS) is a non-invasive breast malignancy in which malignant epithelial cells are confined to the ductal system without breaching the basement membrane. It is Stage 0 (TisN0M0) breast cancer. In a patient with:

• Low-grade DCIS
• Breast-conserving surgery (lumpectomy)
• Clear surgical margins (≥2 mm)

The standard next step is adjuvant whole-breast radiotherapy, which significantly reduces the risk of ipsilateral local recurrence.

Why not the other options?

• A. Mastectomy: Reserved for multicentric/extensive DCIS, persistently positive margins, or when breast conservation is not feasible.
• B. BCT (Breast-Conserving Therapy): Lumpectomy has already been performed; breast-conserving therapy consists of lumpectomy + radiotherapy.
• D. Tamoxifen: May be offered in ER-positive DCIS after surgery ± radiotherapy to reduce recurrence but is not a substitute for radiotherapy.
questions.learning: Radiotherapy Ductal Carcinoma — In Situ (DCIS) is a non-invasive breast malignancy in which malignant epithelial cells are confined to the ductal system without breaching the basement membrane.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is the most characteristic feature of Kallmann syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Anosmia

Anosmia is the most characteristic feature of Kallman's syndrome.

Kallman's syndrome is a hypothalamic disorder that occurs due to defective gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH).

It is mainly associated with anosmia or hyposmia or hypoplasia. Other associated features such as colour blindness, optic atrophy, deafness, cleft palate, renal abnormalities, and cryptorchidism may be present.

The presenting features in males are delayed puberty and micropenis while females present with primary amenorrhoea and failure of secondary sexual development.

The condition is characterised by low luteinizing hormone (LH), follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH), testosterone and estradiol.

Treatment includes human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) or testosterone in males for restoration of puberty and secondary sexual characteristics. In females, cyclic estrogen and progestin can be given. Fertility is restored by giving gonadotropins or pulsatile GnRH
questions.learning: Anosmia Anosmia is the most characteristic feature of Kallman's syndrome. Kallman's syndrome is a hypothalamic disorder that occurs due to defective gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: The lab technician notices a urine sample from a 4-year-old male that was normal on collection but turns into the colour shown in the image after a few hours. It further darkened over the next few hours. Deficiency of which of the following can cause this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Homogentisic acid oxidase

Urine turning dark in colour on long-standing is a characteristic feature of alkaptonuria caused by the deficiency of homogentisic acid oxidase.

The dark colour of the urine on standing is due to the oxidation and polymerization of homogentisic acid.

Features of alkaptonuria:

* Uncommon autosomal recessive disorder

* Occurs due to the deficiency of homogentisic acid oxidase.

* This results in the accumulation of high amounts of homogentisic acid.

* The formed homogentisic acid is deposited in tissues or is excreted in urine.

* Clinical manifestations of alkaptonuria consist of ochronosis and arthritis in adulthood. Arthritis predominantly involves the spine, hip, and knee. Radiologically, it is characterized by intervertebral calcifications.

Ochronosis : Bluish black discoloration of sclera and ear cartilage due to deposition of homogentisic acid, beginning in late adolescence.

Other options:

A. Beta-carotene: Beta-carotene is a pigment that can give a yellow or orange color to certain foods and, to some extent, can affect the color of urine. However, beta-carotene deficiency is not associated with the darkening of urine on long-standing. It is not a characteristic feature of beta-carotene deficiency.

B. Tyrosine aminotransferase: Tyrosine aminotransferase is an enzyme involved in the metabolism of the amino acid tyrosine. However, deficiency of tyrosine aminotransferase is not known to cause darkening of urine on long-standing. Tyrosine aminotransferase deficiency is a very rare condition and is associated with symptoms related to impaired tyrosine metabolism, such as neurological and developmental issues.

C. L-ascorbic acid: L-ascorbic acid, also known as vitamin C, is an antioxidant and plays a role in various metabolic processes. While high doses of vitamin C supplements can sometimes cause changes in urine color, such as a more yellow or orange hue, deficiency of L-ascorbic acid is not associated with darkening of urine on long-standing. Vitamin C deficiency (scurvy) is characterized by symptoms such as fatigue, joint pain, and skin changes.
questions.learning: Homogentisic acid oxidase Urine turning dark in colour on long-standing is a characteristic feature of alkaptonuria caused by the deficiency of homogentisic acid oxidase.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A child presents with thinning of hair and scaling of the scalp. On taking further history, it is found that she consumes raw eggs in her diet regularly. The given manifestations are due to the deficiency of which of the following vitamins?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Biotin

The given clinical scenario of scaling and alopecia and the history of raw egg consumption are suggestive of biotin deficiency.

Raw egg white contains a glycoprotein known as avidin, which tightly binds to biotin and renders it unabsorbable from the intestine. Hence, there can be a biotin deficiency state.

Biotin deficiency may cause:

• Dermatitis, scaling, seborrheic, and erythematous rash
• Mental status changes (depression, hallucinations)
• Hyperesthesia
• Alopecia
• Atrophic glossitis

In infants, biotin deficiency presents as hypotonia, lethargy, and apathy. In addition, infants may develop alopecia and a characteristic rash that includes the ears.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following is the first step after fitting the pessary to check if the pessary is adequately retained?
options: Asking the patient to void and see if the pessary is in place
Seeing if the patient feels any discomfort, which means that the pessary is retained
Asking the patient to perform the Valsalva manouvre and see if the pessary is in place
Being able to admit two fingers between the ring and the pessary.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Asking the patient to perform the Valsalva manouvre and see if the pessary is in place

The first step after fitting the pessary to check if the pessary is adequately retained is to ask the patient to perform Valsalva's maneuver or cough and see if the pessary is in place.

There is some level of descent of the pessary with these maneuvers is to be expected, but the pessary should return to its normal position when these efforts are stopped. If the pessary descends to the introitus with these maneuvers, then a larger size pessary should be tried.

The pessary is well-fitted if you are able to slide the ring of the pessary up and down along the vaginal sidewall. It is well-fitted if you are able to insert one finger between the vaginal sidewall and the edge of the pessary. When the labia are separated, a well-supported pessary is not usually visible.

The patient should be comfortable, and able to void urine with the pessary in place before leaving the clinic.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Name the parasite whose microfilaria have a sheath with no nuclei at the tail end.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Wuchereria bancrofti

A sheathed microfilaria with a pointed tail free of nuclei is suggestive of Wuchereria bancrofti.

Wuchereria bancrofti causes lymphatic filariasis and most cases are seen in India.

Clinical features include massive eosinophilia, hepatosplenomegaly, pulmonary manifestations like dry nocturnal cough, asthmatic wheezing, and dyspnea. It can also cause arthritis, glomerulonephritis, thrombophlebitis, etc. The classical features seen in lymphatic filariasis are usually absent.

Elephantiasis refers to the painful swelling of the legs and genital organs seen in late-stage disease.

Image showing elephantiasis-

Investigations:

Demonstration of the microfilaria in peripheral blood, chylous urine, hydrocele fluid, etc is done.  The specimen of choice is peripheral blood. Night blood samples between 10 pm and 4 am are preferred. This is because the microfilaria shows nocturnal periodicity.

DEC provocation test: In this test, a small dose of DEC is given 20-50 minutes before sample collection so that the microfilaria appears in the blood even during the daytime.

The image below shows the life cycle of Wuchereria bancrofti.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 40-year-old male patient presented with complaints of drowsiness and was admitted for evaluation. Sodium was found to be 98 mEq/L, which was corrected to 110 mEq/L with 3% saline in 24 hours. The patient recovered for a while and had an altered sensorium later. Now, he developed quadriparesis and bilateral conjugate gaze palsy. Which is the investigation to be done in this case?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. MRI brain

| Clue | Interpretation

| ---- | --------------

| Severe hyponatremia (Na⁺ = 98) | Chronic adaptation likely

| Rapid correction with hypertonic saline |  Risk factor

| Initial improvement → then deterioration | Classic biphasic course

| Quadriparesis + gaze palsy | Brainstem (pons) involvement

Rapid correction of severe hyponatremia predisposes to osmotic demyelination syndrome (central pontine myelinolysis).

Features like delayed altered sensorium, quadriparesis, and bilateral gaze palsy are classic for pontine involvement.

Chronic hyponatremia

↓

Brain adapts (↓ osmoles)

↓

Rapid Na⁺ correction

↓

Extracellular osmolality ↑

↓

Water leaves neurons

↓

Cell shrinkage + myelin damage

↓

Demyelination (pons)

| Feature | CPM (ODS)

| ------- | ---------

| Cause | Rapid Na⁺ correction

| Site | Pons

| Symptoms | Quadriparesis, gaze palsy

| Best test | ⭐ MRI brain

| CSF | Normal

The investigation of choice is MRI brain, which shows pontine hyperintensities on T2/FLAIR.

CSF and EEG are non-diagnostic, and BAEP is not useful for confirming demyelination.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A study was conducted among nursing staff to analyze the time spent on different aspects of patient care, including bed preparation, monitoring vital signs, attending doctors’ rounds, blood sampling, and drug administration. Which of the following management techniques is most appropriate for this type of analysis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Work sampling

The management technique that is being applied for the above study is work sampling.

Work sampling is a quantitative management technique. It refers to the systematic observation and recording of the activities of one or more individuals. It is done at predetermined or random intervals. It mainly includes analyzing the type of activities performed and the time needed to perform the same.

These studies have been done on doctors, nurses, pharmacists, and laboratory technicians. This technique can find the appropriateness of the current staff, job description, and training. This may standardize the methods of performing activities and determine the manpower needed in an organization.

Management is the purposeful and effective use of resources such as manpower, materials, and finances for the fulfillment of a pre-determined objective. They consist of four basic activities: planning, organizing, communicating, and monitoring.

Management techniques are of two types:

Quantitative methods

Methods based on behavioral sciences

• Cost-Benefit analysis
• Cost-Effective analysis
• Cost-Accounting
• Input-Output analysis
• Model
• Systems analysis
• Network analysis

• Program Evaluation and Review Technique (PERT)
• Critical Path Method (CPM)

• Planning–Programming–Budgeting System (PPBS)
• Work sampling
• Decision making

• Organizational design
• Personnel management
• Communication
• Information systems
• Management by objectives (MBO)

Other options:

Option A: Network analysis is a systematic approach used to plan, organize, and manage complex projects by breaking them down into interconnected tasks. It helps in identifying the sequence of activities, estimating time requirements, and optimizing resource allocation.

Option C: Critical pathway method is a type of network analysis technique. The longest path in the network is called the critical path. If any delay in activity along the critical pathway, the entire study will be delayed.

Option D: Systems analysis is a quantitative method of management. Systems analysis helps decision-makers by identifying the problem, setting objectives, exploring and evaluating alternative solutions for cost-effectiveness, and reviewing objectives when necessary.
questions.learning: Work sampling — The management technique that is being applied for the above study is work sampling. Work sampling is a quantitative management technique.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Determine the classification of the myoma denoted as '4' in the provided image.
questions.explanation: A pedunculated submucosal myoma is a type of fibroid that arises beneath the endometrium and projects into the uterine cavity, remaining attached by a thin stalk. These fibroids can sometimes extend toward or even through the cervix. Because of their intracavitary location, they commonly cause heavy menstrual bleeding (menorrhagia), infertility, and recurrent pregnancy loss. In contrast, a submucous myoma (option D) refers to a broad-based lesion beneath the endometrium without a stalk. The presence of a distinct pedicle in the image confirms that this is not a simple submucous fibroid but a pedunculated variant. Why other options are wrong: (B) Subserous myoma → grows outward from uterus (C) Parasitic myoma → detached and vascularized externally (D) Submucous myoma → no stalk
questions.learning: A pedunculated submucosal myoma is a type of fibroid that arises beneath the endometrium and projects into the uterine cavity, remaining attached by a thin stalk.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A cohort study was conducted with drinkers and non-drinkers of green tea to study its effect on diabetes mellitus. The risk ratio was found to be 0.84. Which of the following statements is correct?
options: Green tea reduces the risk of diabetes
Green tea increases the risk of diabetes
Data insufficient to establish causal association
The value (0.85) tends to be close to 1, hence there is no effect
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Green tea reduces the risk of diabetes

Green tea reduces the risk of diabetes mellitus is the correct statement since the risk ratio is 0.84.

Relative risk (RR) or risk ratio is the ratio of the incidence of the disease (or death) among exposed and the incidence among non-exposed. It can be determined from a cohort study.

It is a direct measure of the strength of the association between suspected cause and effect. The larger the RR, the greater the strength of the association between the suspected factor and disease.

• RR < 1 indicates inverse association(protective effect).
• RR = 1 indicates no association
• RR > 1 indicates a positive association.
• RR of 2 indicates a 100% increase in risk.

In the question, the risk ratio is less than 1. Hence it implies the incidence of diabetes mellitus is reduced when exposed to green tea.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: The probable diagnosis based on the below clinical image of the breast is?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Mondor's disease

The image shows a thrombosed subcutaneous cord attached to the skin of the breast which is the pathognomic feature of Mondor's Disease.

Mondor’s disease is the thrombophlebitis of the superficial veins of the breast and anterior chest wall. It may also occur in the arm or penis. On raising the arm, the skin over the chest gets stretched and a narrow, shallow groove alongside the cord is seen. It is treated by restricting arm movements and usually subsides within a few months without recurrence, complications, or deformity.

The differential diagnosis to be considered is lymphatic permeation from an occult carcinoma of the breast.

Other options:

Option A: Paget’s disease is a type of ductal carcinoma in situ arising from the nipple and commonly presents as nipple erosion.

Option B: Zuska’s disease, also called recurrent periductal mastitis, is a condition of recurrent retroareolar infections and abscesses. Smoking has been implicated as a risk factor for this condition. Managed symptomatically by antibiotics coupled with incision and drainage as necessary.

Option D: Tietze’s syndrome refers to the benign inflammation of one or more costal cartilages.
questions.learning: Mondor's disease — The image shows a thrombosed subcutaneous cord attached to the skin of the breast which is the pathognomic feature of Mondor's Disease.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Among the direct causes of maternal mortality during or shortly after labor and delivery, which is the most common contributor to maternal deaths?
questions.explanation: In the context of global health and obstetric care, Hemorrhage (specifically Postpartum Hemorrhage or PPH) remains the most prevalent and leading direct cause of maternal mortality worldwide. PPH can occur rapidly after delivery and is often defined as blood loss exceeding 500 ml following vaginal birth or 1000 ml after a cesarean section. While Anemia (Option D) is a major indirect cause and a significant risk factor that exacerbates the effects of blood loss, it is not the primary direct mechanism of death. Embolism (Option A), including amniotic fluid embolism or pulmonary embolism, and pre-existing Heart Disease (Option B) are significant contributors but occur with much lower frequency than hemorrhage. Effective management of PPH involves active management of the third stage of labor, use of uterotonics like oxytocin, and timely surgical intervention if medical therapy fails. Reducing deaths from hemorrhage is a cornerstone of global initiatives aimed at achieving Sustainable Development Goal targets for maternal health
questions.learning: In the context of global health and obstetric care, Hemorrhage (specifically Postpartum Hemorrhage or PPH) remains the most prevalent and leading direct cause of maternal mortality worldwide.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 73 old male smoker with a past history of coronary artery disease presents with blackening of the toes. An image of the foot is shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Atherosclerosis

The given clinical scenario of an elderly smoker with past history of coronary artery disease and gangrene of the first three toes is likely to have atherosclerosis.

Atherosclerosis is a chronic inflammatory disease in which there is a build-up of plaques inside arteries.  It is common after 50 years.These plaques are principally composed of lipids that induce an inflammatory reaction causing turbulent flow leading to atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease(ASCVD). This results in atheroma formation in arteries throughout the body hampering the blood flow and leading to ischemia.

Risk factors include smoking, hypertension, diabetes, and elevated cholesterol. The infrarenal part of the abdominal aorta, coronary arteries, iliofemoral vessels, carotid bifurcation, and popliteal arteries are the common arteries involved. The presence of atherosclerotic disease in one part of the body suggests there could be blockade in other parts as well.

Patients with chronic limb ischemia present with rest pain and tissue loss such as gangrene and ulceration. An ischemic ulcer is painful, pale, and cyanotic in appearance with absent pulsations. It may be associated with transient ischemic attacks, chest pain, eye problems, mesenteric ischemia, and altered renal function.

Doppler or angiogram can be done to identify the block. It is important to evaluate these patients for intercurrent cardiac disorders.

Management involves cessation of smoking and modification of other risk factors such as hypertension, diabetes, and hypercholesterolemia. High-intensity statins should be given irrespective of cholesterol levels in ASCVD. Other drugs that can be used include pentoxifylline, aspirin, clopidogrel, and cilostazol. Surgical options include thrombectomy, endarterectomy, bypass grafting, and amputations if the limb is gangrenous.

Complications of atherosclerosis include

* Narrowing of the arteries: Coronary, cerebral, renal, mesenteric, iliofemoral. > 70% narrowing (severe) causes reduced blood flow.

* lschaemia, ulcerations, gangrene

* Embolism: From atheromatous plaques

* Aneurysm formation: Mainly abdominal aorta and also in peripheral arteries

Option A: Buerger’s disease is a progressive nonatherosclerotic segmental inflammatory disease that most often affects small- and medium-sized arteries, veins, and nerves of the upper and lower extremities.

* Typically presents in young male smokers, with symptoms beginning prior to age 40.

* Patients initially present with the foot, leg, arm, or hand.

* Claudication may progress to rest pain to calf claudication and eventually ischemic rest pain and ulcerations on the toes, feet, or fingers and even gangrene.

If the patient continues to smoke, the disease progresses into the collaterals, blocking them eventually, leading to severe ischemia which is called decompensatory peripheral vascular disease/ critical limb ischemia which presents as rest pain, ulceration, and gangrene.

Option C: Raynaud's disease usually occurs in females and affects bilateral upper limbs. Patients present with pallor/blanching (syncope), dusky cyanosis (asphyxia), and rubor/painful red de-engorgement (recovery). Peripheral pulses are normal.

Option D: Giant cell arteritis is characterized by giant cell infiltration of the arterial wall (giant cell arteritis) involving superficial temporal, facial, retinal, upper limb, coronary and vertebral arteries. Patients present with severe headaches, visual abnormalities, jaw claudication, and a tender superficial temporal artery.

Pearl PF1741: Ankle–brachial Pressure Index (ABPI)

The ankle-brachial Pressure Index (ABPI) is the ratio of systolic pressure at the ankle to that in the arm.

The numerator is the highest pressure in the dorsalis pedis, posterior tibial, or peroneal artery and the denominator is the highest brachial systolic pressure.

ABPI Reading
Interpretation

>0.91 < 1.3
Normal

<0.9
Diagnostic of occlusive arterial disease in patients with symptoms of claudication or other signs of ischemia

0.5 to 0.9
Arterial obstruction often associated with claudication

<0.3
Critical limb ischemia (multilevel obstruction i.e any combination of iliac, femoral or tibial vessel disease and may be associated with non-healing ulcerations, ischemic rest pain, or pedal gangrene.

>1.4
Signifies poor compressibility of the arteries. Mostly due to calcification because of increased age, diabetes etc.

Note: A fall in the resting ABPI of more than 20% after exercise is indicative of arterial disease.
questions.learning: Atherosclerosis — The given clinical scenario of an elderly smoker with past history of coronary artery disease and gangrene of the first three toes is likely to have atherosclerosis.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: The Model for End Stage Liver Disease (MELD) score includes which of the following variables? 1. Serum bilirubin 2. Serum albumin 3. Serum creatinine 4. International Normalised Ratio (INR) Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1, 3 and 4

The Model for End-Stage Liver Disease (MELD) score is used to assess the severity of chronic liver disease, estimate 3-month mortality, and prioritize patients for liver transplantation.

The MELD score is calculated using three laboratory variables:

• Serum bilirubin
• Serum creatinine
• International Normalized Ratio (INR)

Serum albumin is NOT included in the MELD score.
questions.learning: 1, 3 and 4 The Model for End-Stage Liver Disease (MELD) score is used to assess the severity of chronic liver disease, estimate 3-month mortality, and prioritize patients for liver transplantation.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of the following is not a feature of the optic disc in glaucoma?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Roenne's nasal step

Roenne's nasal step is not a feature of the optic disc in glaucoma.

Roenne's nasal step is a visual field defect. It is the result of two arcuate scotomas running in different arcs and meeting at the horizontal meridian. This forms a right-angled defect in the nasal side of the visual field.

Early glaucomatous changes of the optic disc include an increase in cup-disc ratio (C/D ratio) to more than 0.4, splinter hemorrhages near the optic disc margin, and atrophy of the retinal nerve fiber layer.

Advanced glaucomatous changes of the optic disc include a marked increase in C/D ratio (0.7 or more), thinning of the neuroretinal rim, nasal shifting of the retinal vessels or bayonetting, and pulsations of retinal arterioles at the disc margin.

If the damage progresses, all neural tissue is destroyed and the optic nerve appears white and deeply excavated.
questions.learning: Roenne's nasal step Roenne's nasal step is not a feature of the optic disc in glaucoma. Roenne's nasal step is a visual field defect.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: When a family member volunteers to donate blood for a patient injured in a road traffic accident, which of the following tests is not routinely required before proceeding with the blood transfusion?
questions.explanation: To ensure the safety of the blood supply, all donated blood must undergo rigorous mandatory screening for major transfusion-transmitted infections. Standard screening protocols include testing for Hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) (Option B), Hepatitis C virus (HCV) antibodies (Option C), and HIV types 1 and 2 antibodies or p24 antigen (Option D). Additionally, screening for syphilis and malaria is typically required. Hepatitis A (Option A) is NOT typically tested in routine pre-transfusion protocols. The Hepatitis A virus is primarily transmitted through the fecal-oral route, has a very short-lived viremic phase, and does not cause a chronic carrier state. Because the risk of transmission through blood products is negligible compared to the chronic, blood-borne nature of HBV, HCV, and HIV, it is not a part of mandatory blood safety testing. Thus, Hepatitis A is the correct "except" choice for routine donor screening

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: What is the usual method of collecting a sample of urine to detect UTI?
questions.explanation: In toilet-trained individuals, the "clean-catch" midstream urine sample is the preferred method for detecting a Urinary Tract Infection (UTI). This technique minimizes contamination from skin flora and urethral commensals. The patient is instructed to clean the area and discard the initial portion of the stream before collecting the sample. Early morning samples (Option A) are used to screen for proteinuria but are not specific for UTI. Suprapubic aspiration or catheterization (Option C) is the gold standard for accuracy but is invasive and usually reserved for infants or patients unable to provide a voided sample. Starting stream collection (Option D) is avoided because the first voided portion typically contains the highest concentration of contaminating urethral bacteria. Thus, midstream catch offers the best balance of diagnostic accuracy and ease of use
questions.learning: In toilet-trained individuals, the "clean-catch" midstream urine sample is the preferred method for detecting a Urinary Tract Infection (UTI). This technique minimizes contamination from skin flora and urethral commensals.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: What is the best imaging study for diagnosis of cerebral infarct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Diffusion weighted MRI

Diffusion-weighted MRI is the most sensitive investigation for diagnosis of cerebral ischemia.  It is particularly useful for identifying acute ischemic changes in the brain due to its ability to detect diffusion restriction of water molecules in the brain tissue.

Diffusion restriction: hyperintense on DWI and hypointense on ADC.

●       Diffusion restriction is seen with:

1.     Acute stroke

2.     Hypercellular tumors

3.     Abscess

4.     Epidermoid cyst

5.     Keratin-Craniopharyngioma/ Cholesteatoma

Other Options:

Option A: FLAIR MRI: Fluid-Attenuated Inversion Recovery (FLAIR) MRI is useful for identifying older infarcts and chronic changes but is less sensitive in the acute phase of a stroke.

Option B: Non-contrast CT: While commonly used for initial assessment due to its availability and speed, it is less sensitive in the early stages of a stroke, often not showing changes until several hours post-onset.

Option D: СECT (Contrast-Enhanced CT): Typically used to assess for complications or other causes of symptoms but not as sensitive as DWI for early detection of cerebral infarcts.

Educational Objective

Diffusion-weighted MRI is the optimal choice for early detection of cerebral infarcts, making it an indispensable tool in acute stroke management. Its ability to show diffusion restriction provides critical information that can influence therapeutic decisions.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Dense irregular collagen is found in:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Dermis

Dense irregular collagen is found in dermis.

Irregular connective tissue is of three types: Loose, dense and adipose. Dense connective tissue is located in regions which are under consistent mechanical stress and where protection is required for the ensheathed organs. The abundant collagen fibres in the dermis run in a haphazard manner. This protects the skin.

It is usually present in :

• Reticular layer of the dermis
• Superficial connective tissue sheaths of the muscle and nerves
• Adventitia of large vessels
• Capsules of various organs and glands (e.g, testis, sclera, periosteum, perichondrium)

On the other hand, dense regular collagen fibres are found in tendons.
questions.learning: Dermis Dense irregular collagen is found in dermis. Irregular connective tissue is of three types: Loose, dense and adipose.

questions.text: A 32-year-old man is diagnosed with sputum-positive pulmonary tuberculosis at a district hospital. As part of the public health response, his household members and close workplace contacts are identified and screened for tuberculosis. Asymptomatic contacts are followed up and offered appropriate preventive therapy. This activity is best described as:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Secondary prevention

The described activity includes:

• Identification and screening of contacts of a sputum-positive TB case
• Early detection of disease among contacts
• Follow-up of asymptomatic contacts with preventive therapy (e.g., TPT)

These actions are aimed at early diagnosis and prompt intervention, which defines secondary prevention.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: What is the name of the technical platform developed under India’s National Tele Mental Health Programme (NTMHP) for delivering mental health care through a multi-tiered system using telephone services, digital platforms, and online portals?
questions.explanation: Tele-MANAS, which stands for Mental Health Assistance and Networking Across States, is the dedicated technical platform launched by the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare under the National Tele Mental Health Programme. It aims to provide accessible, high-quality, and free mental health services across India through a 24/7 toll-free helpline and digital portals. The system operates on a multi-tiered structure, with Tier 1 providing immediate crisis counseling via trained professionals and Tier 2 offering advanced care at district levels. NIKSHAY (Option A) is the national surveillance and management platform for tuberculosis. Quinidine (Option C) is a medication used for malaria and arrhythmias, entirely unrelated to digital health platforms . e-Sanjeevani (Option D) is a general national telemedicine portal for online OPD consultations but is not specifically the platform developed for the NTMHP. Thus, Tele-MANAS is the correct answer. Would you like me to extract the next set of questions (Q.16-Q.30)?
