questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 35 year old farmer presents with a painless swelling of the foot that has developed gradually over several months. On examination there are multiple discharging sinuses with black granules seen in the discharge. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Madurella mycetomatis

Madurella mycetomatis Causes eumycetoma (fungal mycetoma)

→ Presents with classic triad:

• Painless subcutaneous swelling
• Multiple discharging sinuses
• Black granules in discharge

Common in farmers due to traumatic implantation (thorn/splinter injury)

Granule color differentiation (high-yield):

• Black granules → Madurella mycetomatis (fungal mycetoma)
• White/yellow granules → Actinomyces, Nocardia (actinomycetoma)

Why not others:

• Actinomyces israelii → sulfur granules (yellow), not black
• Chromoblastomycosis → verrucous lesions, not sinus + granules
• Staphylococcus aureus → acute painful abscess, no granules

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Relative bradycardia occurs in:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. All of the above

In the given options typhoid, Q fever, and leptospirosis are infectious causes of relative bradycardia.

Relative bradycardia, also known as Faget's sign, is observed when patients exhibit a lower heart rate than anticipated in relation to an increase in body temperature. Body temperature is commonly regarded as a factor that independently influences heart rate. It is estimated that for each 1°C (1.8°F) rise in temperature, the heart rate typically increases by approximately 15-20 beats per minute.

While this pulse-temperature dissociation is not highly sensitive or specific for establishing a diagnosis, it can still prove beneficial in resource-limited settings due to its easy accessibility and simplicity.

Infectious causes of relative bradycardia include:

• Salmonella typhi
• Francisella tularensis
• Coxiella burnetii (Q fever)
• Leptospira interrogans
• Legionella pneumophila
• Rickettsia spp.
• Orientia tsutsugamushi (scrub typhus)
• Corynebacterium diphtheriae
• Plasmodium spp. (malaria)

Noninfectious causes include:

• Drug fever
• Beta-blocker use
• Central nervous system lesions
• Malignant lymphoma
• Factitious fever

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A patient with asthma on inhaled corticosteroids and LABA continues to have exacerbations. FEV1 is normal, and there is no improvement with salbutamol challenge. The symptoms worsen seasonally. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step? LABA – Long-Acting Beta Agonist LAMA – Long-Acting Muscarinic Antagonist
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Add Omalizumab

The given clinical vignette points towards a probable diagnosis of allergic asthma, which is treated with omalizumab.

FEV1 is normal, which indicates that the obstructive lung disease (asthma) has not worsened. As the symptoms worsen seasonally, this strongly suggests allergic asthma.

Omalizumab is a recombinant humanised monoclonal antibody against IgE. It is used in severe allergic asthma (IgE-mediated) and is effective in treating chronic urticaria. When applied subcutaneously, it neutralises circulating free IgE without triggering the activation of mast cells and other inflammatory cells. When exposed to an antigen, the mast cell surface receptors (Fcε R1) release a limited amount of IgE, resulting in bronchoconstriction.

Pearl PF1790: Monoclonal antibodies nomenclature

Murine - 0% human: “omab” (Tositumomab)

Chimeric - 65% human: “ximab” (Rituximab)

Humanized - 95% human: “zumab” (Trastuzumab)

Fully human - 100% human: “umab” (Adalimumab)

Pearl PF2058: Treatment of Asthma based on severity of symptoms (GINA-2022)

Asthma management - GINA 2022
questions.learning: Add Omalizumab — The given clinical vignette points towards a probable diagnosis of allergic asthma, which is treated with omalizumab. FEV1 is normal, which indicates that the obstructive lung disease (asthma) has not worsened.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following statements about polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS) is not true? (NEET PG 2015)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Follicle-Stimulating Hormone (FSH) levels are reduced.

Polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS) is characterized by hyperandrogenism, chronic anovulation, and polycystic ovaries. Typical hormonal findings in PCOS:

• Increased LH levels
• Normal or mildly decreased FSH levels
• Increased androgen levels
• Increased estrogen (especially estrone) due to peripheral conversion of androgens

The LH:FSH ratio is often elevated because LH secretion increases disproportionately.

Why option B is NOT true: FSH levels are usually normal or only mildly low, not markedly reduced

Pathophysiology:

• Increased LH stimulates theca cells → excess androgen production
• Hyperinsulinemia further increases androgen synthesis

Failure of normal follicular maturation leads to anovulation
questions.learning: Follicle-Stimulating Hormone (FSH) levels are reduced. Polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS) is characterized by hyperandrogenism, chronic anovulation, and polycystic ovaries.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient was asked to copy the face of a clock and his drawing is shown below. What is the correct term to be used here?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hemispatial neglect

Hemispatial neglect is the inability to report, respond, or orient to stimuli in one-half of the space despite having no motor or sensory deficits.

A patient with neglect is asked to draw a clock, their drawing might show only the numbers 12 to 6, or all 12 numbers might be on one half of the clock face with the other half distorted or blank, like the image shown in the image below.

Neglect patients may also ignore the contralesional side of their body; for instance, they might only shave, or apply makeup to, the non-neglected side. These patients may frequently collide with objects or structures such as door frames on the side being neglected.

Other options:

Option A: Confabulation is a phenomenon in which the patient fills in memory gaps with inaccurate information. Further investigating the statement made by the patients may reflect past experiences or bizarre, fantastic stories.  This fabrication of false information is not done on purpose.

Option C: Apraxia: Inability to perform a movement or task when asked despite having the desire and physical capability to carry it out.

Types of apraxia:

* Kinetic: Inability to execute the fine acquired motor movement, the lesion is in the precentral cortex.

* Ideomotor: Fails to perform on command. The lesion is in the parietal lobe.

* Constructional: liability to reproduce simple geometric figures by drawing. The lesion is in the pathway between the occipital or parietal area.

* Ideational: Loss of ability to formulate an ideational plan for the execution of the complex act. The lesion is in the dominant parietal lobe.

Option D: Astrexis/Flapping tremor is a type of negative myoclonus characterized by irregular lapses of the posture of various body parts. Mostly associated with hepatic encephalopathy.
questions.learning: Hemispatial neglect Hemispatial neglect is the inability to report, respond, or orient to stimuli in one-half of the space despite having no motor or sensory deficits.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is the true statement regarding measures to prevent typhoid transmission in the community?
options: Typhoid vaccine administration is the best method of preventing transmission
Hygiene practices and clean sanitation control is more important than typhoid vaccine
In 10% cases, person to person transmission occurs
Drug resistance in typhoid is not as big a problem as in TB
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hygiene practices and clean sanitation control is more important than typhoid vaccine

The true statement regarding typhoid transmission preventive measures is that hygiene practices and clean sanitation control are more important than the typhoid vaccine. It helps in breaking the chain of transmission.

Typhoid fever is caused by Salmonella typhi and is mainly transmitted to humans by the fecal-oral route.

Clinical features include high fever with chills associated with headache, malaise, cough, sore throat, abdominal pain, and constipation or diarrhea are seen in the early phase. The fever occurs in a step-ladder fashion reaching a plateau in 7-10 days. A maculopapular rash may be seen on the trunk and chest known as rose spots. In the late stages, hepatosplenomegaly, abdominal distension, relative bradycardia, and a dicrotic pulse can occur.

Diagnosis is by isolation of the organism from blood, bone marrow, and stools. Blood culture is mainly used for the diagnosis. Other tests such as the Widal tests are useful.

Management is mainly by sanitation. It is the ultimate method to control typhoid. It breaks the transmission of the disease. It is combined with proper health education.

Antibiotic therapy is started early and the choice of antibiotics depends on the susceptibility of the organism to the drug. In the case of drug-susceptible typhoid, ciprofloxacin is useful.

Drug resistance to typhoid has been emerging. Similar to drug resistance in TB, there are multidrug-resistant (MDR) and extensively drug-resistant (XDR) S. Typhi strains. MDR strains are resistant against at least 1 out of 3 or >3 categorically differentiated antimicrobials, such as ampicillin, cotrimoxazole, and chloramphenicol. XDR are those which are resistant to all except 1-2 antimicrobials.

Ceftriaxone, cefotaxime, and (oral) cefixime are effective for the treatment of MDR enteric fever.

Immunization is a complementary approach in management since the protective efficacy can be overcome by a high inoculum in the case of food-borne diseases.

The typhoid vaccines available are the Vi polysaccharide vaccine and the Ty21a vaccine. Ty21a is a live attenuated vaccine recommended after 6 years and is given orally on days 1,3,5 and 7. Vi polysaccharide vaccine can be given after 2 years as a single dose with a booster dose for every 2 years.
questions.learning: Hygiene practices and clean sanitation control is more important than typhoid vaccine The true statement regarding typhoid transmission preventive measures is that hygiene practices and clean sanitation control are more important than the typhoid vaccine.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following bands will increase in serum electrophoresis in Nephrotic syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Alpha 2 globulin

• Massive proteinuria (>3.5 g/day)
• Preferential loss of small proteins:

• Albumin
• Some immunoglobulins

Liver response:

• Compensatory ↑ synthesis of larger proteins:

• α₂-macroglobulin (very large → not filtered)
• Lipoproteins

Result: α₂ band increases

In nephrotic syndrome, there is urinary loss of low–molecular weight proteins like albumin and gamma globulins.

The liver compensatorily increases synthesis of α₂-macroglobulin, a large protein that is not lost in urine.

Hence, α₂-globulin band is increased on serum protein electrophoresis.

| Fraction | Change | Reason

| -------- | ------ | ------

| Albumin | ↓↓↓ | Urinary loss

| Alpha-1 | ↓ / normal | Mild loss

| Alpha-2 | ↑↑↑ | Large proteins retained + ↑ synthesis

| Beta | ↑ (mild) | Lipoproteins

| Gamma | ↓ | Ig loss

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 24-year-old woman who is being treated for infertility with human menopausal gonadotropin came with complaints of sudden abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and breathlessness. The finding of the ultrasound is shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome

The above clinical scenario and the sonogram showing enlarged ovaries having large cysts are suggestive of ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome.

Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS) is characterized by multiple ovarian follicular cysts accompanied by increased capillary permeability. It happens most often as a complication of ovulation induction therapy for infertility. It occurs due to the stimulation of vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) expression in granulosa-lutein cells by hCG.

They often present with shortness of breath, abdominal pain, and gastrointestinal disturbances like nausea, vomiting, and oliguria.

Abdominal pain occurs due to ovarian enlargement and accumulation of peritoneal fluid. Increased vascular permeability and loss of fluid, protein, and electrolytes into the peritoneal cavity cause ascites and result in hemoconcentration. Hemoconcentration causes hyperviscosity and leads to hypercoagulability.

Hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, leukocytosis, pleural effusion, and pericardial effusion can be associated with OHSS.

Some of the risk factors for OHSS:

• Polycystic ovarian syndrome
• Young age
• High estradiol during ovulation induction
• Pregnancy

This condition can be prevented by

• Using lowered FSH dose to decrease follicular stimulation
• Coasting- withholding FSH administration for 1 or more days prior to the hCG trigger injection,
• Prophylactic treatment with volume expanders,
• Substitution of hCG for FSH during the final days of ovarian stimulation.

OHSS is primarily managed with general supportive care. Paracentesis is performed to ameliorate abdominal discomfort and relieve respiratory discomfort.

Other options:

Option B- Polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS) is the most common endocrine disorder of the reproductive age group. Patients with PCOS present with menstrual irregularities, hirsutism, acne, infertility, sleep apnea, and depression/anxiety. These are all short-term consequences of PCOS. The long-term consequences of PCOS include diabetes mellitus, endometrial cancer, and cardiovascular disease.

According to the American Society of Reproductive Medicine (ASRM) and the European Society of Human Reproduction and Embryology (ESHRE), sonographic criteria for PCOS include

• >20 follicles and/or
• Increased ovarian volume (>10 mL), or both

The ultrasound examination image shown below is of PCOS showing enlarged ovaries with multiple cysts.

Option C - Theca lutein cysts are a type of follicular cysts. Hyperreactio luteinalis is a condition in which one or both ovaries develop multiple large theca lutein cysts. They typically occur after the first trimester due to luteinization and hypertrophy of theca interna layer in response to exceptionally high hCG or luteinizing hormone.

They are commonly seen in

• Gestational trophoblastic disease
• Multiple gestational pregnancy
• Fetal hydrops
• Placentaomegaly

Most patients are asymptomatic and the above symptoms are not seen in this condition. Surgical management is only required if it is complicated by torsion or hemorrhage.

The below image shows bilaterally enlarged ovaries with multiple theca luteal cysts as in hyperreactio luteinalis.

Option D - Most women are diagnosed with adult granulosa cell tumors after the age of 30 years, and the average age is roughly 55 years. Heavy, irregular menstrual bleeding and postmenopausal bleeding are frequent and are caused by the endometrium's extended exposure to estrogen. Breast soreness and enlargement are also seen in this condition. Instead of hormones, the mass of the ovary may be the cause of the symptoms. Abdominal pain and distension that is brought on by an expanding tumor that could potentially be hemorrhagic.
questions.learning: Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome — The above clinical scenario and the sonogram showing enlarged ovaries having large cysts are suggestive of ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 10 year old boy with fever, weight loss came to the hospital. On examination he was pale and had significant lymphadenopathy. Bone marrow histology of the person is as given below. Your diagnosis is?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. ALL

The above image shows lymphoblasts with condensed nuclear chromatin, small nucleoli, scanty agranular cytoplasm, which are characteristics of ALL.

ALL is more common in childhood. The child had symptoms related to depression of marrow function including pallor, weight loss due to anaemia and fever secondary to infections. These infections are due to neutropenia and generalised lymphadenopathy, indicating the effect of neoplastic infiltration.

ALL:

* Usually seen in adolescent boys with thymic involvement

* Mediastinal thymic masses occur in 50% to 70% of T-ALLs, which are also more likely to be associated with lymphadenopathy and splenomegaly.

* C/F:

* Abrupt stormy onset within days to a few weeks of the first symptoms

* Symptoms related to depression of marrow function including anemia, fever, infections, bleeding

* Mass effects caused by neoplastic infiltration

* Bone pain resulting from marrow expansion and infiltration of the subperiosteum

* Generalized lymphadenopathy Splenomegaly, and hepatomegaly

* Testicular enlargement

* Central nervous system manifestations such as headache, vomiting, and nerve palsies

* B cell ALL: Pancytopenia due to marrow involvement

* T-ALL: Mediastinal mass, lymphadenopathy, compression of large vessels and airways in the mediastinum

* Ataxia telangiectasia predisposes to ALL

* T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma (T-ALL) is characterized by aberrant activation of NOTCH1 in over 60% of T-ALL cases

Other options:

Option A: AML - Although the presenting symptoms are similar to ALL, bone marrow histology shows the presence of 20% myeloid blasts, delicate nuclear chromatin, 2-4 nucleoli, more voluminous cytoplasm with fine azurophilic granules. Though AML occurs at all ages, it is predominantly seen after 60 years of age.
Option B: Aplastic Anemia - It has a characteristic dry tap on marrow aspiration, bone marrow is markedly hypocellular. It can occur at any age and sex.
Option D: Juvenile myelomonocytic leukaemia - It has characteristics of leukocytosis, monocytosis, hepatosplenomegaly, thrombocytopenia, elevated fetal haemoglobin. It is primarily a disease of early childhood.

Pearl PF1568: Prognostic Factors in Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia (ALL)

Good prognostic markers
Bad prognostic markers

Age between 2 and 10 years

Age younger than 2 years

Presentation in adolescence or adulthood

Low white cell count
Peripheral blood blast counts greater than 100,000,

Female
Male

Hyperdiploidy

Trisomy of chromosomes 4, 7, 10 & 17
Pseudodiploidy or t (9;22)  or t (8;14) or t (4;11)

t (12;21)
MLL gene rearrangements

Early precursor B cell phenotype
T cell phenotype

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: What is the probable diagnosis based on the finding given in the CT image?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Pneumatised superior turbinate

The given CT image reveals a pneumatised superior turbinate.

The superior turbinate, located posteriorly and superiorly to the middle turbinate can become pneumatized. It forms an important landmark to identify the ostium of the sphenoid sinus which lies medial to it. This pneumatization is common in the lateral nasal wall, although it is less frequently seen in the superior turbinate compared to the middle turbinate.

In most cases, pneumatized superior turbinate is an incidental finding during radiological examinations. It can lead to nasal obstruction, headache, epistaxis, anosmia, and postnasal drainage.

Asymptomatic cases of superior turbinate pneumatization generally do not require treatment. However, when symptoms are present, various surgical techniques can be considered, including outfracture, crushing, radio-frequency ablation, turbinoplasty, and microdebrider surgery.

Turbinoplasty is contraindicated if inferior turbinate pneumatization is associated with the maxillary sinus because it may result in the formation of a second ostium. In addition, total turbinectomy is not performed because it may cause atrophic rhinitis.

Other options:

Option A: Pneumatization of the middle turbinate leads to an enlarged middle turbinate that is ballooned out, this is called concha bullosa. The CT image shown below depicts concha bullosa.

Option C: Onodi cell is a posterior ethmoidal cell that may grow posteriorly, either by the side of the sphenoid sinus or superior to it. Onodi cell is surgically important as the optic nerve may be related to its lateral wall.  A CT image of an onodi cell is shown below.

Option D: Haller cells are air cells situated in the roof of the maxillary sinus. They are pneumatized from anterior or posterior ethmoid cells. Enlargement of Haller cells may lead to maxillary sinusitis as it may encroach the ethmoid infundibulum, impeding draining of the maxillary sinus. A CT image of Haller cell is shown below.
questions.learning: Pneumatised superior turbinate — The given CT image reveals a pneumatised superior turbinate. The superior turbinate, located posteriorly and superiorly to the middle turbinate can become pneumatized.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: In cancer treatment, a radiation regimen delivers 1.8–2 Gy per fraction, once daily, five days a week, for 6–8 weeks. What is this radiotherapy technique called?
questions.explanation: Radiation therapy is typically delivered in small, daily portions called "fractions" to allow normal cells to repair while tumor cells succumb to accumulated damage. The protocol described—1.8 to 2.0 Gy per day, given once daily, five days a week (Monday to Friday), over a period of 6 to 8 weeks—is the definition of Standard (Regular) Fractionated Radiotherapy. Hyper-fractionation (Option B) involves giving smaller individual doses (e.g., 1.2 Gy) more than once a day (e.g., twice daily) to reach a higher total dose. Accelerated fractionation (Option C) involves reducing the overall treatment time by giving more frequent fractions without significantly changing the individual dose size. Brachytherapy (Option D) refers to placing radioactive sources directly into or near the tumor, rather than delivering external beams. Therefore, the conventional schedule described in the question is the benchmark "regular" fractionation protocol used in most clinical oncology settings
questions.learning: Radiation therapy is typically delivered in small, daily portions called "fractions" to allow normal cells to repair while tumor cells succumb to accumulated damage.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presents with a pansystolic murmur and features of carditis. Echocardiography showed mitral regurgitation.Which of the following is the most common manifestation of this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Arthritis

The clinical vignette of mitral regurgitation is most commonly seen in rheumatic heart disease. The most common manifestation of this disease is arthritis

Major manifestations of rheumatic fever are:

* Migratory polyarthritis of the large joints

* Pancarditis (myocarditis, pericarditis, or endocarditis)

* Subcutaneous nodules (typically on extensor surfaces of extremities)

* Erythema marginatum, an irregular circinate skin rash

* Sydenham chorea, a neurologic disorder with involuntary rapid movements

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: In a family with three siblings, the eldest child leaves the household and a new third child is born. What is this type of change in family structure called?
questions.explanation: The family life cycle describes the sequence of changes a family undergoes over time. In this scenario, the family is growing with the birth of a new member while simultaneously having children in different developmental stages (one moving out, others at home), which is defined as complete extension. This stage features an overlap of multiple generations or stages within the family unit. Formation (Option A) refers to the initial creation of a family unit through marriage or cohabitation. Extension (Option D) refers to the birth of a first child without the loss of existing household members. Contraction (Option B) is the stage where members leave the home (e.g., children moving out or deaths) without being replaced by new births, which is the opposite of the scenario described. Thus, complete extension is the correct term

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 22 year old came with thigh pain. X ray was done as shown below. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Chronic osteomyelitis

The given clinical scenario of a patient with thigh pain and an X-ray of the lower limb revealing involucrum and cloaca in the femur, strongly suggests a diagnosis of chronic osteomyelitis.

Chronic osteomyelitis may occur by direct inoculation of the infective organism during trauma (like road traffic accidents). The infection continues to thrive within the bone leading to alternating quiescent and flare-up stages of chronic osteomyelitis.

Sequestrum is a piece of dead bone. It is formed when a fragment of bone gets separated from the healthy bone due to necrosis. It varies in size from a spicule to a large fragment and acts as a nidus for infection. It leads to abscess and persistent pus discharge in the bone. Sinus tracts are formed when the abscess from the infected bone drains out through the skin.

The involucrum is the dense new sclerotic bone surrounding the sequestrum. It is formed from deep layers of stripped periosteum. Cloacae are the perforations in the involucrum. Pus and tiny spicules of bone may be discharged through them.

questions.learning: Chronic osteomyelitis — The given clinical scenario of a patient with thigh pain and an X-ray of the lower limb revealing involucrum and cloaca in the femur, strongly suggests a diagnosis of chronic osteomyelitis.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: What is a patient's urine analysis most likely to show if they have hematuria and hypercalciuria?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Isomorphic RBCs

Hematuria with hypercalciuria typically suggests a non-glomerular (urologic) source, such as nephrolithiasis or tubular irritation from calcium crystals. In non-glomerular hematuria, urine microscopy shows isomorphic (normal-shaped) RBCs because the bleeding occurs distal to the glomerulus, so RBCs are not distorted during passage.

In contrast:

• RBC casts indicate glomerular bleeding
• Nephrotic-range proteinuria suggests nephrotic syndrome
• Eosinophiluria suggests acute interstitial nephritis

Thus, hypercalciuria-associated hematuria shows isomorphic RBCs.
questions.learning: Isomorphic RBCs Hematuria with hypercalciuria typically suggests a non-glomerular (urologic) source, such as nephrolithiasis or tubular irritation from calcium crystals.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: What are the reasons for choosing coliform organisms as indicators of faecal pollution of water rather than the waterborne pathogens directly? I. They are present in great abundance in the human intestine and excreted in great numbers in faeces. II. They have lower resistance to forces of natural purification. III. They survive less than the pathogens. IV. They are easily detected by culture methods. Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. I and IV

The following statements are correct:

• I. They are present in great abundance in the human intestine and excreted in great numbers in feces: Coliforms, especially E. coli, are normal intestinal flora and are shed in large numbers, making them reliable indicators of fecal pollution.
• IV. They are easily detected by culture methods: Coliforms can be identified rapidly using simple and inexpensive methods such as the Most Probable Number (MPN) test and membrane filtration.

Why are II and III incorrect?

• II. They have lower resistance to forces of natural purification: An ideal indicator organism should have resistance similar to or greater than many pathogens, so that its absence suggests water safety.
• III. They survive less than the pathogens: Indicator organisms should survive at least as long as enteric pathogens, making this statement incorrect.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 25-year-old male patient presented with a penetrating injury to his left eye for which he was treated with corneoscleral suturing and discharged a week later. He returns 2 months later complaining of diminished vision, associated with redness, pain, and photophobia in the right eye. Direct ophthalmoscopy revealed discrete yellow-white nodules in the fundus. What part of the eye is most commonly affected?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Uvea

The clinical case is suggestive of sympathetic ophthalmitis, which is a bilateral granulomatous panuveitis and hence the affected part is the uvea.

Dalen–Fuchs nodules are seen below the retinal pigment epithelium on ophtalmoscopy.

Sympathetic Ophthalmitis (SO) is a bilateral granulomatous panuveitis occurring after penetrating trauma which usually begins 4–8 weeks after the injury to the eye (the exciting eye). It can also develop after surgeries, proton beam irradiation, Nd: YAG photocoagulation, and cryotherapy. It is an delayed hypersensitivity reaction mediated by T cells.

The exciting eye is often red and irritable, and the sympathizing eye may develop irritation, blurred vision, photophobia, and loss of accommodation.

Fundoscopy:

* Multifocal choroidal infiltrates

* Infiltrates corresponding to Dalen–Fuchs nodules are seen below the retinal pigment epithelium

* Exudative retinal detachment, vasculitis, and optic disc swelling

* Residual chorioretinal scarring gives a sunset glow appearance when the inflammation settles

Treatment :

* Steroids are the basis of treatment.

* High-dose oral prednisolone is given for several months.

* Supplementary topical steroids and cycloplegics for anterior uveitis

* Periocular and intraocular steroids, slow-release intravitreal implants may also be used

* Immunosuppressives such as azathioprine, ciclosporin, and methotrexate are used in resistant cases or as steroid-sparing agents.

* Enucleation of an eye with no visual potential within 2 weeks of injury prevents the occurrence of sympathetic ophthalmitis.

questions.learning: Uvea — The clinical case is suggestive of sympathetic ophthalmitis, which is a bilateral granulomatous panuveitis and hence the affected part is the uvea.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: Which of the following is not a feature of melancholia?
options: Profound feelings of guilt over trivial events
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Sleep-onset insomnia

Sleep-onset insomnia is a characteristic feature of anxiety disorder, not melancholia.

Melancholia is one of the oldest terms used in psychiatry, to describe the dark mood of depression. It is still used to refer to a state of depression characterized by:

• Severe anhedonia
• Early morning awakening (terminal insomnia)
• Weight loss
• Profound feelings of guilt (often over trivial events)

Melancholia is sometimes referred to as "endogenous depression" or depression that arises in the absence of external life stressors or precipitants.
questions.learning: Sleep-onset insomnia Sleep-onset insomnia is a characteristic feature of anxiety disorder, not melancholia. Melancholia is one of the oldest terms used in psychiatry, to describe the dark mood of depression.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A young primigravida at 32 weeks of gestation was admitted since her BP was 150/90 mmHg and urine dipstick was 2+ on antenatal checkup. On examination, she has pedal edema. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Preeclampsia

The given case scenario suggests a likely diagnosis of pre-eclampsia.

Pre-eclampsia occurs due to the failure of the invasion of extravillous trophoblasts into the spiral artery. It is characterized by blood pressure of >140/90 mmHg on two occasions 4 hours apart with proteinuria or signs of end-organ damage.

Criteria to diagnose pre-eclampsia:

* Proteinuria of ≥ 300 mg (0.3 g) in 24 hours or urine protein:creatinine ratio of ≥0.3

* Platelet count of <1 lakh/cu.mm

* Serum creatinine level of >1.1 mg/dL

* Serum transaminase levels twice the normal concentration

* Headache, visual disturbances, or epigastric pain

* Pulmonary edema

Clinical types of pre-eclampsia:

* Nonsevere pre-eclampsia: Blood pressure >140/90 mmHg but <160/110 mmHg without significant proteinuria

* Severe pre-eclampsia: Persistent increase of systolic blood pressure above 160 mmHg or diastolic above 110 mmHg with any of the following, proteinuria, oliguria (<400 mL in 24 hours), platelet count <1 lakh/cu.mm, serum creatinine level of >1.1 mg/dL, persistent severe epigastric pain, marked elevation of liver enzyme levels, cerebral (convulsions) or visual disturbances, intrauterine growth restriction of the fetus, and pulmonary edema.

Complications of pre-eclampsia:

* Eclampsia

* HELLP syndrome

* Acute respiratory distress syndrome

* Cerebral hemorrhage

* Preterm labor

* Postpartum hemorrhage

* Shock

* Sepsis
questions.learning: Preeclampsia — The given case scenario suggests a likely diagnosis of pre-eclampsia. Pre-eclampsia occurs due to the failure of the invasion of extravillous trophoblasts into the spiral artery.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: What is the probable cause of monocular diplopia in a young boy who has experienced trauma to his right eye?
questions.explanation: The provided image displays a classic iridodialysis, which is a separation of the iris root from its attachment to the ciliary body, usually resulting from blunt trauma. This separation creates a "second opening" or peripheral gap that allows light to enter the eye through a route other than the natural pupil. This results in monocular diplopia (double vision in one eye) as two images are formed on the retina. A festooned pupil (Option A) is irregularly shaped due to old inflammatory adhesions (synechiae). Iris bombe (Option B) is the forward bulging of the iris due to fluid trapped behind it, often seen in glaucoma. Iridodonesis (Option C) refers to a "tremulous iris" caused by a subluxated or absent lens. None of those options classically cause monocular diplopia as directly as the traumatic gap shown. Therefore, Iridodialysis is the definitive cause of the symptom and the diagnosis
questions.learning: The provided image displays a classic iridodialysis, which is a separation of the iris root from its attachment to the ciliary body, usually resulting from blunt trauma.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Which of the following are components of kangaroo mother care?
options: Early discharge, skin to skin contact, prevent infection
Early discharge, skin to skin contact, exclusive breastfeeding
Skin to skin contact, exclusive breastfeeding, prevent infection
Early discharge, exclusive breastfeeding and prevent infection
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Early discharge, skin to skin contact, exclusive breastfeeding

The four components of kangaroo mother care (KMC) are skin-to-skin positioning of the baby on the mother's (or caretaker’s) chest, exclusive breastfeeding, early discharge and ambulatory care, and support for the mother and her family for taking care of the baby.

Eligibility criteria for KMC include all hemodynamically stable low birthweight (LBW) babies. All mothers without any serious illness can provide KMC. Short sessions of KMC can be initiated in babies on medical treatment like IV fluids or oxygen therapy.

The initiation of KMC can differ depending on the weight of the newborn. Babies weighing less than 1200 g at birth may require several days to weeks before KMC can begin. For babies weighing between 1200 g and 1800 g, the initiation of KMC may only take a few days. KMC can be started immediately after birth for babies weighing over 1800 g.

The baby should be placed between the mother's breasts in an upright position, with the face turned to one side, The hips are abducted and flexed in a 'frog position' and the arms are also flexed. The abdomen of the baby should be at the level of the mother's epigastrium. In this position, the mother's breathing would stimulate the baby and prevent the development of apnea.

KMC is not necessary once the baby attains 2500 g of weight or 37 weeks of gestation.

The duration of KMC should be gradually increased from short sessions of more than one hour to 24 hours a day.

KMC is comparable to incubators in terms of safety and thermal protection as evidenced by mortality rates. Additionally, it has been shown to reduce severe morbidity by facilitating breastfeeding.

KMC promotes the bonding between mother and child, fostering a strong emotional connection during the early stages of life.

Note: Incubatory care, feeding via nasal catheter, and prevention of infection are part of intensive care for low birthweight babies.
